Economics, not climate summits, will dictate the net-zero transition

New Scientist November 12, 2026

The stench of hypocrisy is in the air at the COP31 summit in Turkey. UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he wanted to show British leadership on climate action. Meanwhile, his government just green-lit the Jackdaw gas field in the North Sea, which will emit up to 36 million tonnes of carbon dioxide without noticeably reducing energy prices, and it is considering approving the Rosebank oilfield and weakening its electric vehicle mandate.

The summit’s joint hosts, Turkey and Australia, are pushing for a clean energy revolution, but this week Turkey announced two new oilfields that would help boost production 30 per cent, while promising to double natural gas production. Australia has recently approved fossil fuel projects including a “climate bomb” coal mine extension that will emit enough carbon to kill an additional 15 million Great Barrier Reef coral colonies during every bleaching event. Meanwhile, the second biggest emitter, the US, is again boycotting the annual climate summit.

How incredibly simple tech can supercharge the race to net zero

While the world shaved more than 1°C off the warming trajectory after the 2015 Paris Agreement, “collective climate action has effectively stalled”, and current policies put the world on track for a catastrophic 2.7°C rise by 2100, according to Climate Action Tracker.

Advertisement

But there is one piece of good news. The Global Carbon Budget also just announced that fossil fuel emissions are expected to slightly decrease in 2026 – something that has only previously happened during the covid-19 pandemic, the 2008 financial crisis and the break-up of the Soviet Union. Granted, the 0.4 per cent decline wouldn’t have happened without the Iran war oil crisis. But the growth in cheap solar, wind and electric vehicles has offset more emissions than the spike in oil prices.

If clean tech can keep accelerating, “a sustained peak and decline in global CO2 emissions could be a few years away”, the Global Carbon Budget report said. This means that economics, not politics, is pushing the clean energy transition forward, despite the failed leadership on display at COP31.

Free newsletter

“Policy was never the main driver,” says Auke Hoekstra at the Eindhoven University of Technology in the Netherlands. “These technologies are simply superior.”

Hoekstra is known for his graphs showing how solar panel production has repeatedly outperformed International Energy Agency expectations. Solar is now providing 10 times more energy than when the Paris Agreement was signed in 2015, making it the fastest-growing electricity source ever, followed closely by wind.

Money talks, and electricity from solar and wind costs less on average than from natural gas or coal. In the US, the top oil-producing state, Texas, where climate denier Donald Trump won a landslide, has also become the top producer of both solar and wind power. In low-income countries like Nigeria and Pakistan, rather than waiting for governments to update expensive and unreliable fossil fuel-based power grids, people are simply installing cheap Chinese solar panels on their roofs, “leapfrogging” hydrocarbon-fuelled development altogether.

The one drawback had been that solar and wind don’t generate much energy in the evening during peak demand. But cheap batteries are quickly solving that problem. Utility and home battery storage is now growing even faster than renewable power generation.

An ambitious form of climate modelling aims to pin the blame for disasters – from floods to heatwaves – on specific companies. Is this the tool we need to effectively prosecute the world’s biggest carbon emitters?

Of course, early subsidies and regulations by governments like China and Germany created the market conditions for renewables to start coming down the cost curve. While economics is driving the energy transition, policy can speed it up or, as in the case of Trump cancelling electric vehicle subsidies, slow it down. Governments still provide more than $900 billion of annual support for fossil fuels.

The target proposed at COP31 of increasing energy use from electricity to 35 per cent by 2035 would send a positive signal. The biggest bottleneck to this is expanding the grid, something governments could accelerate at home by cutting red tape and offering subsidies and loans.

Kingsmill Bond at think tank Ember Energy thinks the economics of clean tech will let the world limit warming to much less than the projected 2.7°C by 2100. Exactly how much less depends on politics. He proposes that energy-importing countries start their own COP, where fossil fuel-exporting countries can’t delay progress.

“The old system is just being propped up by legacy policy and ignorance,” he says. “We’ve just got to tear that down.”

Brief bursts of ‘pink noise’ played while people with early-stage Alzheimer’s disease sleep might give them a slight memory boost, a small study suggests.

Pink noise is best described as a low-pitched hiss. There is some evidence that exposure to pink noise during sleep may help clear waste products from the brain. As such, researchers are beginning to assess whether pink-noise therapy has benefits for the treatment of Alzheimer’s disease.

Can we harness the brain’s deep-cleaning system to prevent Alzheimer’s?

An international team of researchers has explored this possibility. They worked with 37 people, each with diagnosed with Alzheimer’s and experiencing mild cognitive impairment affecting memory. On two occasions, 14 days apart, the 37 participants were invited into the lab in the evening and asked to memorise 30 word pairs. They then slept in the lab while the researchers monitored their brain activity.

Advertisement

Javier Mínguez at Elevvo Therapeutics in Spain, and a member of the research team, says slow brainwaves and brief bursts of neural activity known as sleep spindles help the brain consolidate memories, a process Alzheimer’s can disrupt. The researchers used a system developed by Spanish neurotechnology company Bitbrain that can identify when slow brainwaves are approaching their peak. Throughout the first night in the lab, the researchers played a 50-millisecond-long pulse of pink noise to the sleeping participants each time these peaks occurred.

“Timing is critical, because the useful window is only about 200 milliseconds wide,” says Mínguez.

On the second night in the lab, the study participants were not exposed to pink noise as they slept.

After both nights, the participants were asked to recall the word pairs they had learned the evening before. They remembered slightly more word pairs after exposure to pink noise than after the night without pink noise: 0.88 word pairs more, on average, after the pink-noise exposure. This is equivalent to about a 19 per cent improvement in memory, the researchers say. The clinical significance of this result remains uncertain.

“These results are meaningful theoretically and fit with an increasingly strong set of findings linking memory storage with overnight brain activity,” says Ken Paller at Northwestern University in Illinois, who wasn’t involved in the study.

The study hasn’t yet been peer-reviewed. Several authors have commercial connections to Bitbrain or its spin-off Elevvo Therapeutics, and three are inventors on a pending patent covering the method, says Mínguez.

Mínguez sees the study as a proof of concept. To find out whether the benefits can last, the researchers are now expanding their experiments. They have given study participants equipment to use at home that offers pink noise stimulation during sleep, and they will assess the effects of continued exposure over a 6-month period.

A chronic inflammatory condition is becoming more common, and its symptoms can be mistaken for a severe allergic reaction.

Eosinophilic oesophagitis (EoE) is a rare condition where a type of white blood cells, known as eosinophils, builds up in the oesophagus. It is thought to affect around 40 in every 100,000 people.

Chronic inflammation messes with your mind. Here’s how to calm it

Eosinophils play an important role in the body’s immune system, helping to destroy invader parasites and pathogens before they cause harm to other cells. They also have a role in regulating inflammation, but can cause tissue damage when it becomes excessive, such as in EoE.

Advertisement

EoE can cause symptoms similar to that of anaphylaxis – a severe food allergy reaction – such as swelling, problems swallowing, drooling and the sensation of food stuck in the throat.

Two new studies on EoE have been presented at the American College of Allergy, Asthma and Immunology Annual Scientific Meeting in Phoenix, Arizona, this week.

Free newsletter

In the first study, Talal Nsouli at Georgetown University in Washington DC and his colleagues investigated 29 adults who were referred to a specialist because doctors suspected they had anaphylaxis. Patients reported repeated episodes of chest pain, drooling and problems swallowing after consuming certain foods. On average, each person went to hospital three times, and received at least one dose of adrenaline, the treatment for anaphylaxis. However, none of the participants tested positive for Ig-E mediated anaphylaxis, a specific type of rapid, life-threatening reaction triggered by the immune system. These patients were then tested for EoE with samples taken from the lining of the oesophagus, which came back positive for the condition.

“Not every frightening reaction after eating is anaphylaxis,” says Nsouli. If EoE isn’t diagnosed early, it can lead to the oesophagus narrowing due to scarring. Each year the disease isn’t treated, the risk of this complication rises by 9 per cent.

“When throat tightness, difficulty swallowing or food impaction recur, especially with food allergy testing, we should think about eosinophilic oesophagitis,” says Nsouli. “Rapid recognition can prevent years of uncertainty and progressive oesophageal damage.”

In the second study, Bushra Tbakhi at the University of Cincinnati, Ohio, and her colleagues used health records from more than 300 million people in the US and identified more than 500,000 people living with EoE. The number of diagnoses has risen about sevenfold since 2009.

The cause of EoE hasn’t been clearly identified, but Tbakhi and her colleagues found several key factors that predisposed patients to the condition. Men were more likely to develop EoE compared with women, and the diagnoses were most common in teenagers and people in their 40s. Those with other inflammatory and allergic conditions, such as asthma, coeliac disease, eczema and food allergies, were more likely to have EoE. Out of the most common food allergies, wheat allergy had the strongest link to the condition.

“We are seeing increased eosinophilic oesophagitis over time,” says Tbakhi. “Associated allergic conditions may help identify patients at high risk for eosinophilic oesophagitis.”

EoE is a chronic condition with no known cure. The aim of treatment is to control inflammation and symptoms, so patients can live a relatively normal life. People with EoE may benefit from changes to their diet, including cutting out foods that trigger their symptoms.

The most common medical treatment for the condition is a class of drugs called proton pump inhibitors. These medications work by blocking the lining of the oesophagus from releasing eotaxin-3, a chemical signal that attracts eosinophils. It also reduces acid production in the stomach, which reduces acid reflux into the throat, allowing the oesophagus to restore its barrier. Swallowed steroids are also used to quickly reduce inflammation in the oesophagus.

Don’t make changes to your diet without first speaking to a doctor

How Nvidia became so crucial to the AI boom

New Scientist November 12, 2026

You have almost certainly seen the headlines – Jensen Huang, the CEO of Nvidia, has resigned after admitting to an affair with Alice Huang (no relation), who is suspected by US intelligence officials of being a Chinese spy (a claim China dismisses). The story has become so big because Nvidia, and by extension Jensen, are at the heart of the AI revolution. But just why has this one company become so important?

For me, Nvidia will always be a video games company, its logo splashed up at the start of the play sessions of my youth. Its graphics processing units (GPUs) were specifically designed for the intense number-crunching required to create a 3D scene from triangles. Initially, these were a few hundred triangles, then thousands, and now hundreds of thousands as computing power has increased, allowing ever more realistic computer graphics.

Why gatekeeping is needed in the age of AI

But 30 years later, gaming hardware only makes up a small slice of Nvidia’s revenue, to the point where it has now stopped reporting gaming revenue as a standalone item. Instead, GPUs have become a raw input for the AI industry, essential for both training and deploying large language models (LLMs) like ChatGPT. This sent Nvidia’s value soaring to become the largest company in the world at a value of $4.5 trillion – at least, that is, until news of the affair broke and wiped out almost $500 billion of that, pushing Nvidia down the rankings. Shares fell further as Nvidia announced Huang’s resignation today.

Advertisement

Nvidia’s transformation away from gaming began more than 20 years ago, when researchers realised they could trick GPUs into performing a wider set of calculations. At the time, computers had a single central processing unit (CPU) that executed instructions on data one at a time, in serial. GPUs meanwhile, operated in parallel, allowing them to process the large number of triangles needed to render a scene. By recasting general computing problems in the language of triangles, researchers could harness this parallel power to do other things.

These hacks were impressive, but in 2007 Nvidia formalised the approach with the release of CUDA, a piece of software that could help with translating algorithms into a form more amenable to running on GPUs. Huang, who had been CEO since co-founding Nvidia in 1993, made what, in hindsight, was possibly the biggest bet in the history of computing. At a time when Nvidia’s customer base was almost exclusively gamers, he decided to build CUDA into every single GPU the company sold, even though this increased the cost and the vast majority of purchasers would never use it. Essentially, gamers subsidised the development of Nvidia’s general-purpose computing business for years.

That bet only began to show hints of paying off in 2012, as researchers were starting to use CUDA in meaningful numbers. The pivot point that year was the release of AlexNet, an artificial neural network capable of recognising images far better than any technique at the time. Neural networks had been tried and dismissed before, but thanks to CUDA and Nvidia GPUs, AlexNet brought the technique back into the mainstream and kicked off the field of “deep learning”, which ultimately led to today’s AI boom.

As researchers raced to try deep learning for themselves, Nvidia sold more and more GPUs. Then, in 2016 it released the DGX-1, a box containing 8 GPUs and billed as the “world’s first deep learning supercomputer”. Huang hand-delivered the first DGX-1 unit to OpenAI, then a recently formed non-profit. Nvidia’s share price began to grow, and grow, and grow in lockstep with the subsequent AI revolution.

It is this combination of hardware and software, GPUs and CUDA, that has made Nvidia so valuable. That isn’t to say other companies haven’t attempted to break its stranglehold on the AI industry. In January 2016, Google’s AI arm, DeepMind, announced it had used 176 GPUs to power its AlphaGo AI in a match against Fan Hui, a leading Go player. While neither company has confirmed, these were almost certainly Nvidia GPUs. But by March 2016, when AlphaGo beat the world champion Lee Sedol, DeepMind had switched to 48 tensor processing units (TPUs), an alternative type of AI hardware developed by Google.

How did the biggest crypto heist in history just happen?

Today, Google continues to use TPUs while tech giants like Amazon, Meta and Microsoft are all experimenting with custom chip designs, but Nvidia GPUs still dominate, in part thanks to the software industry’s decades-long experience of building on CUDA. And this links directly to the scandal the company is currently embroiled in.

Since 2022, the US has banned the export of high-end computing chips to China, including many of Nvidia’s top products, in an effort to stymie China’s AI progress and prevent the use of these chips for military applications. According to the Financial Times, Alice Huang told Chinese investors that she was able to secure access to Nvidia GPUs, while The Information claims she was allegedly involved in a deal to buy 240,000 banned GPUs. Alice Huang hasn’t responded publicly to the allegations.

Following that, the New York Times reported allegations of a second affair between Jensen Huang and an Nvidia executive, but Huang has not confirmed this. Today, Huang resigned as CEO, stepping away from the company, and the AI revolution, he helped build. Nvidia has appointed its chief financial officer Colette Kress as interim CEO, and will now search for a new leader as chip competitors nip at its heels. The AI industry as a whole will be hoping that investors don’t lose confidence following the fall of one its leading figures.

Vast data dump from Euclid space telescope reveals stunning galaxies

New Scientist November 12, 2026

The European Space Agency has just released a vast batch of observations of the sky captured by the Euclid space telescope. Launched in 2023, the telescope is currently on a six-year mission to image about one-third of the sky to build the most detailed 3D map of the cosmos ever created.

The latest observations – catchily titled DR1-Foundation – cover an area of the sky as big as 9500 full moons. The collection includes 900 million galaxies.

The mosaic of 740 images at the top of the article, collected in autumn 2024 and spring 2025, covers 367 square degrees of the northern sky. At full resolution, this snapshot runs to 500 gigapixels.

Advertisement

The bright oval in the lower left portion of the patchwork image is the spiral galaxy Messier 81, which is some 12 million light years from Earth.

The image above shows Messier 81 in greater detail, along with part of the M81 group of galaxies that also bears its name – an honour bestowed on it as the largest galaxy of the bunch.

To the lower left is the smaller galaxy NGC 3077, and the patches of wispy blue cloud throughout the images are galactic cirrus, which are actually in the foreground and part of our own home galaxy.

Here, Messier 81 is shown in even greater detail, in an image taken at the full resolution available to Euclid. The haze dominating the right side of the frame is the disc of Messier 81, inside which individual stars are visible.

This hazy galaxy is NGC 1291, around 33 million light years away. The image was made from two taken by Euclid and then cropped. In the background, even more distant galaxies are visible – the furthest away of which show up in red. Stars are still actively forming within NGC 1291, and can be seen as small blue-hued dots.

The image above shows Abell 3128, a cluster of hundreds of galaxies lying around 800 million light years away. The cluster is home to a diverse array of galaxies, including whirling spirals and fuzzy ellipticals. In the centre of the image is a strong gravitational lens, where the light travelling to us from a more distant galaxy has been warped by a massive object in the foreground.

UK military taps up astronomers to spot snooping foreign satellites

New Scientist November 12, 2026

The UK’s military and spy agencies are working with civilian academics to develop new ways to spot snooping by foreign satellites, researchers have revealed.

The US, China and Russia have spy satellites as well as counter-surveillance satellite and spacecraft programmes that can spy on other states’ satellites and observe others spying on theirs.

For instance, the US has a space plane – the Boeing X-37B – which can stay in orbit for several years and is thought to be able to approach other satellites and eavesdrop on their electromagnetic (EM) emissions. China has a similar craft and Russia has satellites to perform the same function.

Advertisement

Dead NASA satellite unexpectedly emits powerful radio pulse

“They fly close, have a good look at what the other satellites look like, monitor any EM like radio transmissions, basically just trying to figure out the purpose of anything else in orbit,” says astrophysicist Mark Norris at the University of Lancashire, UK. “[The UK has] a big capability gap there because it’s quite expensive to have something capable of significantly changing its orbit to allow it to approach other satellites.”

Norris says he is aware of a desire from UK government intelligence agencies to discuss how industry, academics and even research observatories could help plug that gap and provide a sovereign UK capability, in particular because of concern over how reliant the UK has been on assistance from the US.

“There are people with ideas for small, relatively cheap inspection satellites. There are also people like myself who have ideas for things you can do from the ground, a lot more cheaply,” says Norris. “Ground-based observations give you the ability to watch a lot of these suspect objects at once, to help you figure out whether they are a threat against our own space infrastructure.”

Free newsletter

Norris wouldn’t describe the techniques that might be possible in detail, but says ground telescopes could garner some structural information about an adversary craft just from images or even the wavelength of reflected light. This could reveal information about its composition, or the presence and size of particular components such as solar panels or antennae for example.

“There are things we think we can do from the ground that will get you 90 per cent of the way there. Not as good as if you’re in orbit, but it could certainly help you figure out [whether] the structure of this satellite does not match its claimed purpose,” says Norris.

The UK’s space surveillance and protection capabilities are managed by the National Space Operations Centre, a partnership between the UK Space Agency, UK Space Command and national weather service the Met Office. But with an annual budget of around £20 million, it has limited capabilities and essentially just collects observations from various sources in order to piece together an image of what is going on in space.

“They would go and hoover up observations and then try and do an analysis of it. And my own gut feeling is if you can’t control the quality of your data, all you do is produce crap out the other end,” says astronomer Don Pollacco at the University of Warwick, UK. “So, now there’s a push to get their own sovereign capability.”

Why the US military could replace spy satellites with solar planes

In a statement, a spokesperson for the Ministry of Defence said: “The National Space Operations Centre (NSpOC) makes space safer and more secure, supporting international security and defence while helping to grow a strong domestic space sector. Since its launch, NSpOC has monitored the uncontrolled re-entry of over 1350 objects from space, issued 45,000 collision alerts to UK-licensed satellite operators, monitored 11 satellite break-up events and played a major role in international space hazard response.”

Snooping on the electronic emissions from satellites was easy in previous decades, says Pollacco, as they tended to broadcast in a wide cone that could be intercepted on the surface of Earth, even vast distances from the intended recipient. But now satellites tend to broadcast in narrower, more focused beams that mean the easiest way to intercept messages is to drift near them in space.

However, even for nations with a space plane, this approach has limitations, like only being able to target one object at a time. “So, we’ve been trying to think ahead as to what that situation will be like in a decade,” says Pollacco, if adversaries are able to launch many satellites into orbit. “Being able to even know that it’s been launched would be difficult and knowing what it’s trying to do [would be] even more difficult.”

Part of Pollacco’s work, initially designed for civilian monitoring of satellites for logistical purposes, involves running data on reflected light from satellites through AI models to identify them. “They’ve all got their own signatures,” he says.

Pollacco is also working on the Digital Telescope project, which uses an array of small telescopes to monitor a vast area of the sky at once. The project is funded by the European Research Council and will have scientific uses for observing phenomena such as supernovae. But it also has military and intelligence applications.

“The military are on to this,” says Pollacco, “and they offered an opportunity to make [something similar] for them. Anyone sneaking around to take pictures of your spacecraft, we see them.” The Digital Telescope will be able to capture images of satellites every 10 seconds with a resolution of around 10 centimetres. “It’s transformational,” he says.

A powerful new telescope in Chile is set to transform astronomy, and its first pictures of stellar nurseries and galaxies have just been unveiled

James Blake at the University of Warwick says some academics working on satellite observation for civilian purposes already supply data on what they see to the UK government, but any groups taking money from intelligence agencies wouldn’t be able to speak freely about it.

“It’s quite complex to do, but we’re slowly getting better at inferring what these objects could be doing based on purely the light that we’re receiving in the telescope,” says Blake. “In this field, I think a lot of the funding is now coming from the more defence-related routes. It’s not something that I’m particularly happy about. I would much rather be working with the research councils.”

Defence funding can come with problems, such as not being able to publish research because of its potential impact on national security, says Blake. “It’s a very murky pool.”

Blake says observers on the ground are seeing more activity by nefarious satellites. “We’re starting to see a lot of behaviour that previously wasn’t really known to take place, or assumed to be plausible,” he says. “This can range from anything from a flyby to quite intimate inspection going on.”

Sometimes these manoeuvres are so complex that they can use up a satellite’s fuel reservoir in a single move. The intention may be purely to demonstrate the nation’s capabilities, says Blake, but such moves are risky.

“New spacefaring nations are, of course, going to launch these fabulous new satellites that they’ve been able to develop with new technology and they’re going to do things that are quite wasteful or reckless, such as this,” he says. “And the consequences are quite bad sometimes: you can create thousands of pieces of debris if you’re not careful.”

Some PFAS chemicals are declining in English rivers but others are appearing

New Scientist November 12, 2026

The concentration of two of the most well-studied PFAS forever chemicals are showing a strong downward trend in English rivers. The finding adds to a mixed story for the power of global restrictions.

The levels of perfluorooctanesulfonic acid (PFOS) and perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA) in English rivers have fallen by 30 per cent and 29 per cent, respectively, over the past decade, according to a new report by scientists at the Environment Agency (EA), a UK government green regulator.

Both of these human-made chemicals take a long time to break down in the environment. The International Agency for Research on Cancer recently designated PFOA as carcinogenic to humans, and both forever chemicals have been linked to reproductive health and developmental impacts as well as other serious health issues.

Advertisement

Fish-based pet food may expose cats and dogs to forever chemicals

Under the United Nations Stockholm Convention on Persistent Organic Pollutants, the use of PFOS was restricted from 2009, and the use of PFOA was restricted from 2019 – although there were country-specific caveats on which uses they applied to.

They had both been used in non-stick coatings on consumer products as well as in industrial processes. Both were also used in firefighting foams, a major source of PFAS pollution entering the environment, with a ban on PFOA in firefighting foams only coming into force in the UK in 2025.

Rob Bradburne, the EA’s chief scientist, describes his group’s results as proof that the global ban was “a really positive move”. But, he adds that the huge range of PFAS chemicals is going to “complicate the story”.

An issue that is clear in the dataset for England is that while these two main PFAS have declined, many other “forever chemicals” that are being used to replace them – such as short-chain PFAS and fluorotelomer compounds – have now emerged in the environment at detectable levels.

Free newsletter

There are around 10,000 chemicals defined as PFAS, and they are used in a huge range of products and processes, from cosmetics to industrial lubricants. But the health and environmental impacts of many of these chemicals are relatively understudied.

One of the short-chain PFAS that is now particularly widespread across the world is trifluoroacetic acid (TFA) – which can form when pesticides, refrigerants and pharmaceuticals break down in the environment. The EA report confirmed that TFA is widespread in England, and a separate study published this week confirmed that it is also widespread across the UK more generally.

“These findings add to the growing weight of evidence that PFAS pollution must be tackled at source if we are to protect our environment and our health,” says Hannah Evans, who worked on this second study and works with the UK environmental charity Fidra.

“Other countries are already progressing towards this end… The UK cannot afford to fall further behind,” says Evans.

Wastewater treatment plants funnel PFAS into drinking water

Currently, the EU is looking at a blanket ban on all PFAS chemicals, so that when specific chemicals are prohibited they aren’t simply replaced by another PFAS that may also eventually be identified as harmful and persistent in the environment. The UK government has said it is following this closely but has given no timescales on when a similar policy might be introduced.

Alistair Boxall at the University of York, UK, says that the decline in legacy pollutants and increase in short-chain replacements was observed in a recently published European-wide monitoring study he took part in. He believes the change shows why bans that target the entire group of chemicals could offer a better way forward.

“We seem to always be playing catch-up with chemicals like PFAS, so need to be much more agile in the way that we monitor and manage these substances. The idea of using grouping approaches could help,” says Boxall.

Patrick Byrne at Liverpool John Moores University, UK, says that the grouping approach is useful and something that scientists have argued strongly for.

Forever chemicals are renowned for their durability and their non-stick properties, but they persist for years in the environment. An alternative inspired by plants doesn’t have the same problem

He also says that the story isn’t over for PFOS and PFOA. Though they are decreasing globally, it’s important to remember they are still highly persistent and found in almost every water body.

The levels of PFOS being recorded are still, in many cases, higher than the UK and EU Environmental Quality Standard, which is set to reflect the concentration above which the chemical will affect ecosystems. Currently, PFOS is the only individual PFAS with such a standard in England, but others are under development.

“This report adds to our growing understanding of how PFAS enter our environment, but we must not wait for a complete picture before acting,” says Chloe Alexander, a campaigner at Wildlife and Countryside Link, an umbrella organisation in the UK that brings together many volunteer and charitable groups.

“History is full of late lessons from early warnings, where ignored science allowed preventable harm to become widespread and, in some cases, irreversible,” says Alexander. “The longer it waits, the greater the risks to people and wildlife – and the higher the costs of clean-up and toxic waste disposal.”

Election 2026: Election wait leaves businesses with ‘decision debt’ – Mike Burke

New Zealand Herald November 12, 2026

With official election results not due to November 27, Mike Burke urges small businesses to get on with decision-making. Photo / Getty Images

For the past six months, one sentence has done more heavy lifting in New Zealand business than most of its workforce: “Let’s wait until after the election.”

It has parked fleet upgrades, held back hiring and postponed more strategy days than a wet long weekend. Prospa’s latest SME tracker found almost a quarter of small businesses were delaying big purchases until the result was in and 15% were holding off on expansion or hiring. The bigger the business, the more likely it was waiting.

Well, good news, “after the election” has arrived. The less good news is that the bill has arrived with it.

ASB’s economists recently went back through the seven elections from 2005 to 2023, looking for the post-election catch-up you would expect if businesses really had been sitting on their decisions.

They struggled to find one.

Confidence dips before polling day, but business investment still grew ahead of five of those seven elections and employment generally kept rising. In short, we tell surveys and anyone else who’ll listen that we’re waiting, but then mostly just get on with it.

So the election is rarely the real reason. Perhaps it’s simply that “we’re waiting for certainty” sounds far better at a managers’ meeting than “I haven’t decided yet”.

And if certainty is what we’re after, I have bad news. Official results aren’t declared until November 27. Then it’s Christmas, then summer, then whatever the world throws at us next.

Certainty since Covid is like the tradie who is “definitely coming on Thursday”.

Every decision you put off is a loan against your future – and it charges interest.

The ute you didn’t replace in July has been eating repair bills ever since. The hire you put off means your best person has been doing two jobs for four months. The price review you parked means you’ve absorbed cost increases on every invoice since winter.

None of it shows up as a line in your accounts and all of it is costing you.

I call it decision debt. Like any debt, it’s manageable when it’s small and you can keep the balance in your head. It becomes scary when it’s big, spread across the business and nobody has been keeping a tally.

Early in a business, you have to back your conviction, because the data doesn’t exist yet. I call that faith over fact. Naivety is an early entrepreneur’s superpower. In an economy this jumpy, the full set of facts never arrives. If you’re waiting for the data to insure all your decisions, you’ve gone too late, or worse yet, you’ll never go at all.

I bought three businesses in the first quarter of 2020, which I would not recommend to anybody. I’ve made plenty more average calls since, but the costly ones were the ones I sat on.

Here’s a recommendation for the next 30 days.

Write down every decision you’ve parked “until after the election”. All of them, big and small.

Next to each one, answer a single question: what, specifically, would the result change? Name the policy, the rule or the contract. If you can’t name it, the election was never the reason.

Then give every decision a date and try to put most of those dates before Christmas. Some will be a yes and some a no. A clear no still counts. It frees up the cash and the headspace you’ve been holding in reserve for a maybe.

Some decisions do hinge on policy, sure. If a big slice of your revenue rides on a government contract or a specific rule, waiting for the detail is sensible. Write down what you’re waiting for and the date you’ll stop waiting. A wait with an end date is a plan. One without is a stall.

“After the election” is here and it looks a lot like Monday. Your debt is due. Start paying it down.

Mike Burke is the founder of Point16, its Business Growth School and co-host of iHeartRadio podcast: Pints, Pies and Profits with Scott Douglas.

A New Zealand bookseller is phasing out works by British author David Walliams after allegations of sexual misconduct made by multiple women.

The allegations include claims that Walliams groomed teenage girls and used his celebrity status to pursue girls and young women for sex. Walliams has denied the allegations.

The joint Guardian and ITV News investigation drew on more than 30 sources who provided first-hand accounts of Walliams’ conduct. The sources were not all women accusing him of sexual misconduct.

The children’s author and comedian sought a High Court injunction preventing the Guardian and ITV News from publishing the allegations and identifying him.

The court ruled against the injunction, but temporarily protected his identity while he considered an appeal. That protection expired on Monday after no appeal was filed. The court did not determine whether the allegations were true.

Independent bookseller Unity Books has not ordered any of Walliams’ books since allegations emerged of inappropriate behaviour towards junior female employees at his publisher, HarperCollins.

In September, HarperCollins confirmed it would stop publishing Walliams’ back catalogue, having already ended plans for new books.

Unity Books, which has shops in Auckland and Wellington, confirmed it was “phasing him out”.

Its Auckland shop had only two copies of his books left, and they were not selling easily, the company said, while its Wellington branch was out of Walliams stock.

Big chains Whitcoulls, Paper Plus and The Warehouse did not appear to have Walliams’ books available online. It is unclear whether this is in response to the allegations.

The Herald has approached them for comment.

Renee Rowland, association manager of Booksellers NZ, said in an interview on Newstalk ZB that “this isn’t a new dilemma” regarding Walliams’ books.

Shops had been deciding whether to stock his books for some time, based on last year’s allegations and rumours within the industry.

She said booksellers had a wide choice of authors to stock, including many “amazing new authors” they could promote instead.

Walliams’ books will remain available in Auckland libraries.

Auckland Council’s head of library and learning services, Catherine Leonard, said it was up to readers to decide whether to engage with an author. Books were not removed from collections solely because of allegations surrounding their authors.

“Our role is to support informed choice by providing access to a diverse collection, rather than making those decisions on behalf of our communities.”

Kai Creighton is a journalism student at Waikato Institute of Technology.

Carterton rural roads: Council delays decision on rates plan

New Zealand Herald November 12, 2026

Under the proposal, forestry owners faced average rate increases of 1260%. Photo / RNZ, Kate Newton

Carterton councillors appear unlikely to green-light a “nuclear” rates option to pay for the maintenance of rural roads.

The council wrapped up its two-day rates review hearing on Thursday mid-deliberations and is to meet again next Wednesday to decide next steps.

It had consulted on rates changes that would have resulted in rates rising more than 1200% for forestry owners and almost 100% for dairy farmers to help pay for the damage done by heavy trucks on rural roads.

During deliberations on Thursday, councillors agreed that the current funding model to pay for maintaining rural roads was “broken”, but none was keen to see the changes proposed become an immediate reality.

Councillor Brian Deller said it was important the council didn’t “rush into any half-cocked solutions”, while councillor Steve Laurence likened the proposed changes to a “nuclear weapon” if it was applied at the level suggested.

Councillor Simon Casey agreed and said although rural ratepayers needed to pay more towards roading, “the amount is a bit of a nuclear option at the moment and is unpalatable”.

Councillors heard from more than 40 submitters across the forestry and farming sector who spoke passionately against the council’s proposed rates review, citing inaccurate modelling and unfair outcomes.

Despite this, all acknowledged funding rural roading fairly was a problem that needed solving.

The council’s rates review proposal included introducing a targeted roading rate and increasing the rural differential from 0.8 to 1.0 (the amount rural ratepayers pay compared with household and commercial rates).

Under the proposal, forestry owners faced average rate rises of 1260% to help fund roading, and dairy farmers faced increases of 92% on average.

About 4700 residential and lifestyle properties would have had rates decreases of 14%.

Submitter Colin Jacobs of Lewis Tucker said the modelling the council used to inform its proposal didn’t go into enough detail to determine the real impact different activities had on the local roading network.

He also raised concerns that properties classed as mixed use that had forests for harvesting were not accounted for in the targeted charge.

Carterton resident Roger Styles, a former deputy mayor of the Hutt City Council, said he spoke in support of the “silent majority” of Carterton townsfolk and said the proposal was fair.

“Whenever you do something popular, no one says nothing,” he said.

“As soon as you do something unpopular, the room fills up.”

Liam Walker, a 24-year-old employed in the forestry industry, said he would never have considered moving to Wairarapa had it not offered career opportunities for his expertise.

“In a region where young people tend to leave, forestry is bringing young professionals to the area,” he said.

The proposal would drive forestry out of the region to where it was more economical, impacting local jobs, he said.

Harry Livesey, of the Wairarapa Farm Forestry Association, said “no rational council would bring this [proposal] through” and that the modelling was “not robust enough to impose a 1200% increase on ratepayers”.

“Should this go forward, it will go straight to judicial review on process alone,” he said.

Malte Coulmann, of the Southern North Island Wood Council and Forestry Enterprises, said the sector was “prepared to pay its fair share” and was “not seeking a free ride”.

But this was a national problem that needed a national solution, he said.

The council is to reconvene on November 18.

New Zealand Herald November 12, 2026

Joe's Garage Wellington remains closed, a month after it was liquidated. Photo / Grace Symmans

Popular Wellington cafe Joe’s Garage collapsed owing creditors more than $700,000.

The well-known Tory St cafe closed after 13 years of operating in the capital when it was placed into liquidation by the IRD on September 29.

Company Wellybrew took over Joe’s Garage Wellington in November 2023. The first liquidation report has been released, showing the company currently owes $726,260.88 to creditors, with the full amount still to be determined.

The company owes IRD $415,294.33, and $309,183.42 to unsecured creditors, including employees, the Joe’s Garage franchise and food and drink suppliers.

National manager insolvency and trustee service Russell Fildes said the $415,294.33 to the IRD includes preferential GST and PAYE but does not contain any interest and penalties; these are included in the unsecured figure.

He was not able to answer the Herald’s questions about employees and the status of their claims but noted further claims information will be provided in the next report, due 3 May, 2027.

At the time of the initial report, $4,040.86 was the balance of funds on hand.

Reasons given for liquidation were “failure to account for taxation, economic conditions & inability to recover costs”.

The liquidator is investigating the company’s finances to determine any potential recoveries for creditors.

Joe’s Garage franchise services said they can’t confirm what will happen with the future of their Wellington branch but told the Herald they are continuing to explore opportunities with interested parties.

Joe’s Garage started in Queenstown in 2000 and has grown to 19 locations nationwide, including Christchurch, Nelson, New Plymouth and Auckland.

No other cafes are affected by the Wellington liquidation.

The release of the full liquidator’s report is expected in the next six months, with the liquidation estimated to be completed by March 30, 2027.

Grace Symmans is a Wellington-based reporter who covers news in the capital. Grace joined NZME in 2025 as a producer for Wellington Mornings on Newstalk ZB. She can be emailed at grace. symmans@nzme. co. nz.

NZQA chief fronts up over NCEA English Level 2 exam outage

New Zealand Herald November 12, 2026

The chief executive of the NZ Qualifications Authority has apologised after a digital platform crashed midway through yesterday’s English Level 2 exam.

But pushed on how confident he was in the platform’s stability, chief executive Christian Hawkesby would not say with certainty that the outage wouldn’t reoccur – saying instead that NZQA was working with the provider on testing the platform to ensure it was stable.

Hawkesby told Newstalk ZB’s Mike Hosking Breakfast that NZQA was sorry for the disruption to students, and recognised it was a very stressful time for students and their parents.

“We identified an issue during the exam, we worked with our vendor to identify it and resolve it as quickly as we could.

“The system is back up and running and stable and we had exams through yesterday afternoon.”

There were no exams today, but the largest exam was scheduled next Tuesday and NZQA was preparing for that.

Paper copies were available for that exam “to give comfort for students” that there was a contingency in place, he said.

Speaking to Herald Now’s Ryan Bridge TODAY, Hawkesby admitted NZQA still didn’t know how many students had to abandon the exam altogether, but the glitch may have affected up to 37,500 students – the number who were registered on the digital system.

A further 7500 were sitting the exam on paper.

The Herald was told yesterday that students were left panicked and some were in tears after their work was wiped.

Many students then scrambled to sit the exams with pen and paper while some abandoned the exam altogether and have been advised they can use their derived grades from sitting previous “mock” exams.

NZQA confirmed the problem with its digital exam platform was resolved at 10.35am, about 35 minutes after it started.

Hawkesby told Bridge the situation varied widely between schools.

“In some exam centres, we know that students waited patiently for half an hour, 40 minutes and then were given additional time to complete the exam in full.”

There was a well-established process for students to be given the better grade of yesterday’s exam or their derived grade from earlier practice exams, he said.

“We’re also going to work really closely with schools about what other evidence can be provided, and also look at the results from this year’s exam relative to other years to get a gauge of how much of the results may have been driven by the disruption and how we can adjust for that.”

That would have to be done on a “case-by-case, school-by-school basis”, he said.

Manawatū student Finn, 16, told the Herald he was 20 seconds from finishing an essay when the system shut down, while another student from Carmel College had written more than 1400 words in her first essay when her computer froze and her work was lost.

One parent said they were concerned because these results would be “critical” to university acceptance and scholarships.

Education Minister Erica Stanford said students had been “badly let down” and has demanded a clear plan of action by this afternoon to ensure the situation doesn’t recur.

“I have been assured that a plan is in place to ensure no student is disadvantaged because of what happened.”

NZQA said the problem related to the transfer of student responses from the exam platform to the marking platform overnight.

Breast cancer: Pāpāmoa mother calls for wider funded access to Kisqali

New Zealand Herald November 12, 2026

Pāpāmoa mother Heather Johnson was diagnosed with Stage 3 breast cancer in 2021 before it progressed to terminal Stage 4 in 2024. Photo / Kelly O'Hara

A mother with terminal breast cancer believes a drug funded publicly only for late-stage patients could have delayed the progression of the disease if she had been eligible earlier.

Heather Johnson says her “high-risk”, Stage 3 breast cancer diagnosis in 2021 meant her chance of surviving for 10 years was 42%.

But the 58-year-old, from Pāpāmoa, has seen great results from the drug Kisqali. She has been taking it since mid-2024, when it became publicly funded for late-stage patients.

That was about the same time as Johnson learned that her cancer had progressed to Stage 4, considered terminal.

Now she is calling for Kisqali to be publicly funded for people at earlier stages of the disease.

She “wholeheartedly” believed Kisqali would have delayed her Stage 4 progression if she could have accessed it after her initial diagnosis.

An international study by the drug’s supplier, Novartis, showed Kisqali reduced the risk of death by 19% and the risk of cancer returning by 26% when combined with standard hormone therapy.

New Zealand’s medicine-buying agency, Pharmac, said provisional recommendations on an application to fund the drug for early-stage breast cancer were due soon.

Johnson said the first symptom she noticed was swelling in her breast. With no lump, she did not think much of it.

She saw a doctor when swelling increased. She had a mammogram and biopsy.

“Then the news came back … it was cancer.”

Johnson said she had lobular, “aggressive” cancer in her left breast and had a single mastectomy.

Cancer was found in her right breast in 2023.

In mid-2024, she discovered the cancer had progressed to Stage 4, metastasising to her vertebrae. She also had brain lesions.

She began taking Kisqali, which had just been publicly funded.

She had regular CT and MRI scans to monitor her cancer.

“The Kisqali has, by all accounts, kept everything stable.”

Some brain lesions shrank, and her spine showed signs of “healing”, she said. Targeted radiation had also helped.

She had had many scans, drugs and oncologist appointments since her Stage 4 diagnosis, costing the health system money.

“Kisqali’s expensive, but I believe cheaper in the longer run … ”

She advocated for wider access: “We need to do better at preventing progression.”

She acknowledged New Zealand was a small country with limited funding, “but when you’ve got trials and evidence in other countries … I think we need to be looking at that more”.

A Novartis statement said the treatment was publicly funded for eligible patients with early breast cancer in Australia and England.

About 900 New Zealanders with high-risk early-stage (N2) breast cancer were expected to benefit in the first five years if funding was approved, it said.

Breast Cancer Foundation New Zealand head of research and strategic programmes Dr Mehdi Shahbazpour said Kiwis should be given the best chance to prevent breast cancer from spreading and becoming incurable.

Shahbazpour said the study’s findings showed why access to treatment needed to “keep pace” with advances in research.

He said people should be able to make treatment decisions based on clinical needs, not what they could afford.

“That requires sustained investment in New Zealand’s medicines budget, including priority for early-stage treatments shown to reduce the risk of cancer progressing to advanced disease.”

Medical oncologist Dr Sheridan Wilson said a cure was “rarely achievable” when breast cancer spread to organs.

“Enhancing early-stage treatment to minimise recurrence and maximise the potential for a cure remains imperative.”

Pharmac medicines management clinical lead Melissa Copland acknowledged patients who had benefitted from treatment and said Pharmac understood how difficult it could be for people living with breast cancer and their whānau.

Pharmac announced public funding for Kisqali in February 2024, starting from July of that year.

It was funded for people with HER2-negative breast cancer that responded to hormone treatment and had spread beyond the breast.

Pharmac was considering a funding application for people with early-stage breast cancer after surgery, and alongside hormone therapy, Copland said.

Applications were considered separately because the clinical evidence, eligibility, expected health benefits and costs could differ significantly depending on what a medicine was used for.

She said Pharmac’s specialist advisory committees provided objective clinical knowledge and expertise.

The Cancer Treatments Advisory Committee recommended funding Kisqali with medium priority for early-stage breast cancer in November 2025.

It considered the application again on November 6 as further information “was brought to our attention”.

The meeting agenda said the committee would discuss correspondence regarding trial results for Kisqali for early-stage breast cancer.

Provisional recommendations would be published within 30 days, then Pharmac would assess the application.

This included looking at the health needs of people who might benefit, the benefits and risks of treatment and costs, and health outcomes compared with other funding options, Copland said.

The application might then be prioritised alongside other medicines Pharmac would like to fund on its Options for Investment list.

Copland said it could not say when a funding decision would be made, as it depended on available budget, supplier negotiations and the ranking of other medicines.

Megan Wilson is a health and general news reporter for the Bay of Plenty Times and the Rotorua Daily Post. She has been a journalist since 2021.

Rotorua Mayor Tania Tapsell pushes back on conflict questions

New Zealand Herald November 12, 2026

Rotorua Mayor Tania Tapsell and councillor Robert Lee in more amicable times. Photo / Mathew Nash

Rotorua Mayor Tania Tapsell denies having a conflict of interest involving an influential iwi trust, and says in her view a fellow councillor has damaged her reputation by suggesting otherwise.

Councillor Robert Lee has asked whether Tapsell is a beneficiary of the Pukeroa Oruawhata Trust and therefore conflicted on council decisions involving it.

Tapsell says she has no connections with the trust.

The dispute came to the fore after Rotorua Lakes Council’s decision last month to pass administration of Crown-owned reserve land occupied by the Rotorua Thermal Holiday Park to the trust, the post-settlement entity representing Ngāti Whakaue.

Lee argued the change, requested by the Department of Conservation, would deny the council more than $200,000 a year in lease revenue.

His questioning of potential conflicts involving councillors with Ngāti Whakaue whakapapa led to his ejection from a council meeting.

The dispute later spilled on to social media, with Lee and Tapsell publicly addressing the issue.

Speaking to Local Democracy Reporting, Tapsell maintained she had no requirement to declare a conflict of interest regarding the trust.

“I don’t have any connections with Pukeroa Oruawhata Trust and related entities,” she said.

“I have no direct personal involvement with the trust or its related entities, I don’t hold a governance role with them, and I don’t receive any personal benefit from their activities.”

Tapsell said she had been an elected member for nine years and had previously sought advice on the issue. She said it had been “made clear” to her that tribal affiliation did not constitute a conflict of interest.

She said she had never declared, or considered declaring, a conflict of interest in relation to matters involving the trust.

“Because I don’t have one,” she said.

Her uncle, David Tapsell, is the trust chairman.

Lee has commented on the relationship on social media but Tapsell rejected any suggestion the link met the threshold of a conflict.

“Sharing the same surname as others is not a conflict,” she said.

“Rotorua is a small community. If sharing a surname or having distant whakapapa connections was enough to create a conflict of interest, we’d struggle to find anyone who could participate in local decision-making.”

Tapsell said Lee had been told there was no conflict but has continued raising the issue.

In her view: “I’m deeply disappointed he has publicly lied and made defamatory accusations with no evidence to back it up.”

Lee denied defaming the mayor and said he “simply asked a question”.

“The public and I would like an explanation rather than just a denial.”

He said his concerns had “absolutely nothing to do with the mayor’s ethnicity”.

“Her tribal affiliation is only relevant insofar as that may entitle her to be a beneficiary of the Pukeroa Oruawhata Trust,” he said.

Lee said the relationship between the mayor and the trust chairman was one reason he believed questions about beneficiary status were legitimate.

He acknowledged he had not identified any direct financial, governance, employment or beneficiary interest held by the mayor.

“That’s why I asked the question,” he said.

Comments on Lee’s Facebook page have been critical of the mayor.

Lee said he supported freedom of expression but accepted there were “reasonable” limits.

“I don’t hold the public to the same high standard I expect of myself or of my colleagues,” Lee said, stating he had “blocked a small number of people” from his page for “repeated personal attacks”.

Lee said he generally wouldn’t remove comments from his page, although he had done so on occasion, including once at the mayor’s request.

“I do, however, think there is a widespread perception of a conflict of interest among the public and that the public would like an answer to my question,” he said.

David Tapsell told Local Democracy Reporting it was “not his place” to comment on councillor disputes.

Local Government New Zealand chief executive Scott Necklen said conflicts of interest must be assessed on a case-by-case basis.

“It is worth noting that whakapapa to iwi does not automatically mean a conflict of interest,” he said.

Necklen said conflicts generally fell into two categories: financial interests and non-financial interests relating to bias.

“Key considerations include any financial benefit, governance role or close relationship with someone affected by the decision.”

He noted financial interests shared broadly with the public would not necessarily prevent participation in decision-making.

Pukeroa Oruawhata Trust chief executive Mark Gibb was approached for comment.

Mathew Nash is a Local Democracy Reporting journalist based at the Rotorua Daily Post. He has previously written for SunLive, been a regular contributor to RNZ and was a football reporter in the UK for eight years.

- LDR is local body journalism co-funded by RNZ and NZ On Air.

It’s time to rethink one of the world’s most popular cities

Sydney Morning Herald November 13, 2026

It often felt like La Sagrada Familia would never be completed. The basilica’s unfinished nature was a part of its DNA, as vital to its identity in the public eye as any spires or naves.

For more than 140 years, Catalan architect Antoni Gaudi’s masterpiece was a work in progress, a timeline that is testament to the sheer scale of the idea, the expense of bringing it to life, the unlikely nature of a project so bold and ambitious ever coming to fruition.

For regular visitors to Barcelona this structure became a marker of time, its outline subtly altered every time you were in the city – an extra tower here, another facade there.

But in February this year, a 100-tonne cross was erected atop the Tower of Jesus Christ, the basilica’s soaring central spire. Thus, La Sagrada Familia became the tallest church in the world, at 172.5 metres. And it was finished.

Works will continue well into the 2030s – refinement of the Glory Facade, which will become the main entrance; ornamental tinkering on other exteriors; detailed interior work – but officially, the world’s most famous unfinished masterpiece no longer qualifies for that title.

Sign up for the Traveller Deals newsletter

Get exclusive travel deals delivered straight to your inbox. Sign up now.

It’s an exciting time for potential visitors to the Catalan capital, particularly those who have been before and have witnessed La Sagrada Familia in its various states of construction. Now, as Barcelona marks the 100th anniversary of Antoni Gaudi’s death, you get to see the basilica in all its glory. Now, you get to see Barcelona, too, at its best.

Because although the city has been through its share of problems in the recent past, from unrest caused by overtourism to a campaign for Catalan independence, Barcelona is still undeniably one of the world’s great destinations, and there are so many reasons to revisit.

This is truly one of the world’s most spectacular buildings, one of its most beautiful and inspiring. Though Gaudi’s masterpiece is stunning from the outside, with its intricately decorated facades and 14 spires, on the inside it’s perhaps even more impressive. La Sagrada Familia’s soaring, 75-metre-high ceiling appears like the canopy of a Technicolor forest; the basilica’s columns branch out into what looks like concrete foliage, and stained-glass windows cast multi-hued light into every niche.

Even with the large crowds, which are inevitable, a visit to La Sagrada Familia is a moving, spiritual experience. To see it finished is a wonder. Book tickets in advance and book them for as early in the morning as you can manage, to get in before the bulk of the visitors and enjoy the building at its most peaceful. Later, stroll around the perimeter and view the various facades and towers. See sagradafamilia. org

Plenty of other architectural works by Antoni Gaudi have been finished for some time, and are easy to access. The most famous is probably Park Guell, a 17-hectare complex of public parks and gardens on the slopes of Turo del Carmel hill on the north-west edge of the city. This UNESCO heritage-listed site is more than 100 years old, and features numerous structures built in Gaudi’s signature style, a blend of geometric shapes and those reflecting organic forms.

Elsewhere in Barcelona, Casa Batllo is a surrealist apartment block inspired by the ocean, La Predrera – Casa Mila is an apartment building that features warrior-shaped chimneys, and Casa Vicens is Gaudi’s first major housing project. All are impressive from the outside and free to view from the street. See gaudi-foundation. org

As Barcelona has grown and strained at its boundaries, local authorities tinker with way to improve the city. Superblocks are perhaps the most interesting and enjoyable. This is the idea of sectioning off three-by-three squares of city blocks and transforming street spaces into public amenities. Cars are pushed to perimeter roads and inside the superblocks streets are reclaimed as recreational spaces with space for pedestrians, cyclists and residents to relax in a vehicle-free zone.

Not all locals are happy with superblocks – known in Catalan as “superilles” – but as a visitor, these spaces allow you to mix with residents in a leisurely environment away from the touristy crush of the likes of the Gothic Quarter. Find superblocks in Sant Antoni and L’Eixample in central Barcelona, and beachside Poblenou to the north. See ajuntament. barcelona. cat

There’s an exciting, ultra-modern dining scene in Barcelona, which we will get to. First though, let’s talk about traditional restaurants and the dining culture that has developed over hundreds of years, and which remains strong today. Begin with tapas, a style of eating so well-known around the world: Bar La Plata has been around since 1945, serving the same four dishes, though the small plates of fried anchovies are most popular; Quimet y Quimet has served open sandwiches utilising tinned seafood since 1914; and Cova Fumada, opened in 1944, is famous for its potato croquettes stuffed with minced beef.

Sit down for something more substantial at Can Cargolet, a down-home Catalan diner specialising in butifarra sausages and braised snails. Or book a table at Can Sole, a seafood restaurant in the port area that has been around since 1903. Or call in to Colmado Murria, a stockist of high-end cheese and wine, which opened in 1898.

If you love food, and you find experimentation and innovation thrilling, you are going to be overjoyed by the modern dining scene in the Catalan capital, which is filled with chefs doing interesting things. Barcelona is home to Disfrutar, awarded three Michelin stars and a previous No.1 on the World’s 50 Best list. But you don’t have to spend so much to experience this scene: try Ultramarinos Marin for incredible grilled seafood, Estimar for elevated tradition, Berbena for small plates that push the envelope, and Masa Vins for natural wines and imaginative snacks.

Barcelona is also an excellent place to sample the cuisines of the world: there’s a thriving Mexican scene here (Xuba Tacos), high-quality Japanese (Shoronpo), not to mention Italian, North African and more. There is a vibrant, ever-changing dining scene, concentrated in neighbourhoods such as L’Eixample, Passeig de Gracia and Sant Antoni.

Come for the big brands, if that’s what you like: Mango, Zara, H&M, El Corte Ingles. They’re all here, with major outlets on busy streets. But they’re everywhere else as well. If you want to do some shopping in Barcelona, check out the new wave of boutiques and galleries that sell unique pieces you won’t find anywhere else.

Begin your search in El Born. Its narrow streets are lined with boutiques selling the wares of local designers. Gracia to the north is also excellent for indie fashion, with plenty of local designers represented at own-brand shops. L’Eixample, meanwhile, has a host of small galleries featuring the works of Catalan artists.

There was a time when Barcelona was filled with no-go zones, when the city had a reputation for petty crime and visitors needed to be careful with where and when they decided to visit. Those days, fortunately, are mostly over, and many of Barcelona’s neighbourhoods are now pleasant, peaceful places in which to enjoy space and discover some of the city’s finest food and drink.

Start in Sant Antoni, a leafy area that’s only a few metro stops from the Gothic Quarter, but is far more relaxed, with its own covered market and a lively restaurant scene. L’Eixample is busier but also has wide tree-lined avenues and Gaudi buildings. El Born is gritty and energetic. El Raval is multicultural and – if we’re being honest – occasionally a little too edgy. Poblenou is a creative hub. And El Poble-sec has a vastly underrated restaurant scene.

If you’ve been to Barcelona you have probably already visited – or at least know about – La Boqueria, the iconic market accessible from ultra-touristy La Rambla. It’s worth a look around, though on a second or third visit to Barcelona it’s time to explore some of the city’s other markets, which are just as exciting and often far easier to access and enjoy.

Begin close by at Santa Caterina, in El Born, with its mix of fresh produce and on-site restaurants making use of those ingredients. Move on to Sant Antoni, a 19th-century covered market that has recently been renovated and features a blend of fresh and prepared foods. The Mercat de la Concepcio is a flower market in L’Eixample, a pleasure to stroll around, while Mercat de la Barceloneta specialises in seafood, reflective of its position near the beach.

It sometimes feels as if the fortunes of Barcelona the city are very much determined by the fortunes of Barcelona the soccer team. Win, and all is right with the world. Lose and it’s a disaster. FC Barcelona is one of the biggest clubs on the planet – its motto is “Mes que un club”, or “more than a club” – and to attend a match here is to understand something vital about Catalan identity and local obsessions.

Those who have visited before will now find the club’s stadium, the Camp Nou, unrecognisable: it was demolished in 2023 and, much like La Sagrada Familia, is in an extended process of construction, due to finish in two years, though the new facility is already being used to host club matches. Tickets are available via the club’s official portal, which resells unused members’ passes: fcbarcelona. com

If you fancy a sporting experience that’s cheaper and easier to access, Barcelona is home to another top-league soccer team, RCD Espanyol. There’s also EuroLeague basketball in the city, plus motorsports and tennis. Or, just go down to Barceloneta beach for a swim.

There are some big-ticket museums and art galleries that return visitors to Barcelona may have been to before, but almost certainly warrant a second look. We’re talking the Picasso Museum, the Fundacio Joan Miro, the Museu Nacional d’Art de Catalunya, and the Museum of Contemporary Art of Barcelona. All very popular, but with good reason.

If you would like to extend your reach a little, however, there are some excellent options. There’s the Museu de la Xocolata, aka the Chocolate Museum, whose attraction should really speak for itself. The Moco Museum is a smaller modern art gallery housed in a 16th-century palace. And BUAT Gallery has a collection of works by well-known artists that are up for sale.

Consider the great cities of Europe: Rome, Paris, Amsterdam, Prague, London, Berlin. None have a beach. None are even coastal. But Barcelona has multiple, gorgeous stretches of sand that are a cultural experience in themselves. There’s bustle and energy as locals and tourists alike sun themselves and relax.

Barceloneta is the most popular, given its proximity to the city, just a 15-minute walk from La Rambla. Playa de Bogatell is far more relaxed, and the perfect option if you’re staying in trendy Poblenou. Directly to the north of Bogatell, Playa Mar Bella is LGBTQI+ friendly, and has a clothing-optional section. And Nova Icaria is small and low-key.

The city also has a huge amount of green space in which to take time away from the built-up areas. Try Parc de Cervantes, a sprawling area in the west of the city with extensive rose gardens; Jardins de Joan Brossa for excellent hilltop views; Parc del Mirador de Poble-Sec for incredible city vistas; and Tibidabo, a mountaintop reserve on the edge of the city that also features a charming, old-school amusement park.

One of the best things to do after a few days in Barcelona is get out of Barcelona – particularly if you have visited before – and there are two very good reasons why: Cava and calcots. Barcelona is right next to Penedes, Cava country, the home of this globally famous wine.

It’s only about a one-hour drive from the centre of the city to the likes of Sant Sadurni, which is home to Freixenet, a well-known winery with a host of different tour and tasting options, and Recaredo, a high-end producer of beautiful drops. A gentle wander around town there will also bring you to several more cellar doors.

If you visit between November and April, meanwhile, continue your journey another 40 minutes or so to Valls, the birthplace and spiritual home of a Catalan obsession: calcots. The long, sweet onions are harvested in the cooler months. They’re served during “calcotada”, a day-long celebration of all that’s good about Catalan winter cuisine, from smoky, grilled calcots dipped in nutty salbitxada sauce, to fried artichokes with aioli, to grilled meats and, finally, crema Catalana, all served with plenty of cava and red wine.

There are plenty more reasons to escape Barcelona for a day, and plenty of means to do it. Begin with a trip to Badalona, a neighbouring city known for its long stretch of beach and its laid-back, local atmosphere, so different to Barcelona and yet accessible by train in 20 or so minutes.

A little further afield, the city of Girona is only 40 minutes by fast train, and has much to offer in terms of historic architecture, as well as being the home of the world-renowned fine-dining restaurant El Celler de Can Roca. Further north, Figueres is the birthplace of Salvador Dali, and a museum there displays the surrealist’s work.

To the south, Sitges is a bohemian seaside town with a relaxed atmosphere, 40 minutes by train from central Barcelona. Tarragona is about an hour away, and has extensive Roman ruins.

And then there’s Montserrat, a mountaintop area inland from the city, accessible via train and cable car from Barcelona. Here visitors can see an 11th-century Benedictine monastery housing the Virgin of Montserrat, a wood carving also known as the Black Madonna.

Another reason to revisit one of the world’s great cities is a swag of new hotels. The most famous is probably the Grand Hyatt Barcelona, which opened in 2024 after a €20 million renovation of the old Hotel Princess Sofia in Les Corts, making it Spain’s first Grand Hyatt in an urban environment. Around the same time, Borneta opened in El Born. It’s a swish 92-room property with a high-end restaurant on site. There’s also the Social Hub, a relatively new, four-star hotel with co-working spaces in lively Poblenou.

A stay at any of these properties will help visitors avoid contributing to a growing issue in Barcelona right now: the proliferation of short-term apartment rentals, and the displacement of local residents. There’s a plan to phase out these rentals entirely by November 2028.

Barcelona is an easy city to get around, with plenty of public transport options. If you didn’t ride the metro or the buses on your first visit, then it’s time to dive in.

Travel writer

Most major sights around the city are covered by the metro, which has 12 lines and runs until late into the night. Buses and trams are also simple to use, particularly if you plug your destination into your maps app and follow the instructions from there. To ride, either purchase a 10-journey ticket, which will cover metro, buses and trams, or if you’re staying longer, a monthly pass will be better value. There’s also the Hola Barcelona Card, a tourist pass that offers unlimited transport for a set number of days, and includes transfers to and from the airport.

Barcelona has a bike-share system called Bicing, though you’ll only be able to use it if you’re a Spanish resident. See tmb. cat

Barcelona does have issues. It’s a very popular city – sometimes too popular – and locals feel their lives are being impacted in a negative way. So if you’re returning to the city, and you should, it’s an opportunity to visit in a responsible, sustainable way.

That means staying in a registered hotel, rather than a short-term apartment stay. It means shopping and eating in independent, locally owned establishments, supporting places that serve local interests as well as those of tourists.

Learn a few words of Catalan, rather than Spanish, to speak to locals and respect their identity. Visit in off-peak times instead of the height of summer. Behave in ways you would like visitors to behave in your home. Stay for multiple nights instead of ducking in and out.

Treat Barcelona with love, and there’s a very good chance Barcelona will love you back.

See thisisbarcelona. com
