UK appoints world’s first special representative for climate security

The Guardian Wed, 11 Nov 2026 22:30:01 GMT

Exclusive: Madeleine Alessandri, former chair of joint intelligence committee, will take on role of advising No 10 on climate-related national security risks

The UK government has appointed the world’s first special representative for climate security, in the strongest sign yet of fears that climate breakdown will bring chaos to the country.

Prime minister Andy Burnham will announce the move on Thursday at Cop31, the UN climate summit, with the new role designed to advise the government on national security risks from the climate crisis before they spell catastrophe.

Burnham will tell the key climate talks on Thursday morning: “We should all recognise the summer was not normal. The climate crisis is upon all of us now. We saw that with the wildfires that devastated lives and livelihoods everywhere.”

This year’s summer was the UK’s hottest on record, with back-to-back heatwaves supercharged by the climate crisis causing health services and transport to suffer, schools to close and thousands of people to lose their lives prematurely.

Burnham will add: “The message I carry here, in my first Cop as prime minister, is that the UK remains determined to reach net zero by 2050 and to work with our partners to build a clean energy future. The world has changed. The consensus we once enjoyed on science and climate action has broken down. “We will not stand by, and that’s why I’ve pledged a new era of British leadership over the next decade.”

Burnham arrived in Antalya, Turkey late on Wednesday night, before joining scores of heads of state and government for a series of high-level meetings at the talks, which are presided over jointly by Turkey and Australia. He will also confirm UK support for a proposed target of 35% electrification by 2035 and help towards plans to raise £5bn in private finance for clean energy projects across the world.

Madeleine Alessandri, the former chair of the UK’s joint intelligence committee (JIC), which oversees MI5 and MI6, will take on the special representative job.

But campaigners pointed to what they said were Burnham’s failures to take the measures needed to reduce greenhouse gas emissions at home, and to provide the funding needed to protect vulnerable countries overseas from the kind of risks the JIC has warned about. The government is mulling a major weakening of targets for electric vehicles and has given the green light to a gasfield, Jackdaw, in the North Sea while considering a new oilfield, Rosebank, west of Shetland.

“What we’re seeing in part is double standards,” Mohamed Adow, director of the Power Shift Africa thinktank, told the Guardian. “We can’t have Britain preaching a clean development gospel but expanding fossil fuels back at home. You cannot expect one set of rules for Africa and another for Britain.”

The UK’s credibility was “crumbling”, said Asad Rehman, chief executive of Friends of the Earth England, Wales and Northern Ireland. “The prime minister’s first climate talks should be an opportunity to demonstrate he means business. But if this is all the UK has to offer, then the questions piling in about his climate credibility are more than justified.”

Under Alessandri, the JIC collaborated on a secret report warning that within five years the UK could begin experiencing national security impacts from the collapse of ecosystems overseas, driven by the climate crisis and overexploitation of the living world. These impacts included food shortages, rising food prices, mass migration and conflict among nuclear-armed countries.

The report was suppressed under former prime minister Keir Starmer, but its contents were revealed by the Guardian last year, ahead of a redacted publication earlier this year.

Dame Madeleine Alessandri said: “Climate change and nature loss are increasingly shaping the security environment in which the UK operates, placing additional pressure on resources, economies and communities around the world. “The best time to address these risks is before they develop into crises. In this role, I will work with partners across government and internationally to strengthen our understanding of climate threats, build resilience and ensure we are better prepared for the challenges ahead.”

The risks of the climate crisis to national security were also highlighted by Ed Miliband, foreign secretary, who has been briefing foreign capitals on the findings of the JIC report. He is also at Cop31 this week, and told the Guardian: “National security is the next frontier of the fight for climate action – the scenarios once of science fiction are now regular occurrences in the daily news.”

He added: “Climate breakdown is one of the greatest national security threats we face: food security, threats to infrastructure and population movements [are resulting from the climate crisis].

“Those who seek to stick their heads in the sand on climate are putting our national security at risk.”

In common with many wealthy nations, the UK has significantly rolled back its climate finance, funnelling money instead to military spending. In July, Burnham fronted a pledge to lower the cap on UK bus fares, funded by changing international climate donations into repayable loans.

Prakash Dahal of Pro Public and Friends of the Earth Nepal said finance was vital for his country’s adaptation to climate breakdown, and recovery from disasters such as the catastrophic flash flood that struck Nepal in August. “Crucially, this essential funding must come as grants – not loans,” he said. “Nepal is not asking for charity. Nepal is demanding justice.”

The subheading and text of this article were amended on 12 November 2026. Madeleine Alessandri is the former chair of the joint intelligence committee, not the current chiar, as an earlier version suggested. She left the role in May 2026.

‘The world we know is over’ without urgent climate action, leaders tell Cop31

The Guardian Wed, 11 Nov 2026 18:52:08 GMT

Marshall Islands president warns of worsening floods as UN chief calls for a windfall tax on oil and gas firms

Failure to provide an overwhelming response to the climate crisis means “the world we know is over”, the president of the embattled Marshall Islands has warned, as dozens of leaders gathered in Turkey for the Cop31 climate summit.

Hilda Heine, one of a handful of Pacific Island leaders to make an impassioned speech at Cop31 on Wednesday, told other heads of state that overshooting the 1.5C Paris temperature target would mean waves eating away their shores and floods that destroy towns, schools and hospitals.

She described seeing bright, lush coral beneath the water of her home island in July that had been bleached white just months later.

“It’s time to wake up,” said Heine. “Our response to the threat of overshoot must be overwhelming, or the world we know is over.”

Mia Mottley, the prime minister of Barbados, also called out governments who had “not tried hard enough” to curb emissions since the Paris agreement.

“The UN tells us that, even if every pledge is delivered, we are heading for 2.6 degrees,” she said. “On current policies, 2.8 degrees is where we will end up.

“Let me be plain: overshoot is not a new target. It is a debt, a debt of heat, borrowed against our children’s future. And it must be repaid.”

The opening of the summit of international leaders, on day three of Cop31, saw impassioned speeches interspersed with vigorous displays of Turkish music and dancing.

António Guterres, the UN secretary general, blamed a deceitful fossil fuel industry and countries that “keep expanding fossil fuel production while claiming to be committed to 1.5C”. His speech – a salvo aimed at boosting the talks – was one of the last speeches Guterres, a vocal climate advocate, will deliver as secretary general before he stands down next month.

“We need an extraordinary acceleration,” Guterres said. “Our planet is heating up. The clock is winding down. It’s make or bake time.

“Fossil fuels must go the way of the dinosaurs,” he added. “And that won’t happen on its own. The dinosaurs did not have a lobby – fossil fuels do.”

Guterres said oil and gas companies had distorted science and delayed action on the climate crisis, and called for a windfall tax on the bumper profits they have made from the Iran war. “It’s time to kick the habit and end the fossil-fuel addiction,” he said, to applause. “It’s time for governments to tax these windfall profits and use them to help vulnerable countries recover. Polluters must pay.”

Unusually, Turkey is co-hosting Cop with Australia, with the leaders of both countries, Recep Tayyip Erdoğan and Anthony Albanese respectively, each praising the partnership.

Erdoğan said he wants Cop31 to be remembered as a turning point in the climate crisis and called on countries to act, rather than just make promises. “Every minute we fail to meet the targets in the Paris agreement, the risks and costs we face continue to grow,” the Turkish president said. However, on Monday, away from the conference hall, ​​Erdoğan celebrated the discovery of two new oilfields with an estimated in-situ potential of 135m barrels.

In her speech before world leaders, Heine said every new oil well drilled and every piece of coal extracted was a threat to her country’s future. Without naming any individual oil or gas producer, she added: “The discovery of new fossil fuel resources is not something to celebrate but something to fear.”

Albanese said the conference was a “historic moment” for Australia. The country is one of the world’s biggest exporters of coal and liquefied gas. Albanese said governments had a “solemn responsibility” to act on the climate crisis, but he was criticised for failing to mention fossil fuels in his speech.

The gathering of leaders was relatively threadbare. While 91 national leaders attended, according to the UN, major figures such as Donald Trump of the US and Xi Jinping of China were absent. Perhaps tellingly, some other leaders who declined to attend, including the French president, Emmanuel Macron, and the German chancellor, Friedrich Merz, are instead heading to Ireland for a conference on AI.

Almost every country at Cop31 is lagging in cutting emissions, with insufficient finance for the nations most vulnerable to extreme heat, floods, fires and other climate-fuelled calamities.

Although the world is barrelling past the 1.5C limit and is entering the teeth of one of the strongest El Niño events in history, there is little sign that the talks will feature any further progress on phasing out planet-heating fossil fuels.

“I’m getting a feeling of panic from around here, from the science community,” said Bill Hare, a climate scientist and chief executive of Climate Analytics, who described fraught conversations with rainforest and cryosphere scientists. “The mood is gradually darkening among scientists. In fact, people talk about feeling as though things have gone backwards.”

Small island nations face an existential threat from rising sea levels and are some of the countries most exposed to catastrophe when global heating shoots past 1.5C. The UN Environment Programme has found that such overshoot is now inevitable, and warned that its effects on icy regions will be so calamitous it should be kept as brief and low as possible.

Other world leaders stressed the urgency of this moment of multiple crises and the need for multilateralism to finally deliver. Gordana Siljanovska-Davkova, the president of North Macedonia, said: “We are the first generation to fully understand the consequences of our choices – and perhaps the last with time to change course. Future generations will live with the consequences of our decisions.”

Nataša Pirc Musar, the president of Slovenia, said: “If we cannot agree that human dignity and respect for nature must be at the heart of our decisions then, frankly, what is left to unite us?”

National security of all countries at risk due to climate crisis, UK foreign secretary warns

The Guardian Wed, 11 Nov 2026 09:09:47 GMT

Exclusive: Ed Miliband says sci-fi scenarios of destruction ‘now regular occurrences’, as he prepares to address Cop31

The national security of all countries is at risk from the climate crisis, as “science fiction” scenarios of widespread destruction are already coming true and economic shocks from fossil fuels are now the norm rather than the exception, the UK’s foreign secretary is to warn world leaders gathered in Turkey.

Ed Miliband will tell the Cop31 UN climate summit on Wednesday that security and defence objectives are the new “frontier” of climate action, because the rapid heating of the planet will lead to food shortages, widespread economic disruption, migration and conflict.

“National security is the next frontier of the fight for climate action; the scenarios once of science fiction are now regular occurrences in the daily news,” Miliband told the Guardian before his speech to world leaders and governments in Antalya.

“We should be clear that climate breakdown is one of the greatest national security threats we face. Food security, threats to infrastructure, and population movements [are resulting from the climate crisis],” he said.

In a veiled swipe at the Conservatives and Reform UK, which want to scrap efforts to cut greenhouse gas emissions, he added: “Those who seek to stick their heads in the sand on climate are putting our national security at risk.”

Miliband arrived in Turkey on Tuesday evening for the two-day leaders’ summit segment on Wednesday and Thursday of the fortnight-long Cop31 talks, which started on Monday.

Andy Burnham, the UK prime minister, is expected to travel on Wednesday for a series of bilateral meetings with fellow world leaders on Thursday.

Anthony Albanese, the prime minister of Australia, and the Turkish president, Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, will open the leaders’ summit segment on Wednesday. There will also be speeches by the UN secretary general, António Guterres, President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva of Brazil, which hosted last year’s Cop, and the prime minister of Ethiopia, Abiy Ahmed, who will host next year’s meeting.

However, several heads of leading countries are skipping this year’s Cop, including China’s Xi Jinping, India’s Narendra Modi, France’s Emmanuel Macron and Germany’s Friedrich Merz. The European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, will attend.

Miliband will argue that the world must now face the consequences of failures to cut carbon emissions over the past three decades. “It is a disaster for people and the planet, and we must reckon with its implications,” he will tell audiences at Cop31 on Wednesday. “It will drive hardship and insecurity for billions of people.”

He will note that an “overshoot” of the crucial threshold of 1.5C of global heating above preindustrial levels, is now inevitable, as temperatures have exceeded that level for two years and are unlikely to subside significantly. This “overshoot” requires stronger policies to ensure heating does not accelerate, and to seek ways of returning temperatures to safer levels in decades to come.

Fossil fuel shocks, such as the soaring oil price seen this year after the start of the Iran war, which has led to rampant inflation and interest rate rises from central banks in an effort to control it, will wreak further harm, according to Miliband.

He told the Guardian: “A new era of global insecurity means fossil fuel shocks are now the norm – the fossil fuel rollercoaster is here to stay. First Russia, now Iran, next others, have identified global chokepoints and systemic overreliance [on fossil fuels] and the vulnerability of countries around the world that they expose.”

He said the only answer was to “double down” on measures to cut greenhouse gas emissions and build resilience to the effects of extreme weather. “Next year will be the year of climate fightback, as governments, movements and communities across the world step up to defend our shared home.”

Miliband will call for more investment in clean energy and efforts to use it for transport and heating, as well as urgent action to cut methane, a powerful greenhouse gas, and protect and expand forests.

However, Burnham’s government is under fire in the UK for a series of recent and looming policy interventions that campaigners say will push the country off-track from its target of net zero greenhouse gas emissions by 2050, and set a poor example to the rest of the world.

The government plans to weaken a mandate for carmakers to ensure more of their vehicles are electric by 2030, and has given the green light to a new gasfield, Jackdaw, in the North Sea, while considering licensing a new oilfield, Rosebank, west of Shetland.

Arsenal dig deep to earn WCL draw in face of Barcelona dominance

The Guardian Thu, 12 Nov 2026 20:00:16 GMT

Arsenal continue to be a sharp thorn in the side of the European champions, Barcelona, digging deep to hold on to a draw here. Frida Maanum put the Gunners ahead despite a hugely dominant performance from Barcelona, but Caroline Graham Hansen’s equaliser ensured the spoils would be shared.

The last time these two teams met, Arsenal were lifting aloft the Champions League trophy at Barcelona’s expense after the most perfect of defensive performances and a Stina Blackstenius goal in Lisbon in 2025. It was a far less perfect defensive performance this time, but Arsenal showed guts against the team that retook their crown last season and showed they can play ugly when needed.

There was one change to the team that earned a 2-1 win against Liverpool on Sunday, but it was a significant one. Olivia Smith was replaced by Frida Maanum and the Norwegian slotted into the No 10 role with Alessia Russo, who has scored 12 goals in nine games for club and country, moving into the centre-forward position. Russo’s position has been a constant talking point during Arsenal’s struggles, but her exploits have shown where she plays does not really matter.

It was the England forward’s play on the left that provoked the shock first-half goal that temporarily silenced the crowd. The 27-year-old beat two and worked the ball to Maanum. Barcelona got the ball away, but Russo was there again and delivered a perfect cross across the face of goal for Caitlin Foord. The Australian forced a close-range save from Cata Coll, but Maanum was there to power in the loose ball.

The pocket of travelling fans behind plexiglass in the upper tier were jubilant. About 1,000 had travelled despite the late switch of the match to Thursday due to a 24-hour general strike in Spain on Wednesday.

It was a goal decidedly against the run of play, but Barcelona struggled to capitalise on their dominance in the first half, despite some shaky moments at the back from the visitors. Ewa Pajor and Caroline Graham Hansen were particularly threatening as Barcelona targeted Arsenal’s left, made up of the less experienced Taylor Hinds and Lisa Baum.

The scoreline at the break was a little unfathomable based on the run of play and the domestic fortunes of both sides. While Arsenal languish in sixth in the WSL, 12 points behind the league leaders, Manchester City, Barcelona have won nine of their 10 games in Liga F, having scored 41 goals and conceded five and have a five point lead over their nearest rivals, Real Madrid.

Arsenal’s gameplan felt familiar, it was as if they had studied the blueprint religiously followed by teams that have sat back in a low block and frustrated them week-in week-out in the WSL this season.

Pere Romeu had made three changes to the team that earned a 5-1 win over Madrid CFF on Sunday and the surprise was that three-time Ballon d’Or winner Aitana Bonmati was relegated to the bench. It was her arrival shortly before the hour mark that elevated Barcelona’s threat, causing Arsenal’s defending to look even more calamitous at times, and lifted the mood in a frustrated stadium.

Pork fat, a heating pad and a five-storey jump: how a 74-year-old escaped house arrest in Argentina

The Guardian Thu, 12 Nov 2026 19:52:16 GMT

Leonardo Bertulazzi, ex-member of Italy’s radical far-left Red Brigades, fled in dramatic fashion, ‘like something out of a movie’

As dozens of police and sniffer dogs poured into San Telmo, a traditional Buenos Aires neighbourhood with cobblestone streets, on Tuesday morning, one of the clerks at a shop selling dulce de leche asked them why. He said they were “looking for a bomb”.

It was only later that she found out there was no danger of being blown up after all, and that authorities were, in fact, hunting for a fugitive. “An Italian mafioso, right?” she asked.

The escapee was no mobster, exactly: he was Leonardo Bertulazzi, 74, a former member of Italy’s radical far-left militant group the Red Brigades, who had been living under house arrest in Argentina after his arrest in 2024, awaiting extradition to Italy to serve a 27-year sentence.

On Tuesday, however, the 74-year-old escaped from house arrest in dramatic fashion.

“It was like something out of a movie,” said a person with knowledge of the investigation who asked to remain anonymous.

At around 6am, when most security forces “were focused on the Pope’s security” as the pontiff was visiting Argentina, Bertulazzi cut off his ankle monitor, the source said. In order to bypass its temperature and pressure sensors, Bertulazzi apparently wrapped it in a tube with pork fat and left it next to a heating pad.

He then rappelled down from his apartment’s fifth floor, jumped in to a vacant lot behind the building, and then scaled a metal gate to reach the street.

Two weeks prior, an alert in the ankle monitor’s system had gone off, indicating that he might have been tinkering with the machine. On Tuesday, police noticed his ankle monitor had stopped transmitting movement data entirely, and headed to the house – only to find him missing.

“He knew exactly what he was doing”, said the source. “After all, he’s a guy who worked in logistics for the Italian brigade.”

Indeed, Bertulazzi once held a senior position in the Red Brigades, an organization responsible for a series of attacks throughout the 1970s, dubbed Italy’s “Years of Lead”. The group most notoriously kidnapped and assassinated former prime minister Aldo Moro in 1978.

He had been sentenced in absentia on terrorism charges in Italy in 1985 and 1997 and was living in Argentina in 2002 when, after years on the run, Bertulazzi was first arrested by Argentine authorities. He was freed a few months later, and in 2004 he secured refugee status. But it was revoked two years ago, and he was arrested again and put under house arrest, for health concerns. Italy’s rightwing prime minister, Giorgia Meloni, framed the move as a significant political win made possible by her government’s close relations with Argentina’s president, Javier Milei.

After he fled, Italy’s interior ministry undersecretary, Wanda Ferro, said Argentinian police were responsible because they were “supposed to ensure surveillance and the handover [of Bertulazzi] to the Italian authorities”, and urged his swift reapprehension. On Wednesday, Argentina’s security ministry offered a $13,000 reward for information leading to Bertulazzi’s recapture.

The Italian press has reacted to the escape with bemusement, noting his ability to abseil from a fifth-floor balcony despite the 74-year-old’s supposedly poor health – which his lawyer, Rodolfo Yanzon, had used as a reason to argue he couldn’t board a plane back to Italy. Bertulazzi, Yanzon said, suffered three strokes during his two years in detention, and had difficulty walking. He said he told his client on Monday that the judge would not authorise medical testing, however – which he suspects inspired Bertulazzi to flee before he could be extradited. “That was the last thing I said to Bertulazzi,” he added. “He undoubtedly made the decision to prioritise his freedom over his health.”

In an interview with La Repubblica, Bertulazzi’s daughter, Claudia, said he “had no choice” but to flee after an Argentinian court on 3 November rejected his appeal to keep his refugee status, and that he feared spending “the rest of his life in prison” in Italy.

Bertulazzi fled the country in 1980 after being found guilty in the kidnapping of shipowner Pietro Costa, generating a ransom that was allegedly used to fund the Red Brigades’ terrorist activities and to buy a flat in Rome where Moro was held captive. A court in Genoa sentenced him to 27 years in prison.

For years, a complex legal situation meant Bertulazzi could live as a free man in Argentina despite being wanted in Italy. He was arrested in 2002 in Buenos Aires after a joint investigation with Interpol, but was released eight months later because his Italian trials had been held in absentia, preventing his extradition.

Claudi said her father doesn’t fear a retrial: “Partly because, under current laws, we are convinced the only charge that would remain is of participating in an armed group, a charge he has never denied and for which he would accept responsibility.”

She also said she last spoke to her father two days previously and only learned of his escape through the media. “He removed his electronic ankle monitor and lowered himself from the fifth floor using a harness. It’s plausible: he was a mountaineer.”

Trump says no deal needed on Iran war and orders Vance to focus on domestic issues

The Guardian Thu, 12 Nov 2026 19:01:16 GMT

President says vice-president will focus on supposed ‘Massive Corruption and Crime taking place in Democrat run Cities and States’

US politics live – latest updates

Donald Trump has said that the US is no longer seeking a deal to end the war with Iran and ordered JD Vance, who had spearheaded recent efforts to restart negotiations with Iran, to focus on domestic politics instead.

In a post to his social media site on Thursday, Trump said he was redirecting the vice-president to focus his “complete and total attention on the Massive Corruption and Crime taking place in Democrat run Cities and States throughout the U. S”.

Vance had reportedly been talking to intermediaries in Iran and Qatar about restarting negotiations to end the war, which began in February when the US and Israel launched joint strikes on Iran. Iran responded by closing access to the strait of Hormuz, which led to a steep increase for the cost of fuel around the globe.

But on Thursday Trump appeared to shut down the negotiations, redirecting Vance to focus on domestic issues and downplaying the need for a final deal.

“We don’t need a deal with Iran,” Trump wrote. “Those days have long since passed. We’ve got their money, Hundreds of Billions of Dollars, and we’ve got their Strait!”

The announcement effectively normalises a stalemate with Iran. The US has maintained a blockade on Iranian ports and mostly reopened the strait of Hormuz to marine traffic, including crude oil shipments. But the US has not carried out massive strikes against Iran for several months, and Iran has not launched barrages of ballistic missiles against US bases and allies in the region.

Trump last week also downplayed the possibility of new strikes on Iran and said that the war was “effectively over”.

During a White House press conference, Trump said that Israel and Gulf allies in the region were well protected from Iran, and that an escalation was not needed.

“At this point, taking the military action doesn’t seem to be a very necessary thing – but we’re locked and loaded, ready to go for any reason,” he told reporters during a briefing at the White House, which took place shortly after he met with Qatar’s prime minister, Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani.

Trump said he had been lobbied by the leaders of Gulf states not to resume the war.

The decision effectively sidelines Vance from the main foreign policy challenge of his vice-presidency. He had publicly distanced himself from the war, and in April he led a US delegation to Islamabad to negotiate an end to it. Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner and envoy Steve Witkoff have also been involved in negotiations.

Axios last week reported that Vance was speaking “almost daily” with Sheikh Mohammed; Pakistan’s army head, Asim Munir; and other mediators. Several weeks ago he also sent a letter to Mohsen Rezaei, the secretary of the Supreme National Security Council, to resume direct negotiations.

Vance last week blamed the conflict for the historic rout dealt to Republicans in the midterm elections.

“The reason we lost is the war,” Vance said after the midterms in a lengthy post on X. “The president himself said so last night.”

Trump has since doubled down on launching the war on Iran, admitting that it drove up fuel prices but repeating his frequent assertion that it was needed to prevent Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon.

The Guardian view on Gaza’s misery: don’t let Palestinian deaths mount in this bleak winter

The Guardian Thu, 12 Nov 2026 18:54:58 GMT

The formation of a new Israeli government won’t stop the killing, but sustained international pressure must be applied

What do you call a ceasefire when the firing has not ceased? The killings in Gaza decreased when the truce was announced last October, but they did not end. Israel’s strike on Thursday morning on one of the few remaining functioning hospitals, which killed six people and wounded 28 more, was the first on a healthcare facility since then. But it was not an anomaly. About four Palestinians a day have died on average since the ceasefire was declared.

The Israeli military said that it had struck a Hamas commander and other fighters in the attack on Nasser hospital, without providing evidence. Its record does not inspire confidence in the accuracy of its account. Multiple UN experts and health campaigners have warned of the deliberate targeting of medical facilities and healthcare workers. Israeli military personnel have also described the shockingly high level of civilian deaths tolerated as “collateral damage” in targeting even low-level fighters after the brutal Hamas attacks of 7 October 2023.

Many more Palestinians are dying because of the war. With more than four-fifths of Gaza’s buildings destroyed, storms and the cold are proving deadly, killing at least four children and a woman last weekend. The UN says that 940,000 people are in makeshift shelters in areas at risk of flooding. Sewage is spewing into tents. In desperation, families are risking a return to ruined homes – with some dying in building collapses.

Reconstruction is the real need, but even the absolute basics are lacking: the UN says Israel is blocking 150,000 tents that are ready for use, along with other sorely needed goods, including sanitation equipment and nutrient-dense peanut butter. As an occupying power, Israel has a responsibility under international law to meet the needs of Gaza’s people. Allowing in the aid they desperately need should be the absolute minimum expected of it.

Even Donald Trump’s Netanyahu-friendly Board of Peace has urged Israel to allow in all humanitarian supplies and said that its response is insufficient – but it shows no inclination to actually use its leverage. Israel says that it has let in trucks and tents but that reconstruction can’t begin until Hamas “fully disarms”.

Gadi Eisenkot, a former head of the military, has six weeks to form a government following elections last month, in which Benjamin Netanyahu lost his mandate. Substantial improvements are unlikely even if Mr Eisenkot succeeds; the fate of civilians in Gaza was more of an issue in the US midterms than in the Israeli election.

But as Israel gradually begins to digest the extraordinary shift in international opinion underlined by the US midterms – with about three in 10 Americans now believing that it has committed genocide – other governments have a fresh opportunity to press for change. They must use not just words but deeds. Mr Netanyahu has suggested that Israel could become an isolated “super-Sparta”. Yet it is dependent – for security, trade and diplomatically – on the US and Europe.

Other nations must also pay up: shockingly, the World Food Programme said last month that it has had to cut the number of people it can help by half a million because funding has slumped. Israel’s obstruction increases the cost of relief, and its barring of aid groups is another obstacle. Now is the time to exert maximum pressure to ensure that Palestinians can survive this winter – and that they have a future worth living for.

The Guardian view on venture capitalism: investor profits are no industrial strategy

The Guardian Thu, 12 Nov 2026 18:53:12 GMT

Higher returns for backers do not guarantee national prosperity. Public investment should develop domestic capabilities and meet urgent social needs

Britain keeps selling its most valuable companies. The Financial Times calculates that 300 went to foreign buyers, mostly American, over the past decade. What if innovation were scaled up to serve social needs here rather than US investors’ profits? That is the provocation issued by the thinktank Common Wealth in a paper titled We Aren’t the Champions, which takes aim at the UK’s venture capital (VC) industry.

The authors say that as long as the UK is subordinated to US cash, getting startups to a heavyweight size will be a sisyphean task. Britain’s tech pioneers are often sold before they become giants. DeepMind, founded in London in 2010, went to Google just four years later. Britain’s venture capitalists might argue that they are in it for themselves, not for building up British tech.

The conventional wisdom is that if startups are struggling to grow, the problem must be that they lack capital. That is why Rachel Reeves, as chancellor, wanted pension funds to invest in UK assets. But the paper says that this risks making things worse. Putting cash into startups risks inflating eventual sale prices without securing British ownership or control.

The London School of Economics’ Nils Peters and David Kampmann expose a circular logic. The UK lacks tech giants that can acquire successful startups, but selling those startups overseas helps perpetuate that problem. The authors say US and European incumbents won big from the exit of the 38 biggest UK VC-backed tech firms between 2010 and 2023, including businesses at the forefront of AI, fintech and biotechnology.

Selling British technology companies abroad can enrich investors while thwarting ambitions to build domestic champions. The social costs also matter. A system geared towards maximising capital gains favours businesses that promise lucrative exits. The paper argues that this has encouraged surveillance technologies, from wearables to AI chatbots, and exploitative gig platforms, concentrating wealth among a few rather than delivering social benefits.

Gordon Brown is right: Britain should retain ownership of its innovations. But there is a difference between financial returns and industrial development – and improving the former doesn’t necessarily deliver the latter. Although industrial policy has returned rhetorically in the west, this has not translated into meaningful policy. The Common Wealth paper suggests that is a mistake and argues for democratic control over innovation, with investment directed towards social purposes.

The paper’s preferred capitalism is one that is historically associated with the global south: curbing extractive intermediaries, limiting foreign capital and building domestic capacity. India’s publicly funded space programme and Ethiopia’s state-owned airline show how sustained public investment can support homegrown capabilities rather than hastily readying businesses for sale.

Most daringly, Brazil linked universal healthcare for 215 million people to industrial policy, using public purchasing, laboratories and technology transfer. The payoff came during the pandemic: by August 2021, almost three-quarters of Covid vaccine doses administered had been produced at home. Brazil shows that a state can finance, research and produce a universal healthcare system that creates employment and productive capacity. It is surely a powerful idea that providing for people could be a way of sustaining output. Making the fulfilment of social needs a motor of economic development would give Labour a purpose beyond managing scarcity.

Spare a thought for poor Nige, clearly missing his podcast chats with Russell Brand

The Guardian Thu, 12 Nov 2026 18:52:54 GMT

It’s not been a good week for Farage. Aside from that interview and disrespect from the BBC, he’s lost another senior Reform official

It’s a day late, but please observe a two-minute silence for Nigel Farage. Lest we forget. Sad to say, but Nige just hasn’t been quite the same since Sunday’s Remembrance service at the Cenotaph. Like me, you might have thought that he had been in Whitehall to honour those who had died in two world wars and subsequent armed conflicts. Only it turns out he was really there to commemorate himself.

Through his personal valet, Richard Tice, Nige has let it be known that he was extremely angry with the BBC’s coverage of the service. The cameras had spent too long lingering on the faces of the king, other members of the royal family and prime ministers past and present. When what they should have been focused on throughout was Nige. He was the one we were all there to see. The man who had done more for his country than anyone else. To have disrespected him in this way was unforgivable. Let’s hope the BBC has got its act together by next year.

That’s not all. These are tough times for the Reform leader. He’s furious about a lot of things. He’s furious the polls show his party in third place on 20%. Clear establishment bias. Though oddly he was perfectly happy when the same polls showed him 10 points clear of Labour and the Tories. He’s spitting mad that he has had to part ways with the Reform’s general secretary who had been in charge of vetting. Turns out the vetting that Nige had insisted was the best in the country turned out to have been conducted by someone who was the opposite. Schrödinger would have something to say about that.

Then there are Nige’s links to Russell Brand. Guess which politician was happy to go on the now convicted rapist’s podcast, long after allegations against him had become public knowledge and no one else would touch him with a barge pole? That’s right. It’s Nige. Because if Reform is about anything it’s “family, community, country”. And no one sums up “family, community, country” more than Russell. It wasn’t clear whether Russell thought he was there to forgive Nige or the other way round. Or just two narcissists in need of attention.

So it wasn’t altogether a surprise to find that Nige was laying low this week. Perhaps he was just trying to negotiate an appearance on the podcast of another celebrity accused of using his fame to have sex with vulnerable younger women. There seem to be a lot of them around. Or maybe Nige just fancied a break. Needed time to come to terms with the disappointment of only being on screen for a few seconds as he laid his wreath. Whatever the case, it was the Reform B Team that got sent to Thursday’s rally in Wolverhampton. An hour of everyone’s time they will never get back.

First up was Dicky Tice. The person of so little talent or personality that he would still only be the warm-up act if he was the only person on the bill. It’s hard to think of any politician who is so pleased to be so empty-headed. Trying to explain away the cost of living rise of food over the past 10 years as the result of a packaging tax. Dicky, Dicky, Dicky. Please let someone talk you through the costs of Brexit, the wars in Ukraine and Iran – for which you were a cheerleader – and fertiliser and energy costs. There again, this is probably well above his pay grade.

Next up was Zia Yusuf. An altogether more terrifying prospect. Not because he is any brighter or more credible, but because he seems to have been taking acting lessons from Bruno Ganz in Downfall. Every sentence begins with a shout, getting ever louder before reaching a crescendo yell. To be fair to him, it’s possible he’s a bit deaf and this is the only way he can hear himself talk. In which case, someone should help him out.

Zia is also a one-trick pony. Everyone is against him and it’s all the fault of foreigners. “THE ESTABLISHMENT ARE OUT TO GET US,” he shrieked. More upset that no journalists had investigated the Tories and Labour than Reform being found to be packed with racists and dodgy donations. “WE ARE GOING NOWHERE,” he concluded. I wasn’t quite sure that was the message he intended for his audience of largely elderly men and women who had nothing better to do at 3pm on a Tuesday afternoon. But it was hard to disagree. With men like Dicky and Zia in charge, it feels as if Reform have stalled.

Jensen Huang was a busted flush at Nvidia – he had to go

The Guardian Thu, 12 Nov 2026 18:46:48 GMT

CEO was viewed as ‘irreplaceable’, but recklessness of affair with a woman regarded by US officials as a Chinese spy made him a political liability

Half the tech world made up its mind before the facts could be assessed properly. Jensen Huang was “irreplaceable”, said the chorus at the start of this week. Nvidia would melt without the co-founder’s brilliance, apparently. The chipmaker’s board had to find a way to save its genius for the sake of corporate America and the entire AI universe.

It was always nonsense because, after the passage of only a few days since his confession of infidelity, Huang looked less like a towering corporate titan and more like a political liability.

An extramarital affair is not usually a resigning matter in itself – saintliness is not an absolute requirement of the job. But the circumstances here were different. A relationship with the Chinese boss of a Singapore-based firm suspected of smuggling Nvidia chips into China? That displayed recklessness on top of mere unfaithfulness.

Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning

after newsletter promotion

Did he know the Megaspeed executive, Alice Huang (no relation), was regarded as a Chinese spy by US officials? It hardly matters. In the ultra-political world of in-demand AI computer chips, there were enough reasons for him to be careful in the extreme. The conflict of interest, and the risk of landing Nvidia in a quagmire of national security inquiries in Washington, would have been obvious.

Reports of a second affair with a senior Nvidia employee compounded matters – US companies tend to be sensitive about such relationships. But the company’s directors might also have wondered what else could be revealed in coming weeks. Rule number one in these situations is to get all the bad news out on day one.

The kneejerk reaction to Jensen Huang’s resignation was 13% off the share price. That was understandable – some investors truly believed the “irreplaceable” thesis. However, sitting in Nvidia’s boardroom, the job was not to worry about the initial stock market response but about what was best for the business. For multiple reasons, it was time to “rip off the Band-Aid and take Nvidia into its next chapter”, as Dan Ives, a senior tech analyst, put it.

First, the congressional investigations will happen anyway. Democratic senators have asked administration officials to preserve all documents and communications related to the sale of Nvidia’s advanced AI chips to China. At heart, that issue is wider than Nvidia – it’s about whether US officials have themselves jeopardised the country’s lead over China in AI. But, one way or another, the company’s activities, and ties to the Trump administration, will come under scrutiny like never before. Nvidia is better placed to defend itself without Huang in the top job.

Second, his personal lobbying clout on export policy had evaporated. After this week’s revelations, he had no credibility as an advocate of looser restrictions. The political demand will be entirely in the other direction – for loopholes to be closed.

Third, there is the issue Nvidia’s underpowered board has dodged for too long: over-reliance on one individual. Never mind the risk of scandal, there is always a danger in concentrating too much day-to-day power in the hands of one individual. Nobody doubts Huang’s commercial talents, but even “godfathers of AI” in leather jackets don’t go on forever. Better to have a setup that can cope with change at the top.

Colette Kress, the chief financial officer who will stand in as chief executive, is well regarded on Wall Street. Nvidia will not be short of outside applicants on a permanent basis. And the board has heard the governance criticism that a multitrillion-dollar company ought to have an independent chair: Harvey Jones, a former chief executive at semiconductor company Synopsys and a member of the current crew of directors, has got the gig. Then comes the task of creating some proper governance checks and balances, which may require fresh faces among the independent directors.

Within a couple of hours, the fall in the share price had narrowed to 5% as investors remembered that Nvidia still has the best, and most in-demand, graphics processing units in the world and that many pioneering companies have prospered after the exit of an “irreplaceable” chief executive.

Nobody pretends the management job will be easy. Nvidia will be different, not least because the political winds in the US have shifted. But there was no point trying to cling to a chief executive, however successful, who had made himself a busted flush. Huang had to go.

UK ministers look at quick ways to limit NDAs after Walliams allegations

The Guardian Thu, 12 Nov 2026 18:38:13 GMT

Government considers further curbs on non-disclosure agreements after Guardian investigation of TV personality

Ministers are looking at ways to change the law quickly to expand protections that stop non-disclosure agreements being used to cover up harassment or discrimination in the wake of the allegations about David Walliams.

This could involve extending measures that mean an NDA cannot be used this way to silence an employee so that it also applies to others, such as freelancers or volunteers.

Following an investigation by the Guardian and ITV News, which said Walliams used his power and status to prey on young women for sex, there have been reports that NDAs were used by an employer to silence at least one woman connected to him.

Walliams, one of Britain’s best-known television personalities and a top-selling children’s author, denies any wrongdoing.

The Employment Rights Act bars NDAs being used to stop employees disclosing possible harassment or discrimination, and a recent government consultation looked at the idea of extending this protection more widely.

Such moves are expected to be speeded up after a planned meeting next week between Lisa Nandy, the culture secretary, and representatives from TV and film – both of which rely heavily on freelance or contract staff – as well as publishing and sport, to discuss possible new protections.

“We are very much in the space of looking at areas that we can change quickly and without legislation if there are loopholes,” one government official said. “It is still early but extending these protections beyond employees is definitely the sort of thing we are looking at.”

Under other existing legislation, NDAs cannot be used to stop victims or witnesses of crime from giving information to certain specified bodies, for example police or regulators.

Another possible change could extend this protection so that people could speak about crimes to anyone, including the media.

Campaigners had already been pushing for greater safeguards against NDAs before the allegations about Walliams, or the conviction of Russell Brand, who was jailed on Monday for rape and sexual assault.

Zelda Perkins, a former PA to Harvey Weinstein who broke an NDA that barred her discussing the now-jailed Hollywood producer’s predatory behaviour, and has since become a leading campaigner against their misuse, said she hoped the government, led by the Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade (DBIST), would be galvanised by the Walliams allegations.

“I have great confidence that [DBIST] are trying to create the best possible version of this,” she said. “But extending protections over harassment and discrimination beyond employees is absolutely key, and this is something where we need to keep up the pressure. The last couple of weeks have really highlighted the issues around this.”

Answering questions on Wednesday in the Commons, Nandy agreed with a Conservative question about the need to stop NDAs being abused, saying they were “central” to the problem of enforced silence.

“I am working closely with colleagues at MoJ [Ministry of Justice],” she said. “I’ve discussed this issue with them over recent days. This will be part of the conversation that we have with the creative industries when I convene the roundtable next week.”

Separate moves, albeit in the slightly longer term, are likely to lead to a law change so that any adult who has penetrative sex with a child aged under 16 would automatically be charged with rape.

This was recommended by Louise Casey’s review into sexual abuse grooming gangs published last year, following concerns that some gang members had been able to face less serious charges by claiming they had consent for the abuse.

Lady Casey has called for swifter action to protect children and young people from high-profile men, and has urged ministers to change the law to close such loopholes.

Robertson pays tribute to Dalglish as he matches Scotland cap record

The Guardian Thu, 12 Nov 2026 18:06:56 GMT

Tottenham full-back will make 102nd appearance on Friday

‘It’s another reason to honour one of the greatest players’

Andy Robertson insists his matching of Kenny Dalglish’s Scotland cap record by no means brings reputational parity. Four decades after Dalglish, widely regarded as the country’s finest player, ended his international run at 102 games Robertson will hit the same figure with the visit of North Macedonia to Hampden Park on Friday.

The Tottenham full-back is understandably delighted by his own tally – and should surpass Dalglish in Switzerland on Monday – but paid glowing tribute to the man he got to know well during nine years at Liverpool.

“For how long the record stood, for starters, for what he achieved in his career, for the person he is,” Robertson said.

“Tomorrow is another reason for our country to honour one of the greatest players that has played a game. He’s definitely the greatest from Scotland. I think it’s another reason for everyone to speak about him and realise his achievements in his footballing career. And also the person that he has been throughout his whole life.

“Obviously, in terms of number, I will stand side by side with him but I don’t want people to forget how important this man has been to our country.”

The Liverpool connection between Robertson and Dalglish adds an endearing, personal element. “He reminds me all the time that getting into the 100 caps back then was a lot harder than it is now,” said Robertson with a smile. “I never set myself personal goals. For me it’s always about the team and how I best deal with the team and things like that.

“When I overtook Darren Fletcher, when I was in the 80s, it felt like it took ages for me to get to Jim Leighton [at 91]. Then I thought: ‘I’ve only got one more to go.’

That’s when I started thinking about it a little bit more, starting to believe that it might happen a little bit more, starting to wind-up Kenny a bit more that it was going to happen. Sat here today, if it happens, it’s something I couldn’t be more proud of.’’

Why parliament needs to move out – and move on

The Guardian Thu, 12 Nov 2026 17:56:51 GMT

Readers respond to Simon Jenkins’s article suggesting that parliament should relocate out of London

Simon Jenkins is right to characterise parliament as “outdated and immune to reform” (Notre-Dame was restored in five years and under budget. But the Palace of Westminster? No chance, 6 November). However, it is not only cost, practicality and design that are compelling reasons to empty the building and move to purpose-built premises. The building and the institution in their present form are entirely inappropriate for the workplace of a modern democracy.

The self-entitlement evident in the resistance to moving out, such as that voiced by, among others, Jacob Rees-Mogg, illustrates the assumptions of class and leadership roles in those most comfortable with the status quo, and with the arcane, outdated building and rituals, which must seem bizarre and intimidating to anyone not raised in privilege and the traditional public schools.

It is way past time to modernise, to sustain those things that have made parliament a useful model, and to dispense with the decay that extends beyond just the building. Tim Lambert London

Of course parliament should move from Westminster. But instead of Manchester, Liverpool or Birmingham, which have already undergone regeneration, why not move to a city in the north-east of England? There would be several advantages to this.

Property, and the cost of living, is much cheaper, so MPs would require less in subsidies for their second homes and other allowances. It would bring a massive economic injection to a part of the country that needs renewed infrastructure: housing, services, shops and public transport.

And perhaps most important, it would sift out the dilettante politicians who enjoy posing in Westminster, and leave those who take the business of being an MP seriously; could anyone see Nigel Farage or Jacob Rees-Mogg, for example, falling over themselves to work in the north-east? Perhaps then we could move on to politics for the common good. Maggie Hamilton Oxford

Simon Jenkins is right to say that parliament should move north and do its work in a conference centre or some such.

If repairs to the Palace of Westminster take decades, so much the better. By the time they move back, legislators might have stopped caring about maces, prayer cards, division bells and men in tights banging on doors.

Those traditions, never particularly charming, have long since become a distraction and a brake on democracy.

And hopefully, after a generation or two away from Westminster, MPs will have grown out of the embarrassing habit of hooting and jeering when people are trying to speak. We could even find ourselves with a parliament of grownups – one that is bemused by the clanky, dusty, raucous old circus that it used to be. Jonathan Bastable Brighton

I think Simon Jenkins would find that anyone with plans to turn the Palace of Westminster into a “great museum” would first have to deal with the asbestos, update the wiring and make sure it was safe for public use. A not inconsiderable outlay. Jennifer Rees Cardiff

Simon Jenkins is spot-on calling for parliament to leave London, but the UK loves living in the “glorious” past of long ago victories and having a capital that led the world in its ideas of taste and sophistication. Today’s parliamentarians seem to turn misty eyed as soon as they enter their derelict, draughty building, and vote again and again to do nothing about it.

Their attitude pervades the UK’s attempts at capital projects that consume millions of pounds and take for ever, and still don’t take off. Other countries seem to manage capital projects with ease, and they don’t believe they rule the world. Sam White Lewes, East Sussex

We need to rethink climate action away from the Cop talks

The Guardian Thu, 12 Nov 2026 17:56:44 GMT

Readers respond to an article by Fiona Harvey in which she questioned whether progress is being made 10 years on from the Paris treaty

As world leaders gathered in Turkey for the UN climate talks, Fiona Harvey was right to ask, “What’s the point?” (What’s the point? Ten years after the Paris treaty, are climate talks getting anywhere?, 7 November). She pointed to how over 10 years ago in Paris, countries came together for the 21st conference and signed an agreement that aimed to limit global heating to 1.5C above preindustrial levels. For the past two years, temperatures “have exceeded that threshold”.

I was at last year’s climate summit in Brazil, where it was obvious that the Cop process itself is a big part of the problem. The agreed text did not include “fossil fuels”, not to mention any reference to transition away from them. This is largely the result of how negotiations are conducted, as they rely on unanimous consent by all participating countries.

This has pushed a “coalition of the willing” to form outside the formal process that is attempting to drive a transition away from fossil fuels. This is welcome, but maybe it is time to rethink the process entirely?

Some – including Brazil and civil society organisations – have advocated for the creation of a UN climate council or Earth council. This could circumnavigate consensus-based negotiations and drive accelerated climate action. This would empower majorities, such as the 141-country strong coalition that voted in the UN general assembly in favour of the international court of justice’s advisory opinion on countries having an obligation to protect the environment from greenhouse gas emissions.

Other options include strengthening the role of the international court of justice itself to ensure countries implement their climate targets. Both could be achieved by adapting the UN’s founding document, the UN charter, an idea that is generating growing interest.

As Fiona’s article highlighted, the current talks have done their part in advancing the climate agenda. But as the effects of a changing climate become increasingly severe, we need to think about how we can tackle this crisis with far more determination, at much greater speed. Olav Kjørven Former UN assistant secretary general; senior adviser, Article 109

As your report notes, Cop31’s host wants “a tangible outcome … that people can see is real” (Cop31 must deliver climate progress that people can see is real, host says, 8 November). Here is what tangible could look like: receipts.

Two years ago in Baku, governments promised $300bn a year in climate finance. Since then the public has seen pledges, press releases and delivery plans without dates. Adão Soares Barbosa, the chair of the Least Developed Countries Group, a negotiating group of 44 nations, put it plainly: credibility will be measured “not by promises made, but by commitments fulfilled”.

So measure. Every country that signed the Baku goal should table a delivery plan in Antalya naming the amount, the instrument and the year. Grants counted separately from loans. Adaptation counted separately from mitigation. No double-counting private finance toward public promises.

The figures justify the scrutiny. Barely 0.2% of available climate finance reaches small island states for adaptation, for countries whose very existence is at stake. That is not a finance gap; it is an allocation choice.

Cop31 will deserve to be called a success if people can see the money moving. Publish the plans, with dates, and let the public check the receipts. Anything less is another communique. Jackie Omotalade Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, US

Even though the US government is noticeably absent from Cop31, the American people have voted for a new path that prioritises their economic wellbeing (Democrats to attend Cop31 climate talks boosted by midterms and eager to make up for Trump-era setbacks, 9 November). Luckily, we’ve developed a roadmap for the US – the world’s top historical emitter – to take climate action while protecting the energy security of America’s workers.

One proposal for Game Changers, a project of the Political Economy Research Institute at the University of Massachusetts Amherst, would make polluters pay into an extreme weather superfund by levying fees on large fossil fuel companies in proportion to their historical emissions. The fund would support state and local governments and federal agencies in disaster recovery and climate adaptation efforts.

Another game-changing proposal would phase down fossil fuels and provide energy security cashbacks for working families. These cashbacks would come from limiting emissions and compelling fossil-fuel producers to buy non-tradable permits at quarterly auctions. The proceeds would go directly to households to maintain their purchasing power and to community investments in resilience.

Climate action does not have to be expensive for working America. It can, in fact, be a source of economic revitalisation. Our newest crop of US leaders must make it a priority to reimagine economic and environmental policy to centre the wellbeing of people, not corporate profits. James K Boyce Amherst, Massachusetts, US

Participating in art and culture has measurable benefits on our wellbeing

The Guardian Thu, 12 Nov 2026 17:56:34 GMT

William Rees says Ealing council’s workshops have shown that even an hour spent on a creative pursuit can change someone’s day

Reading Emma Brockes’ response to a recent Art Fund study, I felt the significance of the research may have been lost in its packaging (Art is good for your health? Allow me a quick eyeroll, 5 November).

The language of “prescribing” art has its roots in social prescribing. I understand why this might make people uncomfortable, particularly if it suggests that culture is being instrumentalised rather than enjoyed for its own sake.

Yet these findings matter for two reasons. First, they provide evidence for what many of us know intuitively: that participating in and experiencing art and culture are not only enriching, but also have measurable benefits for our health and wellbeing.

Second, with budgets for culture under pressure, this evidence strengthens our case for public investment. Surely that’s another argument for keeping our national museums free and ensuring everyone can access their wellbeing benefits.

Rather than viewing this study cynically, we should recognise the opportunities it presents. As Daisy Fancourt, who is quoted in Brockes’ article, explores in her excellent and insightful book Art Cure, the evidence extends far beyond visiting galleries and museums.

In the London borough of Ealing, we’re piloting a free creative health programme bringing residents and council staff together through activities ranging from clay workshops to Islamic geometric drawing. Almost all participants have reported improved wellbeing following these sessions. But beyond the evaluation, conversations have shown me how even an hour spent being creative can positively change the course of someone’s day, while regular participation can have a lasting impact on their lives.

Art shouldn’t have to justify its existence through its health benefits. But understanding those benefits strengthens the case for everyone to experience, participate in and benefit from art and culture.

And if the thought of visiting a museum makes Brockes’ eyes roll, I’d happily invite her to one of our workshops. She might leave having learned a new skill, but I suspect she’d take away rather more than that. William Rees Culture officer, Ealing council

UK ministers have no plans to publish explosive report on climate crisis

The Guardian Thu, 12 Nov 2026 17:51:24 GMT

Andy Burnham’s newly appointed climate adviser used report to warn of national security risk from collapsing ecosystems

The UK government still has no plans to publish an explosive report showing the national security risk from the collapse of ecosystems around the world – even after handing the key official behind the report a new advisory role.

Andy Burnham addressed the Cop31 climate summit in Turkey on Thursday and said the UK was determined to reach net zero by 2050 and work with its partners to build a clean energy future.

The prime minister also announced the appointment of Madeleine Alessandri, a long-serving civil servant and the former head of the UK’s joint intelligence committee, to be adviser on climate security. The JIC is the committee of the UK’s spy chiefs, which oversees the work of MI5 and MI6.

Alessandri spearheaded the publication of the climate report, which found that food shortages, food price rises, mass migration and nuclear conflict overseas could result from the failure to prevent the collapse of key ecosystems, including the Amazon rainforest.

The report was supposed to be launched at last year’s Cop, but was suppressed by Keir Starmer’s government. The Guardian revealed – through a leak – the key contents of the report ahead of its intended launch last year, and early this year a redacted version was put out. Ed Miliband, the foreign secretary, has briefed foreign governments on the findings and the report clearly influenced Burnham’s decision to appoint Alessandri, but the report itself remains under wraps.

Burnham told Cop31 that Britain was ready to play its full part. “The message I carry here, in my first Cop as prime minister, is that the UK remains determined to reach net zero by 2050 and to work with our partners to build a clean energy future,” he said.

“The world has changed. The consensus we once enjoyed on science and climate action has broken down. We will not stand by, and that’s why I’ve pledged a new era of British leadership over the next decade.”

He said he embraced the focus at the climate summit on electrification, because “if we depend on energy we do not control, we depend on prices we cannot control. The shift to clean energy is the only route to energy security.”

But he insisted that industry must do its part to help people deliver the green transition. He highlighted progress on electric cars and heat pumps, adding: “If you drive a new electric car today in the UK, it costs less than a petrol equivalent. Get on the right tariff and a heat pump can be cheaper to run than a gas boiler.”

Burnham’s public declaration that the climate crisis poses a major national security threat cheered Cop31 and will be noted by governments worried about the impact of global heating on food supplies, the cost of living, migration and infrastructure. He is also one of the few leaders from western Europe to address the summit.

But campaigners, experts and green businesses and investors are worried about his commitment to the climate crisis because his chancellor, John Healey, is known to view economic growth as taking priority even if it means locking the UK into expensive fossil fuels.

Louise Haigh, who is first secretary of state and a key ally of Burnham, is thought to take a similar view, along with Jonathan Reynolds, the business secretary.

Behind the scenes, these concerns are shared by senior members of his government. Significantly, Burnham has no dedicated climate adviser working for him in Downing Street – despite it being an important issue to many voters.

A series of major decisions that have climate implications are being taken largely in isolation, rather than with their cumulative impact in mind, senior insiders have told the Guardian.

While Burnham addressed Cop31, his ministers were thought to be putting the final touches to a weakening of the mandate requiring carmakers to switch an increasing proportion of their sales to electric vehicles.

Burnham has also greenlighted the Jackdaw gasfield, cut funding for heat pumps and is mulling backing a new oilfield, Rosebank. Healey, meanwhile, has told MPs on the Treasury committee that Labour backs a third runway at Heathrow.

Campaigners and business people told the Guardian that the prime minister gave the impression of being swayed by short-term economic thinking from advisers not up to speed with a vastly changed energy world.

Ami McCarthy, head of politics at Greenpeace UK, said of Burnham’s speech to Cop: “[It] hit the right notes, but noises offstage about a massive new oilfield and looser rules on electric cars almost drowned him out.

“Appointing the world’s first climate security envoy is a welcome move, but approving Rosebank would only increase the climate threat level to communities in Britain and around the world.

“There are so many elephants in the room, you’d think it’s a zoo. Burnham needs to start bridging the widening chasm between words and deeds on climate action.”

But the prime minister has influential supporters too, who believe he understands the climate crisis and supports efforts to tackle it.

Burnham missed out on a bilateral meeting at Cop31 with Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, the Brazilian president whose resounding re-election has given renewed hope to leftwing parties fighting the far right.

But he did manage a meeting with Fatih Birol, the executive director of the International Energy Agency and the world’s foremost energy economist.

In between football talk – Burnham is famously an Everton fan, and Birol follows the Premier League closely – they discussed how cheaper energy from renewable sources, and more electrification of the UK economy, could bring down the cost of living.

Birol told the Guardian: “I can tell you that his mind and heart are fully behind the electrification of the UK energy system. I can put my name behind it. I had a very good and in-depth discussion with him.”

The government was contacted for comment.

Vladimir Putin warned US negotiators that Russia would target any foreign troops deployed to Ukraine, in a series of hardline remarks that came as the Ukrainian military faced renewed disruptions to Elon Musk’s Starlink satellite service.

During the talks at the Kremlin with the US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff on Thursday, the Russian president refused to soften his territorial demands, insisting on full control over four Ukrainian regions that Moscow claims to have annexed.

He also ruled out accepting the deployment of foreign peacekeeping troops in Ukraine, describing such a move as a “continuation of war”.

Putin’s comments appeared to severely dampen hopes that a peace deal could be within reach, after Volodymyr Zelenskyy said there was a “window of opportunity” to reach an agreement before the end of 2026.

The latest trip to Moscow by Witkoff and Kushner, who have made numerous visits to Russia, was partly aimed at securing European participation in future negotiations, according to two people familiar with the talks.

Speaking after the meeting, Witkoff confirmed that European representatives would join the next round of talks. “They’re our partners, and it’s important for them to be involved,” he told reporters as he boarded a plane leaving Moscow.

The US envoys will now travel to Dublin, Ireland, where they will meet Zelenskyy and debrief him on the Moscow meeting.

Amid a flurry of diplomatic activity, including the recent talks in Abu Dhabi, the Kremlin appears to have succeeded in reframing negotiations over the war in Ukraine as part of a broader discussion about European security.

But Europe is wary of Russian attempts to focus discussions on a European security architecture, while Moscow continues to pound Ukraine with bombs and missiles.

The EU foreign policy chief, Kaja Kallas, told reporters: “We already have a European security architecture in place.” Kallas pointed to the cold war-era Helsinki accords and the Budapest memorandum, which guaranteed the territorial integrity of Ukraine. “The problem is that Russia is not keeping to those agreements, so right now the focus should be that Russia actually keeps to their obligations … and they don’t attack another country again.” Focusing on a European security architecture was a “distraction” without a ceasefire, she added.

Both Washington and Moscow have been urging European leaders to appoint a single representative to lead negotiations on their behalf.

“Once a representative is appointed, a chief negotiator authorised to speak on Europe’s behalf, there will be a four-way dialogue,” Putin said on Thursday.

EU leaders are due to discuss the issue of who speaks for Europe on Friday, but so far have declined to nominate one person to speak for the bloc. One EU official said the EU would be represented by its institutions when issues concerning the union were on the table, but played down any imminent appointment. They said: “Do I expect an agreement on a special representative? My answer is no, I don’t.”

Kallas suggested she – as the EU’s high representative for foreign and security policy – should represent the EU in talks, alongside António Costa, the president of the European Council.

More than 45 European leaders are meeting in Dublin for the European Political Community summit, a gathering that brings together nearly every country on the continent, apart from the leaders of Belarus and Russia.

The French president, Emmanuel Macron, played down the importance of having a single European negotiator, saying “the content determines the format”. “There is no more US support. So there [are] some mediations, fine,” he said, referring to the process led by Kushner and Witkoff. “But at the end of the day we will be the one to define and decide for our future security as Europeans.”

The German chancellor, Friedrich Merz, said it was first necessary to get Putin to the negotiating table before deciding on a European envoy. Merz said: “It’s not about individuals. What matters is that Putin is prepared to hold talks.”

Meanwhile, Zelenskyy accused Musk’s Starlink satellite service of damaging Ukraine’s ability to defend itself against Russian drone attacks, after Ukrainian military officials reported new restrictions on the system.

According to Zelenskyy, Starshield, a military version of Starlink funded by the Pentagon, has for several days been subject to speed limits of 100mph (161km/h) along the frontline and in Russian-occupied territory.

Similar restrictions last month prompted confusion over who had ordered them, with Musk and the Trump administration pointing fingers at each other before the service was partly restored.

The latest restrictions had made it harder for Ukrainian forces to intercept Russia’s increasingly sophisticated jet-powered drones, Zelenskyy said, accusing the service of “helping the Russians kill more Ukrainians and carry out more accurate strikes against Ukraine”.

Kyiv has contacted Washington to seek an explanation for the disruption, which Zelenskyy said appeared to be deliberate rather than a technical fault.

Norway follows Finland in barring Russian athletes from entering country over Ukraine war

The Guardian Thu, 12 Nov 2026 17:23:51 GMT

Move by Norway ‘a further tightening’ of current rules

Russians ‘have no business’ in Finland, says minister

Norway’s government announced that it would prevent Russian and Belarusian professional athletes from coming to Norway to compete, hours after neighbouring Finland announced a similar move.

The government said it intended to prevent athletes from these countries coming to Norway as long as the war in Ukraine continues. In a statement, it noted that while Norway already had strict rules for visas for Russian and Belarusian citizens, recent “relaxations introduced by international sports federations” meant that more athletes and support staff from the two countries may come to the Scandinavian nation to compete.

In a statement, Astri Aas-Hansen, the minister of justice and public security, said: “Norway already has a restrictive visa practice for Russian and Belarusian citizens, but is now further tightening who is allowed to travel here.”

To this end, the government said it would instruct immigration authorities and police to “to refuse entry to Russian and Belarusian professional athletes and accompanying support staff … if they come to Norway to take part in sporting competitions”. The changes would enter into force “shortly”, the government said.

The statement said that Russian elite sport had close ties to Russian authorities and could therefore not be “viewed independently” from the war in Ukraine.

Norway is preparing to host World Cup in cross-country skiing in December in the town of Trondheim, but this decision means that Russian and Belarusian athletes could be blocked from competing despite having been cleared by the International Ski and Snowboard Federation (FIS).

The FIS has permitted Russian and Belarusian athletes to compete under certain conditions, such as not displaying any country symbols and signing a declaration of neutrality.

The Norwegian move follows a similar decision by Nordic neighbour Finland, which earlier on Thursday announced it would block visas for Russian athletes.

Finland also said it will restrict entry for Russian athletes because of the war in Ukraine, potentially affecting a number of winter sports. The move follows a backlash in Finland to Russia being reinstated for the ice hockey world championships.

“As long as Russia’s war of aggression continues, Russian athletes have no business in Finland,” said Elina Valtonen, the minister for foreign affairs. “Their entry into the country would be a threat to Finland’s international relations. The same is true of other short-term work under visas that is not essential to Finland’s national interests.”

The Finnish foreign ministry said the measure would affect Russians competing under neutral status as well as those competing for national teams.

Finland hosts a figure skating grand prix next week and a cross-country ski World Cup this month. Both sports allow Russians to compete as “neutral athletes”. One major event to be affected is the figure skating world championships in March. Russian skaters are expected to be among the top medal contenders.

The International Skating Union (ISU) said it “has taken note of the statement today by the Finnish government related to Russian nationals entering the country and the possible consequential impact on sporting events, including the ISU figure skating world championships due to be held in Tampere, Finland, and is studying its implications”.

“ISU believes that athletes should not be punished for the actions of their governments in a world where, sadly, many conflicts are ongoing.” The ISU added it was “seeking clarifications” from skating officials in Finland.

The change takes effect from Monday, so should not affect this week’s NHL games in Helsinki between the Seattle Kraken and Carolina Hurricanes or scheduled ski World Cup slalom races in Levi on Saturday and Sunday.

Finland is among a group of European teams to have vowed not to play against Russia at the ice hockey world championships. The men’s championships are scheduled for Germany, which is weighing up whether to go ahead with hosting.

In the longer term, Finland is due to host the European track and field championships in 2030. World Athletics, the sport’s governing body, maintains a blanket ban on Russian participation, though that is facing a legal challenge.
