Women came forward to protect others. They’re heroes

The Guardian Thu, 12 Nov 2026 17:19:19 GMT

So many have contacted me about their experiences. Women used to be blamed for what men did to them, but I can feel things changing

Lucy Beaumont is a comedian and author

At the forefront of everything going on recently are young women and girls. They were vulnerable because of their age or their class, and also because of power dynamics.

These women and girls went through something traumatising, all of them. As did all of the women and girls who I’m sure are coming forward now. Everyone knows there are other men who traumatised girls they’ve worked with, while being paid very, very large amounts of money.

In TV, the very thing that makes working in the industry amazing is also the thing that gives oxygen to misconduct and abusive behaviour. You come to work, “get your head down and get the job done”, which can mean all pulling together on a project and making it work. But that attitude has its dark side. It can mean keeping your head down so as not to see clearly what’s going on right in front of you.

The harmful actions of men were, and are, seen by the people around them. Once they see it, they either worry about it or they ignore it. What happened to the women and girls wasn’t done in secret. I think this is what the very national outcry is about – because it could have been called out, stopped, and women could have been prevented from being in dangerous situations with these men. Because of this culture, the answer to “Why did people do nothing?” is maybe: they didn’t know they were meant to do anything. Or perhaps that’s letting people off the hook?

In the past we told the girls that on some level they were to blame. Women are told to be careful and watch themselves. We had to work around men to feel safe. I asked a female comedian friend the other day: “Why do we get into comedy as women?” I realised it was the result of trauma and defensiveness. I spent years as a young person learning how to be funny to signal to older men who had no business approaching us that they weren’t welcome around me and my friends.

But things have moved on. I can feel it. I can see it in the thousands of messages I’m receiving. I was on Sky News and I said a fraction of the things I feel and the things I’ve heard. And I’ve been flooded with support because people felt something. They feel the same about these young women as I do and for a lot of women watching and reading, they’ve been in their shoes.

I’ve spoken to hundreds of women over the years who have suffered abuse, and then countless more over the past few days. And do you know why they come forward? To protect others. Women came forward, still hurt and confused and dealing with whatever life has thrown at them since then, but they told their truth. They’re heroes, and this is yet another article praising them.

People love telly. They’ve grown up with it in their living rooms. They want it to be a safe place because they want all institutions to be safe. And with telly, well, they decide what shows and channels they will give their time and attention to. They’re the audience. They cut off the oxygen and decide when to turn it on. These audiences are telling us that they want something different now. Things are changing.

Audiences want the truth, as uncomfortable as it can be. They want people keeping it real. Future telly makers take note.

France have spent years trying to beat the Boks but belief and bodies are fading

The Guardian Thu, 12 Nov 2026 17:17:39 GMT

Injury crisis makes the job harder for Fabien Galthié whose side have beaten South Africa once in their past 10 meetings

The final of this inaugural Nations Championship is two weeks away, but regardless of who makes it through to the last match at Twickenham there’s an irresistible sense that the two best teams from either side of the competition will go head-to-head at the Stade de France this Friday night. France, back-to-back Six Nations champions, play South Africa, back-to-back world champions, and the one team that the French – and anyone else with dreams of becoming the world’s best team – need to find a way to beat in the 12 months before the Springboks take a run at winning a third consecutive World Cup.

France have been looking for one of those for a long time now. This is not an even-sided rivalry. South Africa have won nine of the 10 games the two teams have played in the past 15 years, including the last five in Paris. England, Ireland, even Wales all have better head-to-head records against the Springboks in that same stretch of time. France’s one win was in Marseille in 2022, and whatever good it did them was undone a year later when the Springboks knocked them out of their home World Cup in the quarter-finals.

“We tend to get up for the French team, out of respect,” said Rassie Erasmus this week. “It doesn’t take a lot to get the team up. We’ve spoken about it. We enjoy the way the French people get behind their team, this cauldron, it’s not something a lot of our players have experienced, so when they get the opportunity they want to put their best foot forward, to represent themselves, their families and their country.” Erasmus didn’t want to talk about whether his side were favourites or not. After all, he said, what difference does it make? “The only bad thing about being favourites is you might get complacent. And we are definitely not complacent.”

That World Cup quarter-final finished 29-28. The French got so close, but because it was hard to imagine they could play any better they somehow ended up feeling further away than ever. They were still talking about the impact of that defeat two years later, when the Springboks came back to the ground and beat them 32-17 despite playing half the game with 14 men. “What can I say about this South African team?” said Erasmus’ opposite number Fabien Galthié on Wednesday. “Today they are among the best teams to have ever existed in world rugby.”

Galthié has never yet sent out a French team without hope that they can, in his words, do something “improbable”, but that self-belief feels pretty thin this week. They are in the midst of an injury crisis that has left them with existential questions about the toll the domestic game takes on their players. Galthié has used more than 100 players since June 2024. Right now, 30 of them are out injured. Between them the missing players combine for 34% of all France’s total playing time in that period and 41% of the points they’ve scored during it. They’ve lost hookers, props, locks, flankers, centres and full-backs, but the problem is sharpest at fly-half.

They are missing both Matthieu Jalibert and Romain Ntamack, as well as their regular understudies Thomas Ramos and Antoine Hastoy. In the circumstances, Galthié has decided to gamble on picking Antoine Dupont at fly-half, with Maxime Lucu inside him at No 9. With no good fly-half to pick, the French have gone for two great scrum-halves instead. Dupont has done it before, but it has been a while. He played eight games there for Toulouse during an injury crisis in 2024. Lucu has more recent experience in the position, and filled in there last week after Ntamack went off injured during the Test against Fiji.

“It’s been a huge challenge to overcome, but we’ve really enjoyed trying to design a solution,” Galthié said. “They are two icons in France, one at Bordeaux and the other at Toulouse, and we wanted to bring them together to lead this French team on Friday night. It won’t be easy, but we think it’s the best solution.” There’s an idea that the two of them are going to swap back and forth during the match. If nothing else, it’s given then the satisfaction of proving Erasmus wrong: he had predicted they would move one of the centres to play No 10 instead.

Erasmus was keen to point out that South Africa have their own injuries to worry about – Frans Malherbe, RG Snyman, Kwagga Smith, André Esterhuizen, Handré Pollard and Cheslin Kolbe are all missing. But he has still been able to put together a team where the eight forwards have almost as many caps between them as the entire French XV.

after newsletter promotion

Galthié has recalled a couple of old hands – Julien Marchand at hooker and Grégory Alldritt at No 8 – but otherwise his team feels green. They have just 611 caps between them, and seven of them have fewer than five caps each. Galthié puts the blame for these injuries on the domestic set-up, saying the French system makes the players old before their time. But he is hoping that the Top 14 will provide the solution, too. It is a team picked on league form. There have been other changes, too, which have brought the national side a little closer to the domestic game.

France released both the foreign coaches in their set-up, Shaun Edwards and Vlok Cilliers, and have replaced them with men who work in the Top 14. Galthié has brought in Maxime Petitjean from Toulon to work on the team’s kicking strategy and Geoffrey Doumayrou from Montpellier to run the defence. It’s an interesting pick. Doumayrou is only 37, and was playing for the national team as recently as 2019. He moved straight into coaching at Montpellier and within two seasons had turned them into the tightest defence in the league.

Something had to change. France have spent years trying to find a way to beat the Springboks. They’re about to find out if any of it has brought them any closer to actually doing it.

Ebenezer review – Johnny Depp’s Scrooge tries to exorcise ghosts of business past

The Guardian Thu, 12 Nov 2026 17:14:58 GMT

The latest film version of the Dickens classic A Christmas Carol is decent enough, though its star is rather better as the legendary miser before redemption arrives

Here for lovers of Dickens – and fans of subtext – is an unexpectedly watchable new movie version of A Christmas Carol starring a top-hatted and heavily madeup Johnny Depp; it is a film about whether it’s possible for a man to earn redemption before it is too late. (The answer is … sure, as long as you say sorry and change your ways. But Mr Scrooge never launched a libel action against the Sun for calling him an un-Christmassy old meanie.)

In fact, screenwriter Nathaniel Halpern and director Ti West have put together a perfectly serviceable, faithful adaptation – a tradaptation, if you will – of Dickens’s masterpiece about the hideous old miser saved from damnation on Christmas Eve by the appearance of three Christmas ghosts, from yuletides past, present and future. It sticks to the accepted narrative beats and more or less all the familiar episodes, but with a few twists.

There is a witty and ingenious new prologue sequence in which Scrooge’s equally grumpy partner Jacob Marley, played by Ian McKellen, is still alive, going into a full Stadler-and-Waldorf double-act with his old colleague. (Wait – did The Muppet Christmas Carol inspire this?) And West shows us his scary-movie style by having that scene coming to a disturbing close with a kettle’s eerie whistle as it comes to the boil.

As well as pointedly asking about prisons and workhouses, Scrooge now actually accuses the charitable gentlemen of stealing the donations themselves, and there’s a terrible new end in store for cheerful Mr Fezziwig, which the film suggests is what finally embittered Scrooge against the undeserving poor. His lost love Belle is here a novelist, an idea borrowed from romance author Michelle Griep. Andrea Riseborough, Tramell Tillman and Robert Strange play the three ghosts; Rupert Grint is his pinch-faced clerk Bob Cratchit, and Sam Claflin is his cheerful nephew Fred, son of his once adored sister Fanny.

As Scrooge himself, Depp is in fact rather good; theatrically bad-tempered and petulant and, as with his Jack Sparrow, I suspect Depp’s comedy timing and sonorous British accent might have been learned from his old Fast Show comrade Paul Whitehouse. He is better at the unredeemed Scrooge than the saved version at the end, where some of the abject pathos is missing.

This is a decent enough new version, avoiding any big new revisionist takes which might have clunked, though perhaps Dickens himself might not have agreed with the church scene and the solemn use of Silent Night to accompany the Christmas-everywhere montage. He might have pictured something more secular.

Ebenezer is out on 12 November in Australia and 13 November in the UK and US

“We need a new system built around a young person with schools, the NHS and employers all working together to make sure that everyone has the chance to earn or learn.”

The long-awaited report on youth unemployment will promise almost half a million job and education opportunities within a decade, but will also advise sweeping changes to the benefits system for under-25s.

There will be a local fund for young people with disabilities to apply to for money to pay for equipment or for help with short-term expenses such as travel to attend a training course or job interview, the Guardian understands. The fund will be managed by local advisers and the intention is that funds can be transferred quickly when needs arise.

For most young people apart from those with the most severe needs, the fund would replace long-term support such as Pip – a move that has been criticised by some charities and Labour MPs.

Milburn said the trajectory towards 1.25 million young people out of employment, education or training would not be stopped by “crude benefit cuts”, and a life on benefits had to be replaced with relentless support towards work.

“This is a moral crisis. If other countries are relentless in supporting their young people into work and learning, we can be too. A lost generation is a choice. We have a to make a different choice,” he said.

The Joseph Rowntree Foundation (JRF), an anti-poverty charity, said the changes risked taking away vital funds that young people used to keep themselves in work.

There will be a higher rate of youth allowance for young people living independently, including care leavers, according to the Times.

There will also be an additional cost allowance for those who are most disabled – which young people can receive whether they are in work or not – and a new higher insurance provision for those with severe disabilities who will never be able to work.

Milburn, who will deliver his report next Tuesday, told the Guardian that the support for young people outlined in his report would create 440,000 employment and education opportunities by 2036 and raise the net incomes of young people by more than £2bn.

He said the main finding of the review was not a lack of ambition from young people but a lack of opportunities. “I have not met a single young person who wanted to be Neet [not in education, employment or training]. Not one. They want independence, they want to earn their own money and they want someone to give them a chance,” he said.

after newsletter promotion

“I want young people to have more than just enough to get by. I want them to have a future. The system is failing to do that.”

The JRF said the proposals could significantly weaken the safety net for hundreds of thousands of young people with a disability or health condition, leaving many of those on universal credit living on a basic rate of support of around just £80 a week.

“Cutting someone’s income when they’re already struggling to afford food or the bus to college makes it harder for them to stay in education or find work,” said Iain Porter, the charity’s senior policy adviser.

No 10 declined on Thursday to rule out the changes affecting existing claimants. A Downing Street spokesperson said: “We face a choice as a country. We can either invest earlier in young people’s success or continue paying the cost of failure when they become detached from education and work and end up relying on the benefit system. We cannot afford to do both.”

The Labour MP Bell Ribeiro-Addy, who was part of the welfare rebellion last summer, told Radio 4’s Today programme she felt uneasy about voting for cuts to disability benefits.

“The cuts seem to land on young disabled people, and many of them are in college already or already at work. I don’t see how you fix the first by punishing the second,” she said.

But the Treasury select committee chair, Meg Hillier, who was key to the government climbdown on the welfare cuts last summer, told the BBC she was open to the changes. “What happened last year was a cut was being proposed and none of us could explain to people what would happen to them,” she said. “Milburn has done some very good work on this, so I’m giving him a fair wind.”

Jensen Huang resigns as Nvidia CEO after alleged affairs

The Guardian Thu, 12 Nov 2026 16:57:34 GMT

Move follows admission of affair with woman alleged to be Chinese spy and reported relationship with employee

From washing dishes at Denny’s to rockstar of AI: the rise and fall of Jensen Huang

Jensen Huang has resigned as chief executive of Nvidia after reports of extramarital affairs with an alleged Chinese spy and a company employee.

He will be replaced on an interim basis by Nvidia’s chief financial officer, Colette Kress, until a full-time successor is named.

Shares in the chipmaker plunged by 13% when Wall Street opened, after Huang’s departure was announced. After a partial rebound, they were down 7% in morning trading, wiping more than $320bn (£242bn) off Nvidia’s value on the day and more than $600bn for the week – valuing the company at about $3.9tn.

The statement from Nvidia’s board of directors confirming Huang’s departure did not mention the spying scandal and personal conduct revelations that have enveloped the company, instead paying tribute to Huang’s “profound” contributions to the company he co-founded.

“Jensen’s contributions to Nvidia are profound. Nvidia is one of the most consequential technology companies in the world. The board and the company thank Jensen for his immeasurable contributions to the company and the industry,” the statement said.

It added that Huang had resigned as chief executive, president and Nvidia board member “effective immediately”.

Donald Trump, who had defended Huang at first as the scandal threatened to overwhelm the Nvidia co-founder, quickly moved on to potential successors on Thursday, posting on social media that he should be replaced by Tim Cook, Apple’s former chief executive and current executive chair.

“NOW THAT Nvidia CEO JENSEN HUANG, who has done a fantastic job, has resigned, there is only one man to take his place – TIM COOK of Apple,” Trump wrote, adding: “A Legend replaces a Legend!”

The chipmaker’s board earlier this week appointed the leading law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to conduct a “thorough and independent” investigation into the relationship with Alice Huang, an Nvidia customer and Chinese citizen who is no relation to the Nvidia boss. Nvidia had previously denied anything unusual about the relationship, but that changed on Sunday when Jensen Huang admitted he had been unfaithful to his wife, Lori, without referring to Alice Huang directly.

The law firm had directed Jensen Huang to continue to lead Nvidia as the investigation continued.

However, late on Wednesday, the New York Times reported that Huang had a separate extramarital affair with a company employee named Kimberly Powell. She was Nvidia’s vice-president of healthcare and was reportedly captured on video being affectionate with Huang at a hotel during a company conference in March.

The report added to the pressure on Huang, as the board called a meeting late on Wednesday to discuss the CEO’s future.

Powell has been approached for comment.

After Huang’s resignation was announced on Thursday, Reuters reported a third affair. The newly uncovered liaison was another Nvidia employee, according to two people familiar with the matter who spoke to the news outlet. Reuters did not reveal her name.

Nvidia’s board said it would consider internal and external candidates for the chief executive’s role, with Cook featuring among potential runners and riders before Trump’s intervention. Cook stepped down as chief executive at Apple in September but still has a senior executive role at the company. Rene Haas, the chief executive of Arm Holdings, a UK-based chipmaker, has also been mooted, along with Lisa Su, the chief executive of the chipmaker AMD.

Huang ran Nvidia tightly and managed about 60 direct reports. Internal candidates include Kress and Ian Buck, who manages the company’s AI hardware and software products. Huang’s two children, Madison and Spencer, also work at Nvidia but are in their mid-30s and relatively inexperienced. The chipmaker also announced the appointment of Harvey Jones, a tech investor and entrepreneur, as its first-ever chair.

Sign up to TechScape

A weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our lives

after newsletter promotion

Dan Ives, a senior US tech analyst, said the board had done what “it needed to do, which is rip off the Band-Aid and take Nvidia into its next chapter without him” and that the company remained ahead of its competitors.

However, Neil Wilson, an analyst at the investment platform Saxo UK, said Nvidia would need a “great CEO” to replace Huang.

“His technical knowledge and understanding of every last bit of product is basically unique and impossible to replicate,” Wilson said, adding nonetheless that Nvidia was well placed in terms of upcoming products and orders.

Huang’s exit from the company he co-founded in 1993 removes a senior figure in Silicon Valley at a time when the AI arms race between the US and China is at an apex. He owns more than 870m shares, or about 3.6% of the company, and was worth $145bn on Thursday morning, according to Bloomberg, making him the world’s 13th richest person.

Unlike many of his contemporaries at other leading tech companies, Huang has dozens of direct reports, an unusual management structure that emphasises his control over the company.

The entire AI ecosphere relies on Nvidia, which engineers advanced chips used to train AI models and power companies such as OpenAI and Anthropic. It is also one of the most valuable companies on Earth, with a market cap that hit $5tn at one point last year.

Huang has denied any knowledge that Alice Huang allegedly worked for the Chinese government. The pair were seen together around the world, dining in restaurants and attending meetings, over the past few years. Alice Huang is a businesswoman and head of the Singapore-based datacentre firm Megaspeed, who US intelligence services suspect of being a Chinese asset according to multiple reports.

On the same day that Jensen Huang admitted having an affair, Nvidia’s board of directors announced the company was launching an investigation regarding reports that he was the target of a foreign intelligence effort.

Farage was guest on Brand podcast after sexual assault investigation began

The Guardian Thu, 12 Nov 2026 16:43:33 GMT

Reform leader this week criticised the Labour party for ‘cosying up to’ and ‘promoting’ disgraced comedian

Nigel Farage appeared on Russell Brand’s US podcast nine months after police opened an investigation into the comedian after allegations of sexual assault, the Guardian has learned.

The Reform UK leader has criticised Labour for “cosying up to” and “promoting” Brand a decade ago, after the comedian was sentenced this week to more than 10 years in prison for rape and sexual assault.

It has now emerged that Farage was a guest on Brand’s online show in July 2024 – months after allegations of sexual assault against Brand were first made public in media reports, but before he was charged in April 2025.

During the episode, Farage laughed with Brand about their shared interests in taking on the establishment and suggested the west had provoked Vladimir Putin into the Ukraine war because “what you don’t do with a Russian bear is deliberately poke it with a stick”.

Farage was aware of the serious sexual assault allegations against Brand at the time because he had commented on them on GB News the previous year, but they were not mentioned in the episode.

Sitting on a sofa with Brand alongside Dan Bongino, a Donald Trump supporter, and Charlie Kirk, the rightwing activist later murdered, Farage spoke of how “the old left-right divides” were being blown out of the water. He claimed that cancel culture meant people saying racist or homophobic things were “cancelled” but contempt for the white working class was allowed.

At the end of the show, Brand said: “Nigel, thank you for this impromptu opportunity to speak and I hope we get more chances to speak.”

An ally of Farage pointed out that the Reform leader and Brand had previously clashed in 2014 on the BBC’s Question Time, with Farage later claiming that the comedian had an assistant who straightened his chest hair for him and that Brand “didn’t seem to utter a word of sense”.

A number of women accused Brand of sexual assault in a joint Sunday Times, Times and Channel 4 exposé in September 2023, and the comedian was subsequently interviewed under caution by police that autumn.

On GB News in September 2023, Farage said he was not a big fan of Brand but would not prejudge him and remarked on the comedian having “upset big government” and powerful men such as Bill Gates, an apparent reference to Brand’s anti-vaccine views.

On the allegations against the host, Farage said there was “no evidence being produced” and then referred to four or five women having come forward.

He added: “I’m not here to prejudge his guilt or his innocence, but there are many other things in his own autobiography that he’s written about his behaviour with women that are disturbing, abusive and not very pretty.”

Asked about his appearance with Brand, a spokesperson for Farage said: “Nigel regrets his appearance on the show. His thoughts are with the victims who have suffered immensely because of what Russell Brand has done.”

Reform sources said it was not a planned appearance, and he was pulled into the room during a visit to the US.

Since the verdict, Farage has commented on the allegations against Brand on Australia’s News 24, saying: “It’s very difficult isn’t it, because this is two decades old, it’s ‘he said, she said’, although there’s more than one she. So these cases are always very difficult for us to judge at a distance because there is no actual hard evidence.”

However, he came out in support of Jemima Goldsmith, a former partner of Brand, who has accused him of assault. Farage said she was known to him and he believed her account of Brand being violent and abusive, adding: “The judicial system has proved to have actually worked.”

He also criticised Labour for failing to apologise for “cosying up” to Brand a decade ago.

It is not the first time Farage has met a man accused of abusive behaviour. The Reform UK leader was pictured with Andrew Tate, the misogynist influencer, in 2019. Tate was charged with rape and human trafficking in 2023, and the UK is now seeking to extradite him from the US. Tate denies the allegations.

Farage spoke in favour of Tate for defending “male culture” in a Strike It Big podcast which aired in February 2024, while acknowledging that the influencer had gone “over the top” and that he had said some “pretty horrible” things.

Asked about his podcast appearance and comments on Tate, Farage said: “There’s an awakening in a younger generation who have had enough of being dictated to, have had enough of being lectured to. They’re seeing through the rubbish they’re getting taught in schools and universities. If no other politician is willing to reach out to this group of people, then I will.”

Look at the Poundland scandal and see a crisis that goes beyond Britain’s high streets

The Guardian Thu, 12 Nov 2026 16:01:03 GMT

‘I look out for my team,’ a store manager tells me, but Poundland’s US owner doesn’t care. Labour may be too late to prevent it becoming yet another casualty of venture capital

In the Poundland I visit, a treasure trove of bargains, the staff are dejected. The shelves are emptying because the owners have withheld £50m needed for new stock and paying wages. It’s just one of 600 stores in peril, and these employees just a few of 12,000 at risk of losing their jobs – with 30,000 jobs at risk in supply chains.

On Tuesday £10m was released: not enough, but preventing instant collapse. Gordon Brothers, the US owner that bought Poundland for a symbolic £1 last year, specialises in buying and “restructuring” distressed companies. Under pressure, it extended the deadline by 10 working days before putting this profitable business into administration. It profits more by closing Poundland down and breaking it up.

The manager, whom I’ll call Jim for anonymity, is at work an hour and a half after his paid shift ended. “I look out for my team,” he says, though Gordon Brothers doesn’t seem to be looking out for him. He says the outsourced security staff vanished this week as their pay was stopped. “The shoplifting is very bad now. Look, the high-end stuff has gone first”: the well-known brands, not unknown cheaper makes. Despite everything, he is remarkably proud of the shop and boasts of how much cheaper brands are than in Sainsbury’s. He pats the shelf with red velvet Santa stockings and glittery bows, glad some Christmas stock is in before the closure. “But no one is telling us anything.”

Will the staff get jobs if it closes? He introduces me to a man in his late 50s with an easy manner and a wide grin. “My best man, by far,” he says. “He’s been here 15 years, and never a single day off sick, not one. Will any other shop see how good he is? No, because his English is bad and they won’t know his worth to any manager. I don’t know what he’ll do. I keep putting him on the till to try to improve his English, to help him along.” Jim is proud of his eye for picking good staff and keeping them on warm terms, and is fearful for their future.

This is may not be the sort of shop where you expect steadfast dedication to the company. Jim’s attitude is just another reminder of what I often find reporting on work, that most people are attached to their jobs, despite recent British Social Attitudes research reporting their frustrations. Often the greatest aggravations are about lack of control. Jim says he could increase sales if he was allowed to be the buyer. “I know our customers in this area; the centre doesn’t.”

He belongs to Usdaw, the shopworkers’ union, but says there’s nothing it can do. Time and again the union has watched helplessly as these private equity and venture capital buyouts bring down viable retailers. As we talk, a customer asks indignantly why there are no packs of Boost in the cold drinks cabinet. Jim explains the situation and the man looks shocked. “No! You can’t close down! I’m always in here.”

Our surroundings, our streetscape is at the mercy of distant forces. Gap-toothed high streets and boarded-up shops cause us all an ache of loss. Poundland stores teetering on the edge are “anchor stores” drawing people to high streets, but may join those great voids just weeks before Christmas. Woolworths’ 807 stores closed after being taken over, losing 27,000 jobs and lifetimes of local history. BHS, sold for £1, is gone. Debenhams, WHSmith, Toys R Us, Maplin, TM Lewin and plenty more, adversely transformed or taken over by private equity for unkindly “restructure” that usually ends in closures. Some, bought with debts that are loaded on to their balance sheets, stagger but survive – think Asda and Morrisons.

Now it’s Poundland’s turn. At Wednesday’s closed-session select committee on business and trade, MPs heard its long-serving managing director, Barry Williams, challenge the owners, trying to save the business and showing that it made a £18.1m operating profit in the year to September. But Gordon Brothers has turned down offers, notably one from Martin Property Group, owners of NCP car parks.

Through complex financing, it would make more by breaking Poundland up. It has £30m debt to recover but, as it is both the owner and the creditor, it comes top of the list for repayment in administration: after paying tax, it gets paid before any staff who are owed wages. If there’s no money left, redundancy is paid by the taxpayer.

Andy Burnham weighed in demanding answers, but Gordon Brothers has no legal obligation to worry about staff, let alone social or public concerns. The chair of the Commons business and trade committee, Liam Byrne, is campaigning hard to save Poundland, calling Gordon Brothers “much like a wolf on Wall Street, on the British high street”, and adding: “It’s clear that they’ve taken millions out of Poundland at a time when they themselves said the business was on a knife-edge.”

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

But there’s nothing anyone can do if pressure and shame fails. Why should a company, especially a foreign one, care what anyone thinks when the bottom line says close it down?

Byrne is campaigning to prevent this in future, calling for changes to company law that at present gives shareholders primacy above all else, unlike the much preferable situation in Germany. He would stop pension funds making it their sole obligation to maximise short-term gains and thus investing ever more in venture capital. He’d also impose stress tests to stop asset strippers overloading a business with debt then taking the lion’s share when it’s broken up.

On the Poundland shop floor, Jim and the rest of his team serve their customers and wait another two weeks to discover their fate. A future change in the law is essential. Maybe it will come. But it will probably be too late for them.

Polly Toynbee is a Guardian columnist

Daily Apple eau de parfum, 50ml

Glorious.

Discover 25 scent collection, 25 x 9ml

I practically leapt on this as soon as I saw it at the Marks & Spencer press preview because, well, just look at it. A very pretty, deeply satisfying book of individually boxed scents from what is now a very decent fragrance portfolio at M&S. Don’t sleep on it – this will go fast.

Diptyque Nurturing cleansing gel for body and hair, 350ml

Eve Lom cleansing balm, 20ml, and cloth

I predict 2027 will be a big year for the original cult skincare line, Eve Lom. Refresh your memory with this classic balm cleanser, still loved by the most discerning beauty fans for its skin-softening, glow-giving effect and deeply comforting medicinal smell. Yum.

BaByliss Air Style 1000 hot brush

Super Skin Nova moisturising primer, 50ml

Lisa Eldridge Marilyn Monroe collection strawberry blonde lipstick, 3ml

I’m generally dubious about collaborations with the estate of someone not here to consent and oversee, but in this collection, you can see the care, attention and respect Lisa Eldridge gives Marilyn Monroe. Everything is lovely, but who can think of Monroe without picturing a red lip?

Half Magic pressed glitter, 8.5g

I know cheap, fun, festive glitters are everywhere, but if you take your sparkle seriously, please know that Half Magic’s are the very best money can buy.

Neal’s Yard mother’s balm, 180g

I love how Neal’s Yard has never sold out on its values, nor compromised on quality. There’s lots to love throughout the range, but I find this moisturising balm to be a great gift for mothers-to-be (which, speaking from personal experience, should be accompanied by something entirely unrelated to pregnancy, such as a book, gig ticket or good olive oil).

Jumbo hair clips

One of my best buys of 2026. Oversized clips that allow for easy makeup application without leaving dents in my hairline, while holding much more firmly than the standard size seen elsewhere. A stocking filler that will get used by anyone with longer hair.

Charlotte Tilbury Flawless blush blur, 8g

after newsletter promotion

This alone got me back into powder blush. Blurry, non-drying, never-patchy, silken blush in the most perfect neutral rosy beige that flatters every skin tone from pale to deep.

Prequel half and half moisturiser, 168ml

Men, menopausal women, gym-goers and face-cream haters, assemble: this liquid moisturiser drenches skin without suffocating it and behaves beautifully under makeup.

Byoma Longevit-8 peptide serum, 40ml

Among this year’s best high street skincare launches, this is a great serum for anyone interested in state-of-the-art, serious skincare, made affordable enough to maintain long-term. To be applied after cleansing and before moisturiser and sunscreen.

Byoma So Clear set

I’ve recommended this stocking filler to countless parents hoping to set their mildly spotty teen on a solid skincare path. Full sizes can be bought individually to top up favourites when they’re done.

Violette FR bisou balm in chocolat, 2.5g

The most universally flattering, wearable, cool-toned brown, matt, blurry lip balm that is so subtle and easy, you barely even need a mirror. Even a makeup refusenik will enjoy the texture.

Narciso Rodriguez For Her Pure Musc Blanc, 50ml

Not new, not hyped, not trending. Just gorgeous, cosy, clean, elegant and chic. Even the most determined perfume haters will concede that this is hard to resist.

Nest New York three-wick candle

Nest New York candles are too often overlooked. The wonderful quality and festive design – in this case, in collaboration with Parisian designer Pierre Marie – make for a special gift. The scent is unmistakably festive: think sappy Christmas trees and warm log cabins.

Rouge Triomphe travel spray and fragrance refills, 2 x 15ml

A luxurious keepsake and one that, in my case, gets almost daily use. This beautiful handbag atomiser holds, protects and dispenses from interchangeable fragrance cartridges from Celine, which makes exceptionally fine scents for a fashion-first house (try Black Tie, a warm, silken vanilla – it’s exquisite). Kiko Club K lip gloss in Afters Glow, 10ml

The Body Shop whipped matcha body butter, 200ml

Oura Ring 5

Marvis toothpaste trio, 3 x 15ml

Chanel Coco Mademoiselle Crush Absolu, 100ml

Flyaway kit

If you’re a fan of a ponytail, a slick back or a kiss curl, meet your new handbag essential.

Butter Brick face and body cleanser

Ambient Lighting palette limited edition, 6 x 1.4g

Hourglass Ambient Lighting palettes, while pricey, make everyone look prettier in a way that almost nothing else does. Bibliothèque eau de parfum, 50ml

Carolyn Bessette-style headband

The Carolyn Bessette Kennedy trend has proved more than a Disney+ one-season wonder. Nineties-inspired wide, acetate black or tortoiseshell hairbands are still the height of chic, not to mention practical and easy to wear. This one is a steal of a stocking stuffer.

The Fragrance with Benefits, 75ml

If you’ve ever used a Sam McKnight hairspray or styling product, you’ll know they smell better than most scents. Now you needn’t choose. This takes the original signature fragrance created by perfumer Lyn Harris and makes it suitable for use as perfume on skin, hair and clothes.

Dog bags and dispenser

I am not remotely ashamed to say I have a roll of Glossier poo bags hanging from my handbag, and I’m not afraid to use them.

Hair+Me subscription

Is this a suitable or polite gift for someone who has never so much as mentioned their (all too common) thinning hair? Of course not. But for a loved one who has openly despaired in your direction, a subscription to Hair+Me could prove life-improving. One of the team’s physicians will always decide on the appropriate treatment. Opt for the capsules if they have pets, as the key ingredient in the topical treatment, minoxidil, is toxic to cats and dogs.

Makeup bag

These endlessly practical, durable, zip-up clear beauty, toiletries and tech cases are cult classics at this point. Stand in any airport security line, and you’ll see one on the belt.

Snap-on lip tint iPhone case

Wherever I go, whatever I do, one thing I know for sure is that someone will ask me where I got my magnetic lip balm holder. Here’s the answer. Your phone needs to have MagSafe for it to work.

Soothing body bar

Nature of Things is the passion project of Carisa Janes, founder of Hourglass Cosmetics, and it shows: everything is meticulously designed and made. This chunky, fatty, sudsy body bar is 97% plant-based and synthetic fragrance free and, unlike many similarly natural products, lathers properly to leave skin feeling genuinely clean, not just moisturised.

Washable paper makeup bags

Coated paper cosmetics pouches are the easiest (and more responsible) way to cram an excessive number of beauty products into a tiny bag. Which is why I use them, obviously.

Bracelet weights, a pair

Hand weights, a pair

For those of us terrified of fitness clubs and living in normal-sized houses, the threat of ugly, bulky fitness equipment cluttering up the place is enough to keep us glued to the sofa. These discreet, sleek and easy-to-store weights are my solution.

Tobak eau de parfum, 50ml

I love the work of Maya Njie, one of the few black female “noses” working successfully in the privileged, often hereditary, Eurocentric world of fine perfumery. My favourite is Tobak, a warm, cosy blend of spicy cinnamon and cardamom, earthy vetiver and soft, smoky tobacco, but there’s nothing in the lineup that’s not worth a sniff. She helpfully sells travel sizes so you can spread your bets before committing to a full bottle.

Bath salts, 350g

Make bath salts great again. Hotel Mike is set on revamping Britain’s most reviled retro Christmas gift with innovative ingredients, natural fragrance and ferments, and I’m absolutely here for the comeback.

Is It Over Yet? trinket tray

Is it though? Please. While we wait, my jewellery and meds live here.

‘Joni Mitchell sang Both Sides, Now over the phone to me’: folk music legend Judy Collins on her 87 remarkable years

The Guardian Thu, 12 Nov 2026 14:30:42 GMT

As she continues her farewell tour, the US singer-songwriter answers your questions on romance with Stephen Stills, friendship with Carly Simon and how folk underpins all pop

How did you come into Joni Mitchell’s orbit and how did you end up recording Both Sides, Now before she did? Steve-bayley I’m 48 years sober, but in the old days I drank. One night in 1967, I was passed out and the phone rang at about 3am. It was my friend [the musician, songwriter and producer] Al Kooper. He said he’d been at a club and had run into this woman, Joni, who wrote songs. He put her on the phone and she sang Both Sides, Now over the phone. It was brilliant. I said: “I’ll be right over.” I recorded it the next day and it became a huge hit.

I don’t think Joni was too happy that I was the first to record it, but she was very generous and I’ve since recorded many of her songs. She was unknown then, so I’m proud that I was able to help introduce her to the world. She’s one of the great writers of all time.

What is your favourite memory of Leonard Cohen? viennesewaltzer In 1966, a friend at Atlantic Records who always talked about this guy Leonard rang up and said: “Leonard wants to see you. He wants you to sing his songs.” He came to my apartment and said: “I can’t play guitar. I have a terrible voice and I don’t know if this is a song.” Then he played me Suzanne. I said: “Leonard, that is a song and I’m recording it tomorrow.” Which I did – and it became a huge hit. After that, he said: “Now you’ve made me famous. I don’t know why you’re not writing your own songs.” I went straight to the piano and wrote Since You Asked in 40 minutes. That was the beginning of my writing. Leonard was my guru, in a way.

I first encountered the song My Father via This Mortal Coil’s version. Is it autobiographical? mbleeze It’s very autobiographical, although my father wasn’t a coalminer in Ohio and didn’t promise to take us to France. I had to make it rhyme and make sense, but it’s really about the ethereal idea we have of our parents and how they inspire us. My father was blind from the age of four, but he never used a dog or a cane. He went through the world determined to conquer. He went anywhere he wanted – through the city, upstairs in the bus – guided by the sound of his heels on the pavement.

Then he became a great radio personality in three cities. He sang the Great American Songbook and Irish and Scottish folk songs and had books in braille piled up to the ceiling, which he could read to us in the dark. His determination was such that he believed we could achieve anything, which is kinda what the song’s about.

After five superlative traditional folk albums, you got together with [the arranger] Joshua Rifkin in 1966 to produce the groundbreaking album In My Life, in which you treat contemporary song [the Beatles, Leonard Cohen, Bob Dylan, Donovan] with the seriousness usually reserved for classical song. How did you come to do that? hcir321 I’d done Dylan songs before, but for In My Life I’d actually gone back to the songs written in Germany by Brecht and Weill. Once I’d done Pirate Jenny – [sings] “You gentlemen can watch while I’m scrubbing the floor” – I thought it would be interesting to take songs from Berlin from the 1940s and put them with this wonderful music the Beatles and others were doing, so the contrast was really interesting. I was always searching.

Stephen Stills wrote the epic seven-minute masterpiece Suite: Judy Blue Eyes about you on Crosby, Stills & Nash’s debut. Is it your favourite song by the band? raphph When we were making Who Knows Where the Time Goes [with Stills on guitar and bass], we had an affair that lasted four months, but I didn’t like California. He didn’t like New York, or therapy, and I was in both. After we split up, I was in California doing a show on my birthday and he brought me flowers and sang Judy Blue Eyes to me. We were both in tears and I said: “Oh, it’s beautiful, but it’s not going to get me back.” I’d launched into another affair with someone else, but Stephen and I have been friends for 60 years.

After my wonderful husband, Louis, died in 2024, we played a song together and on stage Stephen said: “She married the right guy,” which was so touching – they were buddies. Stephen also wrote Helplessly Hoping about me and I wrote Houses about him. All his songs were incredible, but I’m calling my tour the Sweet Judy Blue Eyes farewell tour and he doesn’t mind that.

How much of the broadening of your repertoire in the 1960s and early 1970s was due to the environment at Elektra Records and to [the label owner] Jac Holzman in particular? Delverie Jac was – is – so brilliant and so cooperative and such a great partner in having things to say about what I was doing and what I was writing. He was always there, for 25 years, and Elektra was a very eclectic label, from Carly Simon to the Stooges. When Jac went to Los Angeles and brought the Doors on to Elektra, he called me first and said: “I want you to know that I’m embracing the Doors as an artist and I want you to hear them.” I fell in love with them and told him they were great. Jac’s still working at 95 and we talk often.

What is at the heart of the sub-genre of folk music that you do? What is it exactly that people are connecting with? eamonmcc I learned all the gorgeous old songs from the Denver Folklore Society – Maid of Constant Sorrow and the like. The folk music genre connects to everyone and everything because they’re stories about people’s lives, their joy and pain. I was lucky enough to find the originals and then the new ones, like Leonard Cohen and the Doors, and they all melded together and became the music of the time, and it’s lasted and is still big everywhere. Inside every great pop song, there’s a folk song.

My favourite album of yours is Who Knows Where the Time Goes. How did you come across the great title track, at the time a completely unknown composition by Sandy Denny? goringgull We were closing up for the day when this guy pulled up to the studio on a motorcycle, raced inside and threw this cassette on the desk of my producer, David Anderle. He said: “You have to record this song.” We played the cassette and I said: “Oh my God, of course, we have to do it.” It’s a beautiful song and I’m so grateful that I got to know her and spent time with her in England and New York. We drank together and it was a time of wonder. An amazing woman. I still have some little flowers that she gave me that I keep in my studio.

Who was the first singer who lit the fire in you? SarahCG An American singer called Jo Stafford, who was very big in the popular arena. When I heard her singing: [sings] “’Twas in the merry month of May when the green buds a-swelling, a young man on his death bed lay for the love of Barbara Allen,” she touched my heart. I told my father I had to have a guitar and that set me on my journey. I never met her, but years later I was very glad to be asked to do the liner notes for a collection of her best songs.

I have about 30 of your albums; which do you consider your best – and why? Cloudberry2021 The most recent, Spellbound, consists of 12 songs that I wrote. It’s the first time I’ve done that and it was nominated for a Grammy, so I’m very happy about that one. I’m writing for another project now and have never lost that thrill of writing songs and working out how to do them.

What led to the collaboration with [the Manchester band] Puressence? axolotly They recorded a beautiful version of Che, a song about Che Guevara that took me four years to write. Nobody else had ever recorded it, but I thought their version was one of the best things I’ve ever heard. So I was intrigued. I found them, met up with [the singer] James Mudriczki in England, we got to know each other and I ended up singing on their album [2011’s Solid State Recital]. James is wonderful.

You did Fisherman’s Song with Carly Simon on her 1990 album. How did that collaboration come about? Micktrick Carly sang a song of mine that Dolly Parton also sang, so I’ve accomplished something I thought would never happen. I’ve known Carly since she was in the Simon Sisters with her sister Lucy years ago. All her sisters were friends of mine, then Carly and I were in Greenwich Village in the 60s when it was a hive of talent. You’d walk down the street and bump into Tom Paxton and he’d say: “I’ve written this song,” and I’d record it.

I met Bob Dylan in that time, but I’d first met him in 1959 and 1960 at a little club in the mountains called the Gilded Garter and we’d get drunk together. He was doing old Woody Guthrie blues then, so when I saw this song written down as “by Bob Dylan” – “How many roads must a man walk down” – I thought it must have been a mistake. I soon realised it wasn’t and started recording his songs. Lately, Masters of War has been too frightening for me to sing, but I’ll try again, because it’s a magnificent protest song and it should be heard.

1939 [when Collins was born] was a long time ago. How do you embrace the magnitude? EdinKyo My mother was married to a blind man she met on a bus in Seattle and they raised five kids and we learned the history of our country and what was precious to our founders. Now, we have AI and it’s a very different world, but the fundamentals don’t change. We’re still making art and music and we’re trying to save the planet. We meet people, get together with our families, get into an airplane and fly to another place. We get through our tragedies and we learn. The way I feel is that if we’re still on the planet, we still have things to do.

Judy Collins’ farewell tour of the US runs until 22 May 2027. Her final Irish concert is at St Michael’s theatre, New Ross, on 24 January 2027 and her final UK concert is at the Palladium, London, on 6 February 2027

NAZA: how and where to watch the Guardian’s acclaimed Gaza documentary

The Guardian Thu, 12 Nov 2026 14:23:50 GMT

Film features testimony from 24 Israeli officials involved in surveillance and remote killing of Palestinian civilians

NAZA will be released in full on the Guardian’s website for free in early December. Sign up here to be notified of the exact streaming date and to be sent a link to the film when it is live.

NAZA has been shown by cinemas in 47 countries and seen by more than 1.5 million people since its release last month, making it one of the most-watched documentary films with a theatrical release in 2026. The film has been offered to a number of distributors and cinemas in Israel but has not been screened there yet.

You can watch a trailer here.

NAZA is a documentary featuring testimony from 24 Israeli military intelligence officers and soldiers involved in the surveillance and remote killing of Palestinian civilians during the war in Gaza. The film’s title comes from an Israeli military acronym used euphemistically to refer to civilians expected to be killed in a military attack.

The interviewees detail the methods used by the Israeli military in Gaza, including AI-based systems built to identify large numbers of potential Hamas operatives, who were then bombed in their homes at night, in the knowledge that the attacks would also kill their families.

Interviews were filmed at night on rooftops in Tel Aviv, on the condition of anonymity, because of the risks involved in speaking publicly. The appearance and voices of participants in the film have been digitally altered to disguise their identities.

The film was directed by the Oscar-winning Israeli directors Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor and produced by the Guardian. It builds on revelations first published by the Israeli-Palestinian magazine +972, the Hebrew-language news outlet Local Call and the Guardian newspaper between 2023 and 2025.

Abraham and Szor were two of the four co-directors – with the Palestinians Basel Adra and Hamdan Ballal – of No Other Land, which documents the destruction of Masafer Yatta, a village in the occupied West Bank targeted by Israeli forces. It won the Oscar for best documentary in 2025.

NAZA was co-produced by James Wilson and executive-produced by Jonathan Glazer, the team behind the Oscar-winning film The Zone of Interest.

NAZA has received widespread critical acclaim and is selling out in cinemas across the world. The New York Times says it is “tough to watch and impossible to ignore”, while New York Magazine describes it as “one of the most important films of our time”. In a five-star review, the Financial Times says that “journalism and film-making brilliantly entwine”. British Vogue calls NAZA a “brilliant and harrowing film”.

The film won the special jury prize at the Venice film festival in September, where its premiere had a 25-minute ovation – a festival record. In November, it won the best political documentary from the Critics Choice Association.

The film, its directors and their confidential sources have faced fierce attacks from the Israeli government and military. The prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, has ordered the attorney general and the head of the Shin Bet security service to reveal the identities of sources interviewed and prosecute them for causing “harm to Israel’s diplomatic and security interests”.

Netanyahu also threatened to strip Abraham and Szor of their citizenship, accusing them of treason. The Israeli military’s chief of staff, Eyal Zamir, said the military would “not allow soldiers to be made targets through lies and blood libels” and would use “every tool at our disposal” against the film.

Far-right groups have vowed to hound the film-makers on their return to Israel and picketed Szor’s family home. Some of the messages included explicit calls for violence, with one protester demanding the “death penalty for traitors”.

The Israeli military claimed there were “substantial errors” in the film and that it had relied on sources who had only a partial picture of the target approval process. It said that while AI was used to help identify targets in Gaza, final decisions on strikes, and the risk of civilian casualties, were signed off by officers.

In response, the team behind the film have revealed they spoke to more than 100 sources with knowledge of the military systems used in the war.

The Israeli government is promoting an online film project, called NAZA: The Real Story, which mimics the style of the genuine NAZA film and is hosted on a website called nazadocumentary. com. It is not the real NAZA documentary and has been misleading some viewers.

Initially, the rival film’s website falsely presented itself as a promotional page for NAZA itself, naming Abraham and Szor as the directors, and listing film festivals where the documentary was to be screened. The site now appears as a platform for the rival film, which has been promoted by Israeli embassies.

Ariel Averbuch, an Israeli attorney and army reservist who co-created NAZA: The Real Story, describes it as an “offensive move” to shift the world’s focus from allegations about the Israeli military’s killing of civilians.

Szor and Abraham have addressed the backlash to their documentary. “Our country is doing so much to hide these systems,” Szor said.

NAZA is in cinemas worldwide and will screen for free on the Guardian’s website from early December. Sign up here to be the first to watch it

‘To them, we’re just NPCs’: the artists and activists challenging Trump’s video game propaganda

The Guardian Thu, 12 Nov 2026 14:00:43 GMT

Order a Diet Coke or invade Iran – that’s the choice facing the US president in one of several satirical games, as designers turn the gamification of politics back on the White House

In early September, the Trump White House announced a surprising new addition to its official website. Named simply Arcade, it is a collection of browser games based on classic titles such as Flappy Bird, Snake, and Tetris, but re-tuned as flagrant works of political propaganda. Designed to court reactionary gamers, they push the administration’s policies on immigration and other hot-button issues, while dehumanising their targets. There have recently been some new additions: a Temple Run clone named Red Scare about crossing the “ration market” and escaping the Democratic Socialists of America, and another simple item-matching game about the threat of socialism. In the midst of increasing fuel, utility and grocery prices thanks to the Iran war, these were naked attempts to distract voters by appealing to their video game nostalgia.

After an explosion of news coverage, Arcade caught the attention of the games industry. The Tetris Company warned on social media that it “took copyright infringement very seriously.” Days later, the game was removed from the White House site. However, aside from a March 2026 statement from the Pokémon Company condemning the White House for using its characters in Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) propaganda, major video game companies have been relatively silent in the face of the administration’s widespread usage of their IP.

But now, video game creators and artists are pushing back, looking to regain ground the industry has ceded to reactionary ideologies over the last decade by turning the gamification of politics back on Trump. Anonymous art collective The Secret Handshake has been known for its political activism since installing a sculpture of Donald Trump and sex offender Jeffrey Epstein at the National Mall in downtown Washington, DC. This spring, the group developed a game entitled Operation Epic Furious: Strait to Hell and made it available online, as well as installing three free arcade cabinets on the National Mall.

A satire on the Trump administration, the game allows players to control the president in a Pokémon-style challenge that starts with an important choice: order a Diet Coke, or invade Iran. As the game progresses, Trump heads to Iran to collect barrels of oil (called “lube” in the game) and encounters administration members such as vice-president JD Vance, secretary of state Marco Rubio, and “secretary of war”, Pete Hegseth. It’s unwinnable, which is the point, though you can get a “Game Over” screen by trying to hold Melania Trump’s hand.

The Secret Handshake had never made a video game until Operation Epic Furious: Strait to Hell. “The ‘form’ was really dictated by the Trump Administration,” a member of Secret Handshake says via email. “It’s not that we wanted to make a video game; it’s that the Pentagon began using video games to promote their war in Iran and make it seem ‘cool’. They actually introduced the idea of a video game, not us. We felt like, well, if they’re going to use video games to promote their war, let’s make a video game satirising that war.”

The collective followed similar logic when creating their second free game, Operation Epic Furious: Nuuk ’Em All which tasks players with speaking to Trump’s advisers, including a UFC fighter as “secretary of combat” and a no-bid contractor helping renovate The White House. The aim is to piece together enough “Big Brainpower” to figure out how to distract voters from the oil crisis. After Trump accidentally hits on his own daughter, Ivanka, and speaks to enough advisers to collect enough partial ideas to make one “big beautiful idea”, he decides to invade Greenland.

For The Secret Handshake, the video game as a medium helps people take in “the insanity” of what’s happening, which the collective believes may be hard to ascertain from just headlines. “When you are using a medium that’s very familiar, like a video game, and you’re going through these actions, it allows you to experience the headlines in a different way,” a spokesperson says. “This game is meant to be a caricature and satire, but it’s full of things in there that aren’t. Trump calling a woman a maggot felt very intense to experience in the form of a game.”

The Secret Handshake had to learn how to build a game on the fly for Operation Epic Furious. “We had no idea what we were doing,” a spokesperson explains. “It was a lot of trial and error, and figuring it out as we went along. We did have someone helping that understood this world and could actually make it happen, but no one was a game designer.” They describe the games as, “held together with duct tape”.

Still, there are avid gamers in the group, and they pulled inspiration from Japanese role-playing adventures, particularly the early Final Fantasy titles, while the invidious, scatalogical tone is similar to South Park games such as The Stick of Truth and The Fractured But Whole. The aim was for the games to be funny and to properly satirise the absurdity of the current administration. So far, more than 350,000 people have played them online.

Two further anti-Trump games mimic the iconic arcade shooter Space Invaders, and they couldn’t have been made in more different ways. This summer, game developer Richie Branson partnered with nonprofit All for America to create Tax Evaders, in which you choose one of four playable pilots (President Trump, vice-president JD Vance, House speaker Mike Johnson, or Senate leader John Thune) before jumping into the first level, destroying healthcare and lining billionaire pockets.

“There’s something a bit unsettling about playing as the ‘villain’,” says Branson, who created Tax Evaders using the free and open-source game development engine, Godot. “The intent here is to drive home the point that these officials are destroying beneficial programmes with the same combination of enthusiasm and indifference as someone blowing up enemy space ships in an arcade game.”

The Trump administration’s aggressive push into online culture is working, according to Branson, who said the White House team is, “on a rampage” with its memelord and gaming culture posts. “It’s a very cunning way of spreading whatever message they’re trying to spread,” he says, before referring to the White House Arcade as “gamified propaganda”, and “garbage, [with] no love for the art”. Tax Evaders has had over 50,000 players and over 2m page impressions since July.

Alfie Souter and Carlota Real work in advertising together. They often chat about breaking news and trending topics, so when they saw the White House release its propaganda arcade, they decided to do something about it. “The craziest thing is the oversimplification of such a complex issue, like immigration,” says Real. “What they’re trying to do is boil this down to the minimum that people understand. A Tetris game; everyone on the planet has probably played it once, and they apply it to the shitshow that they’re doing.”

Angered by the administration’s trivialision of the issues and its demonisation of immigrants, the duo started brainstorming their own version of a simplified game with a political message. With no background in game design, they decided to build it in ChatGPT, which itself is perhaps a satirical message: many believe the Trump Arcade games are “vibe-coded”, or built using plain language to describe a game to a generative AI program, which then codes it.

The result is Corrupt Invaders. Essentially a homage to Space Invaders with an anti-Trump filter, the game tasks you with moving Trump’s “$400m Qatari gift” (his aeroplane) to “collect another $1.4bn in crypto.” Your final score is subtracted from Trump’s reported cryptocurrency earnings. According to Souter the duo wanted the game to be focused on something that felt inarguable about the Trump regime and settled on corruption, using the $400m Boeing 747-8 luxury jet gifted by Qatar. Federal law says US officials can only accept gifts under $480, but the Trump White House insisted Trump accepting the aircraft was legal. “We thought about that jet, and also the $1.4bn earnings in crypto last year – those numbers are so ridiculous,” says Souter. “That’s why when you play the game, you subtract it from the score, because it’s such an unfathomable number”.

The two wanted to focus on the money that President Trump and his close allies have earned since his second presidency and juxtapose that against Americans’ consistent concerns with the cost of living crisis. The games are designed to makes the dichotomy crystal clear. Recently, the duo launched Diesel Kong, a parody of the classic Nintendo platformer Donkey Kong in the context of rising oil prices due to the continued war in Iran. “Prices are going up. Putin’s throwing useless barrels, can Trump be saved?” asks the starting screen. Trump stands in place of Princess Peach, while a nondescript Maga supporter wearing an American flag shirt and red hat tries to make his way up the ramps and ladders.

The developers and activists behind these games are pushing back against the Trump administration’s gamified propaganda while looking to subvert the gaming subcultures the president has co-opted. “Our current administration runs the country as if were a video game, with no real sense of sympathy for the people affected by the losses incurred by their policies,” said Branson. “Gas prices are crazy right now, people’s lives are being affected, but to our nation’s leadership, we’re just NPCs.”

‘It is much, much faster’: could China’s battery-swapping e-trucks be the answer to EV range anxiety?

The Guardian Thu, 12 Nov 2026 14:00:42 GMT

Battery maker CATL aims to have 2,000 swapping stations in China by the end of 2027 and to bring the tech to Europe

Every day, Wang Bing drives his big electric lorry to send about five tonnes of goods between the cities of Haikou and Dongfang on Hainan, a tropical island in southern China. A round trip covers about 500 kilometres (310 miles). But refuelling is not something Wang worries about.

“When my battery runs low, I just drive my truck into a battery-swapping station to get a fully charged one,” says the 53-year-old, who shares the journey with a colleague in eight-hour shifts.

Wang has been a lorry driver for nearly three decades. In the first two of those, he drove conventional lorries fuelled by diesel. About five years ago, he began driving an electric model after the logistics company he worked for upgraded its fleet. In July this year, his old e-truck, which used conventional plug-in charging, was replaced by one with a swappable battery.

In the past, Wang had to spend an hour and half charging his battery each time, but with his new truck, it takes just five minutes or so to have a drained battery removed and a fresh one replaced. “I am very happy,” he says.

Battery swapping is not new in China, where more than 400,000 e-trucks (or over 90% of the global total) were sold last year. The Chinese carmaker Nio commercialised the technology nearly a decade ago for smaller electric vehicles (EVs). But in 2023, the Chinese battery behemoth CATL launched a battery-swapping system for electric lorries through a subsidiary brand called Qiji Energy.

To Wang, the biggest advantage of the technology is the time it saves. “It is much, much faster,” he says. “I don’t even need to leave my truck when the battery is being swapped.”

This swiftness builds on the cost advantage e-trucks already have over their fossil-fuelled peers when it comes to refuelling.

“Electricity is cheaper than oil,” Wang says. The per-kilometre fuelling cost for an e-truck works out about 1.1 yuan (12p) in Hainan, he says, significantly lower than that for a diesel truck, which exceeds 2 yuan (22p) a kilometre. “That means my e-truck can save more than 20,000 yuan (£2,200) per month,” Wang says.

When a truck approaches a battery-swapping station, the station’s cameras automatically identify the type of battery it uses by checking its number plate. “All the driver needs to do is to drive the truck into a designated area, and the battery will be swapped completely automatically,” says Wei Jiuchun, 46, a test driver at a Qiji Energy battery-swapping station in Suzhou, east China. Wei’s job is to help the station test its system for different models of heavy trucks and under different weather conditions.

It is not just time and fuel costs the technology saves but, in China, the initial lump sum a buyer has to put down to get an e-truck, says Mao Shiyue, a Beijing-based researcher at the International Council on Clean Transportation (ICCT).

The upfront purchase price for an e-truck is significantly higher than for a comparable diesel model, a major obstacle for those vehicles’ wider adoption in many parts of the world. In China, a customer opting for battery swapping typically buys an e-truck without a battery, and then rents the battery from a service provider. As the cost of a battery is about 40% of an e-truck’s price, the business model can make e-trucks a lot more affordable, Mao says.

The technology can also help minimise the pressure EV charging brings to the power grid, according to Mao, because swapping stations have more flexibility to spread out the charging time for the depleted batteries.

“If the grid sees a spike in electricity demand during peak hours, those stations can even act as an energy-storage station by returning the electricity stored in their batteries back to the grid to ease the strain,” he says.

after newsletter promotion

CATL, the world’s biggest battery manufacturer, is a key player in promoting battery swapping for heavy trucks in China. The company’s support for the technology is critical for its large-scale rollout, says Phate Zhang, the founder of CnEVPost, a Shanghai-based outlet focusing on EVs.

CATL plans to put 900 battery-swapping stations into operation across China by the end of this year, expanding its current network twice more. By the end of 2027, it wants the number to reach 2,000.

The company has also teamed up with the London-based renewable energy supplier Octopus to bring the technology to Europe. It intends to open its first group of battery-swapping “mega hubs” in the UK next year, and a network of more than 30 hubs in Europe by 2035.

In China, battery-swapping is still a minority charging method for its rapidly growing e-truck fleet. In 2024, about one-third of the zero-emission trucks in the country featured this technology, while the rest largely had conventional plug-in charging, according to the latest available figures.

One downside is that drivers often need to stick to a particular service provider that caters to the specific type of swappable batteries their e-trucks use.

“For example, some batteries are swapped from the chassis, while others are swapped from the top of the truck,” says Xue Lulu, a senior associate at World Resources Institute China. “Even under the same technological route, batteries made by different companies often have different specifications.” This means drivers cannot drop into any random swapping station to get their trucks replenished, which could restrict the journeys they can make, she says.

Plus, battery swapping doesn’t necessarily mean drivers will save time, Xue says. During her field research in China, she found some lorry drivers would wait outside battery-swapping stations for one to two hours before going in because they wanted to avoid using the service during peak hours, to save money. “Logistics firms are extremely sensitive to costs,” she says.

The most suitable users are probably drivers who, like Wang, work on fixed routes served by battery-swapping stations. Mao says the charging method has been rolled out most successfully among companies that use heavy trucks in specific settings, such as those carrying goods in ports and factories, as well as within a city or between two nearby cities. “For unpredicted and long-haul routes, there are still challenges for rolling it out on a large scale,” he says.

Pierre Sage’s failure to fix defensive flaws leaves Crystal Palace seeking new solution

The Guardian Thu, 12 Nov 2026 14:00:42 GMT

A losing run, set-piece struggles and a call for help led Steve Parish to cut ties with the manager after five months

The moment that summed up Crystal Palace’s season under Pierre Sage came five minutes before half-time at Selhurst Park on Sunday. After Palace had gone close to taking the lead on numerous occasions against Liverpool, the Frenchman must have feared the worst when Alexis Mac Allister headed in from a soft free-kick conceded by Jefferson Lerma. The TV cameras immediately panned to Steve Parish in the stands. After the Palace chair removed his hands from in front of his eyes, his expression said everything you needed to know. The only surprise was that Sage had to wait until Thursday before his inevitable fate was confirmed.

Not since the start of the 2017-18 season, after Frank de Boer was appointed as Palace’s first permanent foreign manager and sacked after five matches, have the club found themselves bottom. In their record 14th consecutive season in the top flight, and with preliminary work having started on building a new £200m main stand despite major doubts over funding, Palace cannot afford to be relegated.

Sage has been walking a tightrope since the 5-0 thrashing at Brighton last month when it was made clear to the 47-year-old that he must tighten a defence that had conceded the most goals in the Premier League. Some players are thought to have questioned his training methods, although Dean Henderson, the captain, was among those believed to have pledged their support for Sage after defeats by Newcastle and Tottenham.

There was some evidence Palace’s players were adapting to his desire to play more on the front foot rather than relying on the counterattacking approach that brought his predecessor, Oliver Glasner, so much success. But they have been far too open at the back and Liverpool’s second goal from Florian Wirtz was almost a copy of Hoffenheim’s in Thursday’s 1-1 Europa League draw, when Palace were extremely fortunate to snatch a point in a game Parish did not attend because he was in New York.

Palace have conceded eight goals from set plays in the Premier League, including four in their current run of four straight defeats. Fixing a problem that dates back to Glasner’s spell has to be the priority for Thomas Frank, who looks poised to take over. The Dane met with Palace in the summer but decided he wasn’t ready to return after a difficult spell at Spurs. He is now believed to be very keen for a new challenge and offers proven Premier League experience - a prerequisite for Parish after Sage. Sean Dyche also had his supporters among the Palace hierarchy. The former sporting director Iain Moody, an influential consultant for Palace who was heavily involved in Sage’s appointment after Sage’s success at Lens last season, worked with the former Nottingham Forest manager at Watford and was thought to favour him.

Frank has played with a back three – a consideration that was a major factor in Palace opting for Sage in an attempt to provide continuity from Glasner – more often than Dyche. Palace could benefit, though, from a change of formation, in the short term at least, given the lack of experienced options owing to the long-term absences of Chadi Riad and Takehiro Tomiyasu.

Palace were rescued from the relegation zone by Sam Allardyce in the 2016-17 season and Parish went back to basics again with Roy Hodgson after De Boer’s disastrous spell, and the team finished 11th despite losing their first seven games. That was without the added complication of European football, however.

Palace signed 11 players in the summer and Sage’s suggestion after the Liverpool game that adjustments may be needed in “some positions during the winter transfer window to give more solutions” is not believed to have gone down well with Parish. Last month, the 61-year-old hired the Raine Group to field interest in investment or a possible sale of the club he helped to rescue from administration in 2010. His American billionaire co-owners Woody Johnson, David Blitzer and Josh Harris are understood to have reservations about funding the new stand.

Parish is said to view the squad as too good to be in this position, although Palace failed to adequately replace the key defenders Maxence Lacroix and Marc Guéhi this year, bringing in Tomiyasu on a free and Axel Disasi and the 18-year-old Honest Ahanor on loan. It is telling that Coventry and Hull – Palace’s next two opponents after the international break – have a higher net spend over the past five years despite being in the Championship until this season. Palace broke their transfer record twice last January and providing mid-season funds will be essential.

Much of the blame for the summer’s haphazard recruitment has been pinned on Matt Hobbs, the sporting director brought in from Wolves to replace the influential Dougie Freedman, who moved to Saudi Arabia in spring 2025. Freedman is said still to be a sounding board over transfers and there have been questions over the influence of the agents Unique Sports Group given the large number of players it has, or has had, on Palace’s books, but it is Parish who calls the shots despite owning less than 10% of the shares. His next move will be crucial to their hopes of avoiding relegation.
