You can see everything on this list: the 20 most jaw-dropping documentaries – ranked!

The Guardian Thu, 12 Nov 2026 13:32:25 GMT

Ahead of the UK release of Nathan Fielder’s hotly anticipated Elizabeth Holmes film, we count down the most shocking and affecting true stories ever committed to cinema

A 50-second dispatch from daily life blew the whistle on the approaching juggernaut of cinema and its unbeatable horsepower of verisimilitude. But if we must be strictly factual about the iconic Lumière brothers’ short, the anecdote about audience members fleeing their seats in fear of being crushed by the oncoming locomotive probably never happened.

The dramatic re-enactment is the car chase of the documentary industry: a crude way of keeping our attention. But by using rotoscoped animation, Keith Maitland’s riveting account of the 1966 mass shooting at the University of Texas completely revitalises the re-enactment as part of the documentary toolkit. It leaves us prone under the killer’s crosshairs with the emotional immediacy of a thriller and an oddly elegiac comedown.

Amid the 21st century true-crime deluge, it’s a relief to stumble on a less violent mystery that foregrounds women’s lives rather than their deaths. But the Chilean director Maite Alberdi’s docudrama still skirts the boundaries of credibility: it focuses on Ale, a desperate Mexican mother who, after three miscarriages, duped her husband into believing she was pregnant. With Alberdi also trying to verify whether Ale was a child-snatcher, the story of this bizarre long con doubles up as a metaphysical inquiry into the ultimate knowability of people.

Documentaries often introduce us to indelible personalities, but it’s vanishingly rare when they initiate us, Narnia-style, into entire new realms. Marc Singer unearthed one in the homeless community of “mole men” living in abandoned subway tunnels extending out of Penn Station in New York City. With DJ Shadow’s mindscape compositions lighting the way into the gloom, this is a grimly transfixing voyage to the centre of urban deprivation.

This early Alex Gibney cut was shocking in the mid-00s – surely boardroom cynicism and corporate fraud couldn’t occur on this scale? Now, its revelations about the collapse of the US energy company – and the underlying profit-falsifying – feel like a taster for You Can See Everything’s tech-company chicanery and the post-truth air we all breathe.

A prime cut of Werner Herzogian insanity, yet somehow the great master never laid claim to this high-seas tragedy. The amateur sailor Donald Crowhurst bit off more than he could chew when he entered a 1968 solo circumnavigation race. Floundering in the Atlantic, he faked his own positions for seven months. The quixotic madness seems to infect everyone: a French competitor, Bernard Moitessier, having rounded the globe once, opts to keep going.

From Frank Capra’s recruitment drive to Ken Burns’ Vietnam panorama, war documentaries employ all manner of tactics. But for sheer concussive immersiveness, it’s hard to beat Sebastian Junger’s and Tim Hetherington’s stint embedded with the US’s lost boys in the Korangal valley in Afghanistan. Although it ducks political commentary, the ever-present sense of threat from the Taliban is indictment enough of the forever war.

The city-symphony documentary is as old as cinema – and Godfrey Reggio’s Gesamtkunstwerk is the most monumental. Pulling a Kubrick, it starts by juxtaposing neolithic drawings and a rocket launch, then blasts us through ever-accelerating stages of human civilisation in between, soundtracked by Philip Glass’s incantatory score. How about an update for capitalism’s endgame phase of AI chaos?

Stowed aboard a Massachusetts trawler, this experimental marvel is like swilling around in the chowder of Captain Ahab’s dreams. It’s a narration-free montage of hurtling anchors, churning spume, loitering seagulls and asphyxiated fish sliding into the maw of the boat – presumably the leviathan of the title. Attended to by tattooed, cigarette-toting seadogs, you feel as if you’re merging with the vessel’s consciousness.

Any footage of someone climbing the 900-metre Yosemite landmark El Capitan would have captured our attention. But doing it unroped for the first time, as the daredevil Alex Honnold does here, adds a distinct edge and extra viewing investment. There’s the ethical quandary: to what is Honnold subjecting his girlfriend, Sanni McCandless? Then there’s the possibility that the directors, Elizabeth Chai Vasarhelyi and Jimmy Chin, are heightening the risks by filming this brinkmanship.

The line between Herzog and his gallery of hubristic dreamers is thin – and never so pointedly highlighted as in Les Blank’s chronicling of Herzog’s 1982 adventure epic Fitzcarraldo. Making a rudder for his own back, Herzog drags a steamboat over a mountain – then must make a call on letting Indigenous people murder his ignoble-savage leading man, Klaus Kinski. The director’s much-memed “the birds are in misery” monologue counts as comic relief.

One for the cinephiles and the aestheticians. Dziga Vertov’s city-symphony set out to supply “a truly international language of cinema based on its absolute separation from the language of theatre and literature”. He’s as good as his word: Man With a Movie Camera overspills with slo-mo, double time, match cuts, split screen, rhythmical editing, stop-motion animation and, in the margins of his mosaic of Moscow, Odesa and Kyiv, self-reflexive shots of the creator himself. An ultra-cool pop-up book for the medium.

In many ways flawed in documentarian terms, this cataclysmic tribute to the murdered doctor Andrew Bagby, directed by his childhood friend Kurt Kuenne, is firmly in his camp. But if his accused killer, Bagby’s ex-girlfriend Shirley Turner, receives no shrift, the film’s partisan weakness is also its greatest strength. Kuenne demonstrates the force of love surrounding Bagby, which allowed his grieving parents to survive an unimaginable ordeal: co-parenting their grandson with Turner, then in turn having the infant’s death inflicted on them when he was killed by Turner in a murder-suicide.

Has there ever been a more jaw-dropping verite image than that homunculus impossibly upright in the void between the twin towers? Featuring in this film seven years after 9/11, it was horribly redolent of other visuals, such as the falling man. The inhuman scale speaks for itself, but behind it is the story of the French daredevil Philippe Petit’s 1974 high-wire act in New York City, told with heist-like relish by the director James Marsh.

Meted out in imposing blockbuster beats by the director Kevin Macdonald, Touching the Void is a moral litmus test and shocking survival saga wrapped up in one. Climbing in the Andes, Simon Yates must decide whether to break an alpinist taboo to save his own life and cut the rope on his partner, Joe Simpson. What would you do? Probably not crawl for three days over ice and glacial scree to reach safety, as Simpson did later.

The documentary that cracked Herzog open for mainstream audiences. The goldmine of footage of the failed actor turned bear-whisperer Timothy Treadwell hovers between depicting him as a camcorder-touting holy fool and a reckless transgressor – classic Herzogian ambivalence about the natural world, in other words. He deems the audio of Treadwell’s death too raw for our ears, but makes great play of listening to it himself.

At the head of the early 00s documentary revival, Andrew Jarecki navigates a slippery and disturbing domestic enigma here: whether the Long Island computer teacher Arnold Friedman and his son Jesse were violent child molesters or the victims of local paedophile-panic in which their middle-class neighbours were competing to be the biggest victims. Deceptively jocular in its portrayal of a clan, it proves that the biggest mystery of all can be one’s own family.

Everyone loves a conman flick – but Bart Layton’s masterly investigation is all the more transfixing for featuring a scam with no obvious reward or purpose, other than obscure psychopathological needs. After a Texas teenager, Nicholas Barclay, goes missing in 1994, he appears to resurface three years later in the southern Spanish city of Linares. The young man is in fact a French shyster, Frédéric Bourdin, with brown eyes unlike Nicholas’s blue ones – but he is welcomed into the family home all the same. Stranger than fiction is suddenly a revitalised cliche.

Knowing about the Holocaust isn’t the same as bearing witness. Maybe Claude Lanzmann’s nine-hour Shoah gives greater psychological understanding, but Alain Resnais’s whistle-stop tour of atrocity is the devastating warning shot. In just over half an hour of images never to be unseen, it calmly lays out how mankind surrenders to its worst instincts – and finally reminds us that this could happen anywhere.

Joshua Oppenheimer’s audacious masterstroke takes a step forward from Resnais by daring to empathise with the perpetrators of violence and, in doing so, understand its root causes and ramifications. Investigating the 1960s Indonesian anti-communist genocide, Oppenheimer allows a pair of ageing death-squad hoodlums to re-enact their deeds in the cinematic idiom of their youth: film noir and sappy musicals.

Far more than an excavation of a buried chapter of Indonesia’s past, it’s a searing exposé of the reinforcing links between force, state power, moral self-justification, the authorship of history and culture. Ultimately, it’s a strange kind of therapy: just like in The Zone of Interest, our apparatchik antihero ends up dry-retching out his guilt.

Trump won’t save Ukraine. But Marine Le Pen’s betrayal could be worse

The Guardian Thu, 12 Nov 2026 13:22:27 GMT

European leaders need urgently to prepare for a far-right French president who would cut off Kyiv’s financial lifeline

Europe is consumed by two debates that matter less than it thinks, while neglecting one that matters enormously. The first is who should represent the EU in negotiations with Russia. This is largely irrelevant because there is little prospect of serious Ukraine peace talks before the end of winter - despite the fanfare that has surrounded discussions in Abu Dhabi this week. Russia has powerful incentives to escalate the war over the coming months in an attempt to break Ukraine’s economy and civilian morale.

The second is Donald Trump’s approach to Ukraine. This matters less than it once did – and not only because he is now more constrained by a Democratic Congress. Since returning to office in January 2025, Trump has provided no new US military aid to Kyiv. American weapons sales remain important to Ukraine’s war effort, but Trump’s military interventions in the Middle East have further strained supplies of the weapons Ukraine needs most – notably Patriot interceptors.

Ukraine does remain heavily dependent on US early warning intelligence, particularly to detect incoming Russian ballistic missiles, a capability Europe is unlikely to replicate fully before 2030. But the broader point stands: the US is a less indispensable partner to Ukraine than it was two years ago.

The debate European leaders are neglecting is much closer to home: what happens if Marine Le Pen wins France’s presidential election in six month’s time?

A president Le Pen would suspend France’s bilateral aid to Ukraine. More consequentially, her opposition to increasing France’s contribution to the EU budget could jeopardise EU-wide funding. Le Pen is threatening to veto the bloc’s next seven-year budget, including a proposed €100bn facility for Ukraine. This is the mechanism through which the EU hopes to sustain Kyiv financially beyond 2028.

A Le Pen presidency could also give governments further from the frontline political cover to scale back their support. For Italy, Spain, Greece, Austria, Hungary and Slovakia, Ukraine is a lower priority and Italian support could weaken further after next year’s election.

The resulting bilateralisation of aid could leave a smaller group of northern and western European countries shouldering the burden. They would struggle to compensate for the loss of contributions from much of southern and central Europe.

Le Pen would also threaten Ukraine’s EU membership prospects and the bloc’s sanctions regime against Russia. Ukraine’s membership of the EU would become virtually impossible: key decisions require unanimity, and Le Pen has already opposed Kyiv’s accession. Nor would she be alone in her reluctance. Despite their public commitments, many EU governments harbour serious reservations about admitting Ukraine.

Sanctions would be equally vulnerable. Le Pen has advocated lifting EU sanctions on Russia since 2017. The bloc’s economic sanctions are due for renewal in July 2027, and a French veto could bring them to an end. She could also block the renewal of sanctions against individuals and veto any new packages.

In short, a Le Pen presidency could simultaneously undermine the three pillars of Europe’s support for Ukraine: on financing, EU membership and sanctions on Russia.

Let us imagine for a moment the worst-case scenario – as a result of Europe’s inability to sustain Ukraine after a Le Pen victory, Kyiv is pushed into a settlement on Moscow’s terms. Russia gets constitutional recognition of its annexation of Donetsk and Luhansk (and possibly even Zaporizhzhia and Kherson). Moscow also imposes political and security conditions on Kyiv: a prohibition on Nato membership, a cap on the size of its armed forces, and the political demands Moscow dresses up as “denazification”.

After an unprovoked invasion and almost five years of ruthless Russian attacks on civilians, Ukrainians would see the deal as a humiliating defeat. The humiliation would be greater still if Kyiv signed under pressure from Washington, with support from some parts of Europe and opposition from others.

Above all, the deal would be a humanitarian tragedy. Ceding the rest of the Donbas would leave tens of thousands of civilians under Russian occupation. They would face what occupation has meant elsewhere: mass detentions, forced disappearances and torture. Others, who manage to get evacuated, would add to Ukraine’s internally displaced population.

Because any transfer of territory requires a referendum, Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, would have to hold one and would probably put the whole deal on the ballot. Ukrainians would very likely reject it, opening an unprecedented political crisis. If Ukraine could no longer keep fighting, Zelenskyy would face two bad options: overrule the vote and impose a deeply unpopular deal; or resign and leave a vacuum for the next government to fill.

The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment

after newsletter promotion

Either way, protesters would probably fill the streets, opponents would challenge the agreement in court and whoever signed it would lose office. The deal would also need to clear parliament, where it could be voted down because few MPs would want their names on it. If it were instead imposed outside the constitution, politics would splinter into factions, some vowing to scrap the settlement and others insisting on moving on.

The economy is likely to follow. Donors and investors who had planned to fund reconstruction would pull back, leaving billions in potential deals on the table. The threat of Russia’s re-invasion and political instability would stall reconstruction. Millions more Ukrainians would then head west to rejoin their families, escaping a deal that fails to provide proper security guarantees and leaving economic devastation behind. At the same time, many soldiers would refuse to lay down their arms and keep up a guerrilla war in the ceded parts of Donbas. These units would be hard to rein in, possibly handing Moscow a pretext to resume full-scale fighting.

Over time, the sense of betrayal is bound to harden into resentment of western partners and Kyiv’s wartime elites alike. Most dangerous of all, Russia would probably use the pause to rebuild its economy and army. Soon, Vladimir Putin may feel tempted to exploit Ukraine’s chaos and invade again. The weak security framework of a deal on Russia’s terms would make this possible. Europe would be left with a broken, embittered and heavily armed state on its border, and an emboldened Russia behind it.

None of this is inevitable. Ukrainians have shown little appetite for capitulation, and weeks of US pressure have not shifted public opinion. Kyiv also understands that Moscow’s terms are probably designed to produce exactly this kind of turmoil. Ukraine would accept such a deal only if it had no other choice.

Getting there would necessitate a combination of things going wrong at the same time: a full US cut-off of intelligence and military support that lets Russia push the front back; European funding drying up with no bilateral substitute; and a Russian escalation backed by new mobilisation. Each is possible; together, they are unlikely. Nonetheless, this scenario should give EU capitals serious pause for thought. Policy should be built on the worst-case scenario rather than wishful thinking that Le Pen, in power, will moderate her view of Ukraine, in the way that Meloni has.

Ukraine’s outlook is bleaker than at any point since Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022. Putin’s strategy has always been to outlast the west and achieve politically what he cannot secure on the battlefield. That prospect is becoming more plausible – not because Ukraine is losing the will to fight, or even because of Washington’s retreat, but because of what may happen in Europe next year, making it the weakest link in its own strategy to defeat Russia.

Mujtaba Rahman is the managing director for Europe at Eurasia Group, a political risk research and consulting firm

AI helped UK defy expectations – but will economy’s resilience fizzle out?

The Guardian Thu, 12 Nov 2026 13:08:12 GMT

Despite John Healey’s defiance, the economy faces threats from a tech slowdown and energy bills this winter

AI helps UK economy grow at fastest pace for more than two years

The forecasters were clear when John Healey became chancellor in July: Britain’s resilience to the war in the Middle East would not last. The global economic headwinds were too strong, inflation was beginning to rise and growth would slow to a trickle.

Four months into the job, the economy is continuing to defy expectations after growing by 0.7% in the third quarter – the fastest expansion in two and a half years. It puts the UK on course to be the second-fastest growing G7 economy this year.

On his first day in Downing Street the memo from the Treasury showed the most optimistic City analyst expected 0.3% quarterly growth. Most had pencilled in a figure close to zero. Some were warning that the UK could edge towards a recession.

Despite the gloomy outlook households have continued to spend and business investment has powered ahead, driven by the rollout of AI.

Underneath the bonnet, growth is being spearheaded by IT and professional services – together contributing about half of the rise in activity. As the central sectors in the AI boom, that is hardly surprising – with analysts at ING suggesting the strength in IT was “very clearly a datacentre story” thanks to the UK’s status as a leading destination in Europe for investment.

Overall, Deutsche Bank estimates that AI-related spending has added about 0.3% to 0.4% to GDP growth this year. It is clear to see why Healey is keen to build on the groundwork laid by his immediate predecessor, Rachel Reeves, to harness AI amid government efforts to court global business investment.

Meanwhile, household consumption is up by 1.6% so far this year – helped by spending over the warm summer months even as consumers faced a living standards squeeze because the Iran war fuelled a surge in petrol and diesel prices.

However, the fear is that the UK’s initial resilience to the global economic storm emanating from the Middle East will soon fizzle out.

Both of Britain’s recent growth engines face a tougher period ahead.

After the US midterm elections and revelations at the chipmaker Nvidia, the outlook for the AI investment boom is less certain. Financial markets have been rocked in recent weeks amid fears that a bubble in AI stocks could be about to burst. A slowdown in technology investment could hit the UK. Still, the hope is that swelling demand for AI will not evaporate overnight.

For households, however, a tough winter lies ahead. Energy bills are poised to increase by about a quarter in January, with the average annual household gas and electricity bill expected to climb to more than £2,000. Analysts say it is hard to see how consumer spending would not come under greater pressure in the new year.

In the latest data there were some early warning signs: retail sales and consumer discretionary spending fell in September. Real wage growth is cooling and the headline inflation rate is on track to reach a fresh peak of close to 5% next year.

With growth proving resilient, the Bank of England will feel emboldened to raise interest rates to combat imported inflation. City investors expect at least two more quarter-point increases to 4.5% before the end of next year. That will hit the brakes on the economy and add to the cost of living squeeze.

At last month’s budget Healey struck a defiant tone by arguing that the UK could continue to defy forecasters expectations. That task, however, is becoming increasingly tough.

‘I was home alone when the glacier collapsed. My mum called and told me to run’

The Guardian Thu, 12 Nov 2026 12:00:48 GMT

Location: Bidur, Nepal

Disaster: Floods, 2026

This is Isha Rimal’s story

Isha Rimal is a 17-year-old volunteer for the Red Cross Society in Bidur, Nepal. This summer, her family was caught up in the floods that crashed through the country after a glacier collapsed – an event made more likely by climate change

From the roof of our home we can see the Himalayan goddesses. That is what the mountains mean to us: they are goddesses. I grew up here in Bidur, Nuwakot, two hours from Kathmandu. It is a beautiful place with a perfect climate. Or so I used to think, before the Bhotekoshi flood waters from the glacier collapse tore down the Trishuli River, destroyed many homes and killed some of my friends.

It changed my life. Until then I had planned to study in the US and become a neuroscientist. But now I want to stay here, train as a medical doctor and help my people.

I thought it was an earthquake at first. The house was shaking. My bed was shaking.

I was alone at home. My younger brother and sister were at school, but I was sleeping in because I’d just graduated. At about 9am I got a call from my mum. She told me to come as fast as I could to the college where she worked. She didn’t say why, but she sounded worried. So I got out of bed, locked the house and left as fast as I could. I only had 10% power on my phone.

It is a 10-minute walk from my home to the college. My mum had told me to hurry, so I ran. Everyone was in a hurry and running. Many were going down towards the river – the opposite direction from me. I remember a strange smell.

I didn’t talk to anyone, so I didn’t know what was happening. All that was going through my head was trying to guess why mum had called me. She had never done that before, not while she was at work.

I never imagined the threat could come from the river. That’s also 10 minutes’ walk from my home. My friends and I used to go there as children. People would bathe there. We live among rivers. They had never been something to be scared of.

When I reached the college, I found my mum. She had been informed about the flood. We never imagined it could be so big. Everybody was chattering; there were rumours that all the buildings had collapsed. Mum started crying. She said my brother and sister’s school had been affected, and she hadn’t been able to reach them.

It is difficult for me to remember all my frightened feelings at that time. We didn’t know if we were safe. We learned the bridge had been washed away, so there was no way to go to the other side. There were rumours of more floods. And my brother and sister were missing.

We had no way of knowing where they had gone. Police had turned up at their school in Bidur and told the students to flee. Teachers packed as many as they could in the school bus, but there was only one bus and hundreds of students. The others were just told to run as fast as they could. We asked a relative to look for them on a motorbike. He found my sister. But my brother took more time. He had hitched a lift with some foreigners and reached very high ground. We were crying with worry, and it turned out he had been eating ice-cream!

When the river calmed, we went home. But everything was chaotic. The flood had knocked out two hydropower plants. The phone signals in many areas were down, and there was no electricity. The fans and air conditioning didn’t work, so it was too hot to sleep at night. There was also so much noise from the rescue helicopters.

It has been traumatic. Many died. One of my childhood friends was killed. Others lost their homes. After a while, the bodies of dead people and animals started to smell. Many people are psychologically affected by what happened, by seeing the collapsed homes. My brother and sister were so scared that we sent them to Kathmandu for four days.

Two days later, we had another flood. I don’t think anyone reported it. From then on, there were constant rumours about other floods. And fake alerts, even at 2am. These made people evacuate, and some homes were robbed.

I didn’t dare visit the disaster area for many weeks. When I finally got the courage, I was shocked to see that places in Devighat I used to visit were gone. A temple where I had worshipped, gardens where our family had spent happy times together, markets where we used to shop, all gone. All those memories, gone.

I volunteered for the Red Cross. At first I worked for 30 days in the pharmacy of the emergency clinic. With the local bridge broken, many community members were left stranded and unable to reach Trishuli hospital for urgent care. As a volunteer, I’ve been on the ground assisting our pharmacists with medical inventory, listing treatments and dispensing free medicine directly to those in need.

Seeing people leave our clinic relieved, happy and deeply grateful to the Red Cross for providing what they needed most during this disaster has been the most rewarding experience.

After that, I trained with the sanitation team and learned how to advise people to wash their hands and use water purification tablets. This was important, because many water sources were contaminated.

In some areas the need is still very great. There were many NGOs here immediately after the flood, but most of them have gone. I guess there was no way for them to leave enough for everyone for a lifetime. But many didn’t even provide for five months.

I will continue volunteering until the end of December, then I will go to Kathmandu to study for my entrance exam for medical school.

My thinking has changed. I used to think that life was sorted, and now I have seen how quickly people can be affected. I used to want to be a neuroscientist and have fun in New York, but after seeing the doctors in the clinic I want to help people like they do. I love that. Now I feel happy to stay here and distribute medical treatment. It makes me feel happy when people thank me for doing that. I realise now that I don’t want to leave my country. I want to be here. I want to be a good doctor.

But we must change things. I still love mountains, but now I think people must be more respectful of mountains. We should not treat the climate as a big joke. We shouldn’t mess with it. The Bhotekoshi flood proved that climate change does not respect borders. While our nation contributes almost nothing to global emissions, our people are left rebuilding their lives inside cracked and damaged walls. I think other countries should take more responsibility, but we cannot be negligent here. This is a sign. We need to take the climate as a serious issue. Everyone around the world should do what they can. I am not asking for donations for Nepal; I am asking that everyone minimise the way they are affecting us. If we continue to ignore the melting Himalayas today, the consequences will flow down to everyone’s doorstep tomorrow.

World Cup triumph would be only half the story for England’s wheelchair rugby league squad

The Guardian Thu, 12 Nov 2026 11:58:11 GMT

England go into Friday’s final against France hopeful of retaining their title – and inspiring more to take up their fast-growing, compelling sport

Sport in Britain is so often judged on various key metrics. Attendances, TV viewing figures, revenue and, arguably the most important one of all, trophies. On Friday morning, a group of men will represent England in a World Cup final against France, hoping to retain the trophy they won in 2022 while still playing for something far more important.

The captain of England’s rugby league wheelchair team, Lewis King, remembers what things used to be like as a wheelchair athlete. His life changed in 2009 when, aged 24, he was left partially paralysed after a blood clot on his spine that required an emergency operation. At that stage, playing sport felt impossible.

A few years later King was convinced to try wheelchair rugby league by a friend who he met while rehabbing in Stoke Mandeville hospital. To suggest it was low-key would be putting it mildly. “It started as a bit of fun and you’d only ever have a couple of family members watching; maybe a dog too if you were lucky,” King says. “But I fell in love very easily.”

He, like so many was captivated by the sport’s big selling point. “It is everything great about any version of rugby league, just in a wheelchair: it’s identical in so many ways,” he says. “The big hits, the line breaks, the incredible athleticism … I don’t know how you couldn’t be amazed when you see it for the first time.”

The public clearly agreed four years ago, when a TV audience of almost 2m and 5,000 in attendance in Manchester watched England lift the World Cup. Despite the tournament being behind a paywall in the UK this time, the BBC will televise the repeat showdown with France, offering more crucial exposure.

It is a sport on the rise. It is the most popular wheelchair sport in England by some distance and since the World Cup triumph in 2022, participation has risen by 110%. Four years ago, there were 19 teams playing in formal leagues; there are now 42, and rising.

Clubs such as Leeds Rhinos, Wigan Warriors and the new men’s Super League champions, Wakefield Trinity, do not just have wheelchair teams, they have girls and juniors teams too, offering a pathway into sport for anyone of any age that may not be able to play the running version of rugby league.

But as well as winning, King and his squad are aware their stories inspire a new generation of young men and women. Rob Hawkins, the best player in the world who won the Golden Boot for the third successive year this week, lives with chronic fatigue syndrome and had previously been bedridden for 18 months.

Luis Domingos, who played professional wheelchair basketball before switching to rugby league, contracted polio as a child and no one sums up this story quite like Halifax’s Finlay O’Neill. Diagnosed with hyper-mobility in his knees and forced to give up able-bodied rugby league, O’Neill was inspired by England’s win four years ago.

after newsletter promotion

He is now part of the 2026 squad and the reason why England’s players are performing for something bigger – the vehicle to help rebuild lives after trauma. “We speak about that regularly,” King says. “Finlay was watching us at the last World Cup and now he’s scoring tries and playing in a final himself.

“There is a pathway for anyone and we want to show people trauma in life doesn’t mean you can’t play and enjoy sport. We had some young players present our shirts before we came to Australia. That’s the win for us: seeing the next generation want to do it because of us.”

The game itself has plenty of promise. England and France are the world’s two best teams and the final four years ago was won by four points. Both teams expect a similar scoreline in Wollongong, when another big crowd will be watching. “I would have liked to have played Australia in the final, with it being over there,” King says. However, England dismantled Australia in the semis on Tuesday.

When you watch England in action at the very least you will find yourself in awe of their ability in the midst of their inspiring back stories. You may even find you have just stumbled across your favourite other sport: one England are pretty good at too.

Billions lost and markets roiled by one man’s indiscretion. Isn’t it now clear that these tech bros are too powerful?

The Guardian Thu, 12 Nov 2026 11:17:51 GMT

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair must be the costliest fling in human history – and a preview of what awaits when the tech bubble bursts

One thing we all know about the tech billionaires is they are super-smart. We know this largely because they never stop telling us. The “cognitive elite”, to use their favoured phrase, are entitled to shape our future without our say-so. When Elon Musk goes hiring, he wants “super-high-IQ small-government revolutionaries”. Long before they got private jets, what fuelled these boys was faith in their own brainpower. As a teenager, Jensen Huang wooed his future wife, Lori, thus: “If you do homework with me every Sunday, I promise you you’ll get straight As.”

Lord Byron: I believe it’s your move.

Which raises the question: if you’re that clever, why act so dumb? At last week’s midterms, it was Musk who backed Team Trump to the tune of $446m. With unhedged bets like that, why wouldn’t you want him gambling with your livelihood? This week, it is 63-year-old Huang and his affair with a much younger woman, who the US government strongly suspects is a Chinese spy. That scandal wiped more than $400bn off the value of his company in just two days, making it the costliest fling in human history. But who knows? Perhaps she loved the centibillionaire for his mind.

Forget Sam Altman and Dario Amodei: no one is more central to the future of technology than Huang. He runs Nvidia, which makes the chips powering AI. Previous generations of chips have been compared to kitchen knives: however sharp, they only chop one vegetable at a time. But the graphics-processing units made by Huang’s business are more like food blenders – they can blitz an entire veg patch. That’s what makes Nvidia the foundational infrastructure company of AI and one of the most valuable businesses in the world. And it uses its power: in some of the biggest funny-money deals over the past year in AI, Nvidia has been the money printer. It also stumped up at least $20m for Donald Trump’s new ballroom. Smart!

Not only is Huang one of Trump’s favourite businessmen, he’s warmly welcomed by leaders around the world – including Andy Burnham, who last month in London sank a whisky with him. Even as he falls from grace, Huang’s supporters have brought out the superlatives: “torchbearer”, “irreplaceable”, “incredible human”.

Huang is boss of the most strategically important business in the fastest-growing, biggest-spending industry in the world’s No 1 capitalist economy. He is part of a tiny coterie of people, who may well feel they sit above the norms and laws that govern the rest of us. That’s certainly the way he has been treated so far by Trump, who was personally warned aboard Air Force One that Huang’s love interest is believed to be a spy for Beijing. Not only is China an ever-greater threat to US AI dominance, it has been banned by Washington from getting Nvidia’s top-of-the-range chips. And the US president takes no discernible action.

Some people are in a huge tizz about the spy part of this story, notably the Tory MP Tom Tugendhat, who, after Vladimir Putin invaded Ukraine, demanded that every Russian in Britain be rounded up and expelled. The force is not strong in that one. Personally, I can’t get too excited about the threat to the Trumpian model of AI. Neither, it seems, can Washington: it’s been more than a year since Nvidia was revealed to be selling some of its best stuff to a “dilapidated storefront” outside Kuala Lumpur, which sounded awfully like a pit stop on the way to China. Again, no action. The message ordinary Americans can take from this is that a company so vital to America’s AI-military complex is too big to subject to ordinary laws.

In the everyday world, a CEO who gets into both a sex scandal and a national-security imbroglio wouldn’t stay CEO for more than a minute. At Nvidia, the board has moved with incredible sloth. It declared on Sunday that it “has no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised” – before any independent investigation. It finally met on Wednesday evening after further revelations of a separate extramarital affair with an Nvidia executive. Huang’s fate now reportedly hangs in the balance, but the company board, it may surprise you to know, includes several of his longstanding business associates. You’ll also be gobsmacked to learn that several members of his family are serving in senior positions at Nvidia.

One of the protections for Huang, like Musk and Zuckerberg and Altman, is that there appears to be no succession plan in place should any of those men fall under a self-driving automobile. A suggestion doing the rounds is that the father may now be replaced by one of his children. The Vatican has a more codified succession process for the pope, even if it includes white smoke and Ralph Fiennes.

This scandal is different from the allegations over David Walliams or the convictions handed down against Russell Brand – but one black thread that connects them is the grace afforded to each man by enablers and the powerful. Asked about the Huang affair, Trump described him as a “fine person”. Many of us will remember Trump defending the white nationalists who stormed Charlottesville in 2017. They were “some very fine people”, he said.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

after newsletter promotion

This is the very same sense of impunity that drove so many Americans out last week to protest against Trump, datacentres and AI. At the midterms, the Democrats rode a wave of populism: the many v the money. Nearly two decades after the banking crash, the public anger against an unaccountable, ruinous elite is finally finding a political vehicle. Yet it still lacks the policies to match.

What do even the brightest minds in the Democratic party, or Labour for that matter, want to do about the tech billionaires? A moratorium on datacentres, certainly. A wealth tax, maybe. Given the largeness of the moment, the scale of popular anger, these are tiny measures. What about breaking up private monopolies such as Nvidia and socialising AI? How about combining that with a refoundation of welfare and other essentials of everyday life?

The tech bubble hasn’t burst, but this week we got a small taste of how it might end. When America’s AI bets do collapse, that will be a financial failure, an economic failure and a political failure. Given the strategic importance of these companies and their technologies, there will be demands for huge bailouts. The left should start preparing its own response. Through diffidence and a lack of preparation, it squandered the crisis of 2008; it mustn’t this time. To do so would not be, well, smart.

Aditya Chakrabortty is a Guardian columnist

I’ve had a stinking cold this week – and I’m longing for good advice

The Guardian Thu, 12 Nov 2026 11:00:47 GMT

Heavy and light colds tend to pass more quickly than middle-of-the-road ones. But should I stay in bed or continue mixing with others?

How to define the cold that’s ruining your day? There’s a hierarchy. We start with the sniffle, the mere runny nose, scratchy throat or just feeling a little off. This is the slight cold. The nose becoming more blocked than runny, and a cough coming into play, entitles you to call it a heavy cold. Any of the aforementioned symptoms worsening, accompanied by hotness, shiveriness, aching and general misery, gives you the right to call it a stinking cold. There’s also a malady known as man-flu, but I have no truck with such a lazy, gender-specific categorisation.

The only good thing about the stinking cold is that you have the green light to do sod all and repair to bed. This was me for three days this week, and it has firmed up a theory I have long held that you’re better off getting a stinker because it tends to come and go and be done with more quickly than the other varieties. This theory, I should point out, is based on my lived experience rather than any clinical expertise or any kind of research. Sorry – I felt too ill to bother with anything of the kind.

The kind of cold I really can’t bear is the middle-of-the-road, magnolia, vanilla, neither-here-nor-there type. When you don’t feel up to doing much, but neither, if you’re honest, are you feeling ropey enough to justify doing nothing. And these kinds of colds, for me anyway, seem to drag on for ever.

But seriously, what do you do? What’s the right call for your own health and for others in your workplace or friendship group? Do you stay at home for the greater good, or do you soldier on bravely and be quietly commended for toughing it out, while running the risk of infecting friends, enemies and workmates with a dose of whatever you’ve got?

The NHS advice is as useful and detailed as it can be in what is inevitably a grey area. It’s well worth reading, but boils down to staying at home if you have a temperature and maybe going to work if you haven’t, while acknowledging you might still be infectious, so be careful with your coughs, sneezes and general hygiene.

Message received and understood. Be careful out there. May any colds you get this winter be as light as a mere dusting of snow.

Adrian Chiles is a broadcaster, writer and Guardian columnist

The Booker prize winner described a dystopian Britain. But haven’t we been living in that since Brexit?

The Guardian Thu, 12 Nov 2026 08:00:13 GMT

It didn’t need a novel: even Leave voters understand the damage that has been done, as does the PM. Now all he has to do is persuade his party

Earlier this week, some people on the radio were talking about a very British dystopia. The government had disintegrated, but everyone was carrying on pretty much as they had before. Britain was isolated on the world stage and people missed Europe like hell, but weren’t allowed to visit, let alone live there.

I thought the radio people were discussing Britain post-Brexit, circa 2022. In fact, they were talking about the plot of the Booker prize-winning novel The End of Everything. Its author, M John Harrison, is renowned now for being, at 81, the oldest winner of the award, as well as the first science fiction writer to win it. But let’s also carve out a space for him on the podium of dystopian fiction, as a writer who can describe an indeterminate future in terms that are both terrifying and sound like a couple of years ago.

The past 10 years of British politics have had the dreamlike quality of a novel – not because they are dense with allegory or challenging to interpret, but for a much more basic reason. The morning after the 2016 referendum, a new reality simply arrived. For the next four years, we would discuss nothing but Brexit, and the language of compromise and practicality was banished.

If any other decision forced itself upon the electorate – for instance, who the prime minister should be – it would be filtered through which candidate would do the best on Brexit, which itself became more and more of a magical concept.

Like a novel, this phase took on its own rhythms, put the spotlight on characters who worked within its arc but made no sense in real life (Mark Francois, anyone?). The period since 2020, when Britain officially left the EU, has been the sad, humbling process of watching this fiction try to impose its rules on reality, and reality always winning. It turns out you can’t destroy your relationship with your biggest trading partners and not take a hit to prosperity.

Ancillary, Brexit-related fantasies, such as “immigrants leech money”, have taken their own toll, and we’ve stood by and watched as a reduction in net migration bleeds yet more money out of the economy, and a crusade against foreign students has created chaos and desperation in our universities.

If 2016 was the beginning of the “we’ve all had enough of experts” universe, in 2026 we’ve all had enough of that fictive universe, the place where facts don’t matter. Remainers gonna remain and we will insist on pointing out that Brexit has had no upside until the end of time.

But leavers have had a sea change. It’s true that only 57% of Britons agree that Brexit was a bad idea; but only 30% think it was the right choice (we should file the remainder under “please make this conversation go away”, rather than the traditional “don’t know”). More striking is the fact that 73% of Tories, 59% of leave voters and even a majority of Reform voters now back a youth mobility scheme – that radical idea Keir Starmer ruled out as soon as he became prime minister for being far too remainey.

Many politicians, on both sides, will be wishing what I used to wish when every week saw new data on attitudes to immigration, showing them to be hardening: if only these pollsters would just stop asking. Apart from a handful of Tories who were frozen out of their party, even the staunchest opponents of this fandango have, for electoral expedience, obeyed its precepts: that we all care more about sovereignty than prosperity and that we all want to take back control and either believe, in some distant future, that control will come to pass, or are sick enough of the conversation that we’re prepared to pretend we already have it.

Andy Burnham’s first big statements as prime minister still, after an underwhelming budget, look like a radical improvement on the politics that came before. His framing of Brexit was deceptively mild – shall we just take another look at this? Ideology aside, we’re in the economic doldrums, and we’d do well to take another look at our relationship with the EU. While easy answers remain elusive, it was far closer to the electorate, which just wants this nightmare to end, than it was to the political establishment, which can only conceive of the discussion in terms of which old wounds can be tolerably reopened, rather than asking: were those wounds a rhetorical construct? What would happen if we turned the page?

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

after newsletter promotion

Brexit differs from fiction or nightmare in so far as some of its effects will be permanent; we’ll never get back the wasted time or lost growth. It’s nevertheless possible to wake up from this fantasy world – ditch the red lines, the specious idea of a fixed, unified “red wall” and deal with the world as it is, where circumstances both here and in the EU have changed in a kaleidoscope of ways. Burnham catching up with the electorate has been heartening and necessary, but insufficient: his party needs to catch up with him.

Zoe Williams is a Guardian columnist
