‘We can’t be at the bottom indefinitely’: Can Britain’s most maligned service station be turned around?

The Guardian Thu, 12 Nov 2026 05:00:10 GMT

In 2022 and 2023, Hartshead Moor East, near Leeds, was voted the worst in Great Britain. Ever since, staff have been on a mission to redeem its reputation

The crime issue of the Long Read magazine is out now. Click here to order

In October 2023, at Skelton Lake service station on the M1 south-east of Leeds, Janine Gray received some bad news. She was surrounded by journalists and leading lights from the transport industry: people from the AA, the RAC, motorway service area chief executives, officials from National Highways. The big dogs. And it was among these gathered dignitaries that Gray heard the news she had been hoping, for the previous 12 months, not to hear. For the second year running, Hartshead Moor East – one half of the motorway services near Leeds that she managed – had been officially declared the worst service station in Britain.

This poll, conducted annually by the consumer watchdog Transport Focus, always makes the news. It produces gags on Have I Got News For You, punning headlines in the papers, “and finally” segments on local TV channels. Now Gray and her staff would be subjected to another round of ridicule. Of all the country’s service stations, which have a sort of aura of shitness to them anyway, theirs was apparently the shittest. Again.

These findings could not be easily dismissed: the Transport Focus poll is not some tinpot online survey, but a shockingly vast and serious operation. Each year, over a period of about seven weeks, pollsters are dispatched to almost every one of the 120-odd motorway service stations in Great Britain (a handful choose not to participate). About 70 people undertake 700 shifts across the survey period, ensuring each service station is visited on at least five occasions. More than 30,000 members of the public are surveyed. In other words: to lose one Transport Focus Motorway Services User Survey may be regarded as a misfortune. To lose two looks like carelessness.

Like airports and shopping malls, service stations are often described as “non-places”, a designation used by the French anthropologist Marc Augé to describe characterless spaces in modern life that are defined by the transience of people moving through them. The very term “service area” is itself about as unspecific as can be imagined – a non-name, you could say – as if the person inventing the concept thought up a placeholder name and forgot to come back to it.

But to the people who work there, each service station is far from a non-place. What is it like, not to pass through a service station but to stay there, year in and year out? How did it feel, for Janine Gray and her colleagues, the people who make Hartshead Moor East tick, 24 hours a day, every day of the year, to be told it is the worst services in the whole country – a country that has a strange preoccupation with deciding which services are good and bad – not once, but twice? To know they were staring down the barrel of a third humiliation if things didn’t change? What were they going to do about it? And more than all that: what do Britain’s service stations, and our need to quantify their goodness or otherwise, tell us about ourselves?

These were the questions that preoccupied me when I came across Hartshead Moor’s story. I did not know, when I set out to answer them in late 2023, that getting those answers would take me almost three years, and nearly cost me my life.

It was in March 2024 that I first made the journey to Hartshead Moor. On my way there, I investigated how things looked at the other end of the Transport Focus poll. Rugby services on the M6 opened in 2021, and ranked first in 2022 and 2023. On the day I visited, daffodils lined the approach to the station, which overlooks the rolling countryside of Warwickshire. A fountain tinkled at me as I entered through sliding doors into a bright, airy space, with seating booths clad in plausibly Scandinavian pale wood. Outside were picnic tables set back far enough that you could almost imagine you were in a national park, rather than a few hundred metres from a motorway. The bathroom facilities were huge and spotless. I left feeling calm, recharged and ready to get back on the open road.

I continued north for two hours and arrived at Hartshead Moor East. It made a different impression. No vistas, no daffodils – just a squat, grey-white building with Welcome Break branding plastered over the front entrance. An apologetic-looking sign announced that there was a KFC and a Waitrose here, but you’d have to go “over the bridge”, exposed to the elements, to the westbound site. Inside, it was cramped and paint was peeling. On the first floor, beneath a low ceiling, was a Starbucks, a Subway and a forlorn seating area. There was no Scandinavian wood.

Between the Burger King and the toilets I met Gray, the woman whose job as manager was to get this place back on track. Gray – mid-40s, long black hair, gossipy manner – is a rare person for whom motorway services constitute not an occasional necessity, but the core of a life. She has worked at Welcome Break, the UK’s second-largest operator of service stations after Moto, since 2011. She talks without explanation about EVs, SCOs, NPSs and UBMs. For Gray, it is impossible to go to another service station and just “enjoy it”. Where the rest of us are getting in and getting out, she can’t help but notice dirty corners, the particularities of the lighting, any room for improvement. “It’s a busman’s thing,” she said.

We sat at a table on what is known to staff as the upper deck, outside what is known to staff as the Starbucks unit. There were a handful of other customers. I would, on future visits, get talking to some of these patrons, but I felt curiously inhibited today. There is an almost sacred anonymity to the service station. It is a place to slip out of yourself. I tried to imagine a stranger with a recording device approaching me as I ate a KFC Zinger Meal alone at a plastic table, and felt sure that it would be a violating experience, to be caught in flagrante delicto of being no one. You can see me, here? Here, where I hardly exist?

Gray and I were talking five months after the 2023 Transport Focus poll results came out. She was disappointed, of course, but the bad showing hadn’t been a shock. Welcome Break had been refurbishing the toilets when the pollsters came, and customers were having to make do with the portable toilets outside. The previous year, Gray reckoned that Hartshead Moor’s last-place finish was mostly because those toilets had been outdated. And too green. (Photos of the facilities pre-refurb do indeed show luridly lime green paint on the walls, Brat summer avant la lettre.)

The importance of toilets cannot be overstated. It is the one place that almost every visitor visits. The toilets dictate the economics of the service station, Gray explained. You’re paying more for your coffee here than on the high street because that coffee is subsidising the majority of people – about 60%, said Gray – who are here only to use the toilets. That, at least, is the official line from operators. Plus, there’s the fact that service stations are expensive to build and maintain. More cynical observers might also note that at a service station, you are a captive audience. Once you’re through those automatic doors, Welcome Break and the like have you over a barrel, pricing-wise.

As Gray and I spoke, other staff members came to join us. Millie Thornton, 22, worked in the Starbucks inside the main building, Sarah Hunter, 35, managed the cleaning team and Wendy Clarke, 55, was the shift manager at Subway. They represented a tiny fraction of the total Hartshead Moor workforce. Nearly 200 people work there, across East and West. That’s what is required to keep this place open 24 hours a day, every day. Cleaners, staff for each outlet, managers for those staff, finance people, assistant finance people, people to staff the hotel, people to handle fuel deliveries. “It takes an army,” as Thornton put it.

But army isn’t quite the right metaphor. A more apt one – though one that, I admit, sounds painfully like Welcome Break PR – might be “family”. It was a word I heard from staff many times over, and it seemed to have some basis in fact. Sarah, who manages the cleaning team, has worked at Hartshead Moor East since she was 16, when she took Saturday shifts while studying at college. She was still here in 2024, 18 years later. That year, one of her colleagues retired after 30 years of service. It’s steady work, with opportunity for progression, and it’s common to find a couple of generations of a family working at the same services. Thornton worked in the Starbucks on the upper deck, and her older sister worked in the Starbucks drive-thru.

When I brought up the poll, I was met with groans, eye rolls, shifting in seats. “The first time, fair enough. Like, take it on the chin,” Thornton said. “But the second one was a bit of a kick in the stomach. We were in the middle of a refurb. It’s not exactly ideal, but it was like: ‘Oh God, everyone’s been trying so hard for the past year.’” Gray told me she had driven home from the Transport Focus presentation at Skelton Lake in October 2023 with her head held high. “I’m not hiding,” she said, sounding like a football manager after a bruising defeat.

On that first visit, back in March 2024, I asked them what they were hoping for when Transport Focus returned in a few months. Gray said it would be business as usual. “We don’t put any airs and graces on,” she said with noble forbearance. “It is what it is, isn’t it?” Thornton was less phlegmatic. “It should surely improve, like come on!” she said, hands in the air in exasperation. In the months between the 2023 poll result and my visit, they had completed the toilet refurbishment, and had the WH Smith refreshed and a new unit put in, which operates as The Good Breakfast in the morning and Chopstix in the afternoon. “There’s nowt else we can do, apart from knock it down and start again.”

In the months that followed, it became clear that Transport Focus approached their Motorway Services User Survey with the seriousness of a pre-Trump US intelligence agency. I have come to realise that the company name is meant literally: when they say they’re focused on transport, they’re not screwing around. Service station managers are not informed when the Transport Focus pollsters are coming, to prevent them from influencing the results by, say, putting their best staff on shift. Transport Focus even do spot checks to verify that the surveying is being done properly. “It’s a huge operation,” said Louise Collins, Transport Focus’s director. So seriously does Transport Focus take this endeavour that I could not persuade them, even with the promise of signing an NDA, to tell me when the pollsters would be visiting Hartshead Moor East in 2024. My requests to speak to pollsters who had previously worked on the survey were swiftly knocked back. I would not be allowed to interfere in any way with the rigour of the process.

Unable to size up the pollsters myself, I turned to Gray and her colleagues. Mostly, they were pleasant, Gray said, but not always. She remembered feeling that one of them was going into her conversations with visitors with a negative bias against the services. “She was just like [here Gray pulled a sneering face]: ‘It’s not as good as Wetherby, is it? Have you been to Wetherby?’ And I just thought, hang on a minute.”

Gray and her colleagues had wondered whether the station itself was holding them back. Hartshead Moor opened in 1973, and the main buildings have remained largely unchanged. I told them about my visit to Rugby, and there were weary nods. That one was nice, they agreed. “But that’s a new one,” Gray pointed out.

Service stations arrived in the UK in 1959, with designs borrowed from Italy and the US, countries where motorways had a longer history. At first, service stations were government-owned but operated by private companies, and they were glamorous destinations. When Leicester Forest East M1 services opened in 1966, it housed a restaurant modelled on an ocean liner designed by Terence Conran, complete with a baby grand piano and waiters in sailor suits serving Jamaican fish jambaraya (sic) and flambe curry. In the 1960s and 70s, Peartree services near Oxford had an outdoor swimming pool at their Excelsior Motor Lodge hotel. Watford Gap services, also known as the Blue Boar, was once a bustling, all night hub where bands took to stopping in their tour vans as they travelled between venues in the north and the south of the country. For a few years, motorists collected tales of knocking elbows with the Rolling Stones, Dusty Springfield and the Beatles as they tucked into their plates of ham, egg and chips.

As early as the mid-1960s, though, with about a dozen motorway services now up and running, operators were struggling to make money. In 1967, a government-commissioned review of service areas recommended adopting a “policy of least commitment”. Fancy restaurants disappeared and in came bolted-down furniture, disposable plates and cafeteria-style service on easy-clean trays. By the time Hartshead Moor opened in 1973, the glamour days were long gone. Football hooligans often clashed at service stations. In 1975, Leeds and Chelsea fans attacked each other at Birch services on the M62, ripping small trees from their stumps and smashing windows. A further government study published in 1978 found that the general quality of British service station food was awful. The same study described Hartshead Moor, only five years old at the time, as “scruffy”.

By March 2024 – and with Hartshead Moor East now being called “a right mess”, per one Google review – the staff were getting fed up with the way their workplace was perceived. “You can hear people when you’re walking around saying: ‘I don’t know why they’re saying this is the worst, it’s alright isn’t it?’” Gray told me. To the staff, the reputation felt like a cruel joke. When I met them in March 2024, they were more than ready to stop being the punchline.

A couple of months later, however, Gray and her team received unexpected news. Transport Focus had decided not to run the poll that year. To allow service providers more time to implement changes based on the previous year’s poll, they would not be returning until spring of 2025. For staff at Hartshead Moor East, this was a blow. Another year as Britain’s worst.

I wondered whether Welcome Break could use this time to do something drastic for their most maligned site. I thought about what Thornton had said, about knocking it down and starting again. Could they just go ahead and build something nicer? There is a sort of precedent here. While almost all UK service stations are run by a handful of private operators – Moto, Welcome Break and Roadchef are the largest – there is a family business that runs three boutique service stations with their own distinct characters. Connoisseurs speak reverently of Gloucester and Tebay, picturesque pit stops with more of the flavour of a village farm shop – local produce, lakeside views – than services. Could Welcome Break build something a bit more like that at Hartshead Moor?

According to Glenn Howells, the architect who designed Gloucester, this is a tactic Welcome Break and the others have been pursuing for some time. They emulate some of the visual language of that beloved building: a swooping roof, some nicer finishes. But to him, it ends up feeling hollow. The reason Gloucester works is because it feels genuinely local and un-corporate. “You can’t just put on a veneer of a soft rural finish,” Howells said. “A bit of Cotswold stone walling and a wobbly roof isn’t going to do it.” Even when trying to take architectural tips from Gloucester, he said, big corporations were still big corporations. “They make the money from the same concessions that you see everywhere,” he said. “And they hide the loos somewhere at the back, so you go past as many of the concessions to get to them, and that’s how they make their money – if I was being cynical about it.”

This uniformity is perhaps what makes the Transport Focus survey so competitive. It really is a comparison of like for like. What could be more galling than being told you’re the worst in a bunch that are, fundamentally, all pretty similar to you? But, paradoxically, this very sameyness may help account for why people have strong opinions about service stations. Small differences – which are really the only kind of differences that exist in this context – make a big difference.

For Hartshead Moor East, the extra year without a poll was not wasted. In the early months of 2025, as the survey period drew nearer, potholes were filled and extra showers were installed for lorry drivers. Welcome Break gave the front of the building a new coat of paint, replaced all the lighting in the lower deck to brighten up the place, and installed new ceilings. The Subway got self-service ordering screens.

By May 2025, there was a new manager, too. Akib Neamat, a quietly good-natured, practical sort of a guy in his early 30s, has spent his whole working life at service stations. At 19, he started working at Hartshead Moor in Welcome Break’s now defunct own-brand restaurant Eat In. Over the years, he moved around different services, but was happy to be offered the role of manager at Hartshead Moor in December 2024. He met his wife there, early in his career, when she was his supervisor. “It was quite nice to come back to a place that I’d always called home,” he told me. “I grew up quite a lot here.”

No wonder. The staff here see it all. There is joy: minibuses disgorging hen parties, ladies on race day doing their makeup en masse in the toilets, celebrity sightings. Roy Keane used to come into Hartshead Moor East when he managed Sunderland. He would buy a Twirl and tell people wanting photographs that he was Roy Keane’s brother. There are also darker sights. Police sometimes base themselves there to deal with road deaths. The staff have had to prevent drunk drivers getting back on the road. The night before I visited in 2024, a woman had been attacked by her partner in the car park. She had fled into the service station, locked herself in the toilets and asked another woman to go and get staff. The police were called, and they eventually had to pepper spray the man. “It’s like the weather,” Gray had told me. “Never two days the same.”

As Neamat stepped into his new role as manager, the Transport Focus poll was, of course, on his mind. And in the days leading up to the arrival of the pollsters in May 2025, he was feeling confident. Unbeknownst to anybody at Hartshead Moor, however, a series of events were being set in motion that would have profound consequences for their service station. Marks & Spencer was being hacked. Over the Easter weekend, M&S shops around the country experienced payment failures and broken tills, and the company was issued with a hefty ransom demand for the control of their systems.

On 12 May, just one day before the beginning of the period during which pollsters were due to arrive at services up and down the country, Neamat was told that Transport Focus had cancelled the survey. Because Moto and Extra services have M&S units in them, and their service was being disrupted by the hack, the results might reflect customer disgruntlement with a half-functioning M&S rather than a true picture of the station’s quality. Although it is run independently, the survey is paid for jointly by the operators, and if they don’t want it to run, it doesn’t. So it didn’t. Again.

Neamat had broken the news at the weekly Monday afternoon meeting, in a conference room deep in the bowels of Hartshead Moor. He winced at the memory. “Everyone was all geared up, ready for it. ‘Oh yeah, this is going to be great. We can get ourselves off the bottom of that list.’ And then to be told at the last minute it’s not happening?” Thornton had been particularly exasperated: “At that point we were like, we can’t be at the bottom indefinitely,” she told me.

And so it was that, as 2025 disappeared in the rearview mirror, I entered my third calendar year of working on a story about motorway service stations. During the previous 12 months, I had bought my first car, a down-at-heel but sensible VW Polo. I had done a lot more driving. I had grown more familiar with the motorway’s loveless expanse, the minutes slipping into hours behind the wheel. I had got my first flat tyre and experienced the peculiar kind of open-air imprisonment that the hard shoulder provides. What would I not have given, then, for a packet sandwich and a clean-enough toilet? I thought longingly about the simple but restorative offerings of a service station.

Simple, but restorative. That is what we want from a services. But it’s not necessarily what we think we want. Those early days of the motorway do sound delightful, when you could avail yourself of, for instance, half a lobster au gratin at Forton Pennine Tower. Why can’t we have that back, we wonder. Why do we now get sausage rolls and cardboard cups of coffee?

One reason can be summed up in a single phrase, familiar to all in the service station world: “Destination in its own right.” It’s the wording that has been used by the Department for Transport since 1980 to prohibit motorway service area operators from offering anything that might entice people on to the road with the sole purpose of visiting their service stations, thereby overloading the motorways. If an amenity was considered exciting enough to bring in people who would not otherwise be on the road, it was nixed. No swimming pools, no outre shops, no glitzy restaurants, nothing too delicious, nothing too fun. There is, in essence, a legal requirement that service stations cannot be too good.

It is not always easy to stay on the right side of this vague stipulation. In 1990, Newport Pagnell received an official castigation for trying to over-celebrate 30 years of service stations: they wanted to invite Margaret Thatcher to attend a party, but the DfT said no. For Ellie Wilson, Welcome Break’s marketing manager, the rules are a daily challenge, a perverse paradox at the heart of her work. “We struggle with that a lot, because our role in customer marketing is to improve the customer experience,” she said. She was acutely aware that to pull itself off the bottom, Hartshead Moor East needed to become nice. But not too nice.

Wilson said something else that stuck with me. “Service stations are a good indicator, maybe, of a country’s culture.” How do our services compare with what the rest of the world has put on the sides of their motorways? I found myself at a service station in Albania recently, which contained a statue of the Virgin Mary, a fully stocked bar and people merrily smoking underneath a chandelier. In the US, they don’t have a direct counterpart to our motorway services but a state-by-state patchwork of truck stops, gas stations, behemoth novelty chains such as Buc-ee’s (presided over by a toothy beaver mascot) and “rest areas” that are places for you to stop and eat your own food. Italy’s “autogrills”, which serve fresh pastries and good coffee, and stock a wide range of salami, are beloved by locals and travellers alike. They represent a vestige of the Italian practice of going for a drive on the motorway as a pastime in itself, which came and went in Britain back in the 1960s. In Moroccan service stations, you can reportedly get a genuinely good tagine.

The truth is that not being allowed to be “destinations in their own right” isn’t the main reason our service stations aren’t more exciting. The main reason is us. Customer feedback consistently suggests that people want sit-down meals back, a return to something like the nostalgic era of Little Chef restaurants. To meet this demand, between 2017 and 2020, Welcome Break opened branches of Pizza Express across some of its sites. But people didn’t eat in them. Two of the Pizza Express branches have closed this year alone. “People haven’t got a lot of time to stop these days,” said Rich Cross, a 28-year-old motorway services fanatic from Bristol who has visited every service station in Great Britain and contributes to the extraordinarily exhaustive website motorwayservices. uk. “It’s all sort of focused around speed of service and getting [customers] what they want as quick as possible essentially.”

The occasional Tebay or Gloucester is nice to have, but they are not what the majority of people truly desire. If our service stations say something about who we are, then one of the things they say is that we’re a nation of people who like to complain about how things were better once, or elsewhere. Who relish moaning about how we want something different, but whose actual desires are more basic than we like to admit. We prize efficiency, reliability, mundanity. “There’s an attraction to certain kinds of gone-to-seed parts of English life,” said Joe Moran, author of a 2009 history of Britain’s motorways, On Roads. “Things like seaside resorts out of season, or rainy northern towns.” Our services are not, ultimately, all that great. And that is what we love them for, in our begrudging, irony-inflected way. As Moran puts it, they mine “a rich seam of English ordinariness”.

I asked Cross about his view of Hartshead Moor East. “She’s an old girl. Never going to be able to compete with a Skelton Lake, is it?” he said. Leeds Skelton Lake has an RSPB bird-viewing platform. Hartshead Moor East has Burger King.

Finally, in May 2026, the hi-vis-vest-clad pollsters arrived at Hartshead Moor East. Once again, I had not been permitted to know when they were coming, so I headed back up to the station when the polling period was over. On the August day I visited, the station did, to its credit, look better than it had two years previously. A dad and his pink-haired teenage daughter were eating granola bars and staring at their phones in silence under the freshly installed ceiling panels. Tradesmen were getting a Subway under newly bright lights. Stamping his foot on noticeably shinier white flooring outside WH Smith, a little boy was expressing his need for a travel pillow with a sloth’s face on it.

Millie Thornton was still there, and so was Sarah Hunter, a recent recipient of the Welcome Break 20 years of service badge, which she wore on her lanyard. She had been on shift for many of the Transport Focus visits. It was impossible to know how things had gone until the results came out – “Can’t bribe them. I’ve tried,” said another member of staff – but the pollsters had told them they were hearing good things from customers. “They just kept saying it’s positive feedback, which was really nice to hear,” Hunter said.

Around the station, staff were generally optimistic about their chances. The work done on the building, the effort put in by the teams – it would all surely add up. A hat-trick of last-place positions in the poll would be more than they could take. “I’d be disheartened if we were at the bottom again, massively disheartened,” Neamat told me. I asked Julie Pygott, who has worked in the WH Smith for the past nine years, how she would feel if they came bottom again. Also present for this meeting was Ellie Wilson, the Welcome Break marketing manager. “Keep it clean,” Wilson interjected. Pygott paused. “I just don’t know,” she eventually said. “It’s not true. That’s what I would say: it’s just not true.”

On another visit to the station later that month, I finally got talking to my fellow drivers. I have spent a lot of time in my career approaching strangers to ask them questions, and never have I encountered so uniform a response than at this service station: bemusement shaded with mild panic. Tom, a man in his 30s on his way to Ipswich, was overseeing his St Bernard tucking into something billing itself as an ice-cream puppuccino pop. As the dog slurped, and I explained what I was doing, he started to laugh. What did he think of Hartshead Moor? “It’s got the dog lollies, so it suits me.” Then a pause. “It’s a services really, isn’t it?”

The service station is one of society’s great levellers. There is no such thing as a VIP service station. All life is there: young and old, rich and poor, well- and ill-intentioned, all with empty stomachs and bladders full. It renders us all anonymous. Sometimes, people make intentional use of the benign indifference of services. For instance, a man named David Lawrence told me that during the 70s and 80s, a group of cross-dressers used to meet at a service station near Manchester where they could be with each other freely without fear of being recognised. Less movingly, petty crime has always flourished at services for the same reason.

One of my trips to Hartshead Moor this summer happened to coincide with the partial eclipse. On my drive back to London, I decided to pull over for the moment itself, envisaging a suddenly dark motorway and some lethal rubbernecking that might cause a crash that would result in my death before my service stations piece was finished.

The nearest services was Newport Pagnell, one of the first to open in the UK, in 1959. On its first trading day, it had to open two hours earlier than planned because there was such a crowd of people waiting outside to see it. On the day I visited, 67 years later, the car park was busy. Children sat on car roofs pointing iPads at the sun. One couple were prodding a hole in a piece of paper with an earring. I wandered over to a group of women who had eclipse glasses, and waited for the darkness to fall. The moon slipped over the sun, and then slipped off again as we all gazed upwards, a briefly and randomly assembled cross-section of society, united for this half-hour by the chance circumstance of us being on the motorway at the same time, soon to go our separate ways for ever.

I spent the months before the Transport Focus results were due to be announced in a state of unease. The survey data had been collected. That was certainly an improvement on the previous two years. But so many years into this project, I had learned to take nothing for granted. Perhaps an earthquake would destroy Transport Focus’s Manchester office and bury the survey with it. I was beginning to feel as if some kind of curse had been placed on this article, or that I had absorbed some of the bad luck Hartshead Moor itself had experienced. But I was also nervous on behalf of the staff if the survey results did indeed come out as scheduled. Hopes were high. Thornton was setting her sights on breaking the top half, whereas Hunter’s dreams were more modest (top 75). For both of them, though, the excitement was palpable. “It’s been too long,” Thornton said. “We just want to know.”

As the clock ticked down towards the grand reveal of the first Transport Focus survey in three years, buzz built across the service stations world. I spoke to Ken McMeikan, the chief executive of Moto, the company that runs the celebrated Rugby services. He told me he would “love to win it for a third time”, but he wasn’t being complacent. “I think Rugby and Sawtry will definitely be challenging for the No 1,” he said. I caught up with Janine Gray, the previous Hartshead Moor East manager, on the phone. She works at Leicester Forest East now but, a year on, was still irked that the 2025 poll had been cancelled. “You feel a bit like there’s unfinished business,” she said.

Before I received my formal invitation to attend the unveiling of the Transport Focus survey results, which would be held at Rotherham services, I had been imagining some kind of party. What’s it like? I asked Louise Collins, the director of Transport Focus. Is it a drinks thing? She blinked at me and laughed. No, she said. Everyone drives there.

Everyone except me, it would turn out. You may remember that I claimed, in what no doubt seemed a rhetorical flourish, that writing this piece nearly cost me my life. I was not exaggerating. I had planned to spend the night before the ceremony at Hartshead Moor’s Days Inn hotel (despite Rich Cross advising me, from experience, that I would not find that experience delightful). So, on Monday 9 November, I set off from my house in south London in the car I had bought only six months before, to drive the four hours up to the services. Ten minutes into that drive, on the north side of Vauxhall Bridge, directly beneath Riverwalk, the building immortalised on the front cover of Patrick Radden Keefe’s bestseller London Falling, I was rear-ended by an SUV with enough force to not only destroy my car beyond repair, but to cause a three-car pileup ahead of me, in which another vehicle was lifted clean off the ground by a Maserati rammed underneath it. By some miracle, nobody was seriously injured, and I escaped with a bump on my head and a mild concussion. Unfortunately, I now had no car, 12 hours before I was due to report from a service station. There was, without question now, some kind of curse at play here. And I feared Hartshead Moor East would have to get off the bottom of the poll for it to be broken.

On Tuesday morning I took the train to Sheffield, and an Uber from there to Rotherham services for the Transport Focus ceremony, arriving at about 10am. It was Welcome Break’s turn to host the event, and they had chosen their razzliest, dazzliest new services – completed last year – to show the competition what they were capable of.

What Welcome Break is capable of, it seems, is producing a service station that looks on the outside like a regional airport, and on the inside like a stage set of an English town square. Rotherham is an enormous, 32,000-sq ft re-imagining of a Yorkshire village. Amy Holmes, on Welcome Break’s design team, told me that those two words, “Yorkshire village”, were the only two words they were given by the parent company’s chief executive to steer them. Inside the station, I found lamp-posts, fake flower beds and mock street signs such as “Retail Road” above a branch of Waitrose that had window-shaped holes in the facade. The Burger King had faux mansard roofing, and the top of the Starbucks appeared to be covered in plastic grass. It felt like a corporate slant on the notion of localness, just as Glenn Howells had foretold.

The survey results were being announced at 11am, and by 10.30am, the gigantic station contained pockets of guests from the upper echelons of service station world – a glimpse of open shirts and suits and sensible business heels among the regular punters. After some hobnobbing, during which Ken McMeikan of Moto told me about a recent trip to China to check out what they were doing over there with services (malls with fuel, in essence – and decidedly “destinations”, as he put it), we filed up an escalator flanked by green and white balloons to a mezzanine level that houses a soft-play area and a makeshift presentation space, where we would be hearing which station had soared to victory and which would languish at the bottom.

After opening remarks from Nigel Stevens, the chair of the board at Transport Focus, eventually the time came to announce which services had won: the grand coronation. Or not, as it turned out. “This is supposed to be the moment of the great reveal of who’s No 1, but …” he said, trailing off. “John, you better come up here, because I think you might be the winner.” At this, John Diviney, the chief executive of Welcome Break, stood up. Stevens handed him a glass trophy the size and dimensions of a paperback book, and he sat down again.

It was a strange moment: one which plainly called for some kind of moment of suspense, giving way to the popping of champagne corks. But everyone in attendance already knew that Rotherham had won, squeaking in ahead of Rugby. Transport Focus had given the operators the survey results weeks in advance of this event, so they could get going on making improvements. I was, personally, disappointed by the lack of ceremony. But the decision to do it like this was practical: it served a purpose, and as a consequence was underwhelming. Just like, I suppose, a service station.

I hadn’t come to hear who won, though. I had come to hear about Hartshead Moor East. The news, at last, was good. They didn’t just haul themselves off the bottom spot. They didn’t just break the top half. They came 33rd out of 123, a majestic leap up the league table that made them the single most improved site on 2026’s survey. At the presentation, they were held up as a beacon for other services to follow. “Sites will look at these results,” said Diviney in his speech, “and ask: ‘How can we be the next Rotherham? Can we be a Hartshead?’” To be a Hartshead: now a goal to aim for.

The operators knew the results in advance. The staff at the each of the service stations, however, did not. The first thing Akib Neamat did when he woke up at 6am on Tuesday morning was to Google “Transport Focus”. And there it was. His station, their station, the most improved. I rang him that afternoon. “The vibe on site today has been ecstatic,” he told me. He called a meeting with his staff when he arrived at 8am, and told them the news, which was met with cheers and the biggest smiles he had ever seen at Hartshead Moor. The curse, after three long years, had been lifted.

The Long Read magazine crime issue: out now

A special true-crime edition of the Long Read magazine brings together 10 of our most gripping tales from the past decade. To celebrate its launch, join us for an evening with contributors Imogen West-Knights and Samira Shackle at Funny Weather Books in Highgate on 25 November.

Polls Found Strength for Democrats, but Still Missed Badly

The New York Times November 12, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Democratic gains were expected, but surveys almost uniformly underestimated how well the left would do. Many pollsters seem to have made similar mistakes.

By Caroline Soler and Ruth Igielnik

Graphics by Jillian Vordick

In one important sense, polls got the story of this year’s election right: They showed Democrats winning the House and leading in the race for control of the Senate.

By another measure, this year’s polls were among the worst in recent memory. When looking across all pollsters, surveys systematically underestimated the support of Democratic candidates, and they did so on a scale that rivaled or even exceeded the heavily criticized misses of 2016 and 2020, when polls underestimated Republicans.

Overall, national polls this year underestimated the strength of Democrats by around four percentage points. Across the key Senate races, the polls underestimated Democrats by an even larger five-point miss, compared with an average of about 3.5 points across all Senate races.

Polls generally called the winning party but underestimated the Democratic margin.

New York Times analysis in select states where five or more polls were conducted in the final three weeks before Election Day. Excluding Alaska because results are not finalized.

The New York Times

This error is similar in size to the recent Trump-era presidential polling misfires. In 2020, national polls underestimated Republicans by about four percentage points; in 2016, Republicans were underestimated by three points.

Not every pollster this year erred by so much. The New York Times/Siena Poll, for instance, did not systematically underestimate the Democrats. Neither did a handful of other pollsters, including AtlasIntel and Survey 160.

Overall, the final Times/Siena polls underestimated Democrats by less than one percentage point, with some polls underestimating Democrats and others underestimating Republicans.

Note: In Nebraska, polling miss refers to over or underestimation of the independent, since there was no Democrat in the race.

Sources: New York Times/Siena polls of likely voters conducted Oct. 19 to 26 in Florida, South Carolina and Minnesota, Oct. 23 to 29 in Nebraska and Oct. 23 to Nov. 1 in Iowa, Kansas, Maine, Ohio, Michigan and Texas. Margins are calculated using candidates’ unrounded vote shares.

The New York Times

But across all pollsters, most polls underestimated Democrats, and in some states the error was huge. In Texas, the polls underestimated James Talarico’s margin of victory by nine percentage points. In general, the misses were less extreme in the classic northern battleground states, while pollsters struggled in the Sun Belt, where Democrats made their largest gains.

There are a number of theories as to why the error was so large. One particularly strong possibility is the role of turnout, which appears to have been far stronger for Democrats than many pollsters assumed.

The fact that the polling error has exceeded — or at least been on par with — the worst polling errors in recent history, however, suggests there may be something bigger and systematic at play.

Pollsters have adopted new sampling and weighting techniques to compensate for the voters they are failing to reach. More and more, pollsters are weighting their surveys to the respondents’ recalled vote history. But that approach assumes the composition of the electorate will look mostly the same from one cycle to the next, which this year led to polls being tilted toward Republicans.

When much of the industry responds to these challenges in the same ways, pollsters end up making similar mistakes. The kind of widespread polling error we’ve seen recently may become more common.

While the data isn’t final in much of the country, there are lots of signs that turnout was more favorable to the Democrats than most polls had anticipated.

Take Florida, for example. Unlike most other states, we already know the makeup of the Florida electorate: Registered Republicans outnumbered Democrats by about 8.5 percentage points, according to turnout information available from election officials. That’s not what most polls showed. Our final Times/Siena poll of the race, which overestimated Senator Ashley Moody’s support by three percentage points, had a likely electorate with Republicans ahead by 13 points in terms of party registration.

A similar story might have unfolded elsewhere in the South, where the Black and Hispanic share of the electorate was higher than it had been in previous cycles.

Why did the polls underestimate the Democratic turnout? The answer varies from pollster to pollster.

One factor might be that pollsters are relying on increasingly heavy-handed methods of weighting, where a pollster gives more weight to voters from groups who were underrepresented among survey respondents. Since 2016, and especially since 2020, pollsters have been trying to properly represent Mr. Trump’s supporters, in part by ensuring that they have the right number of people who reported voting for Mr. Trump in the previous election.

That approach may have overshot the mark this year. By weighting their samples to 2024 voting patterns, some pollsters may have assumed a more Republican electorate than the one that actually turned out.

(The Times/Siena Poll’s approach to incorporating the results of past elections is somewhat different than other public pollsters; read more here.)

New voters may have been an especially difficult group for pollsters to represent. Midterm elections tend to attract only the most regular voters, but Times Voter Trends estimates suggest that more than 10 percent of voters nationally didn’t vote in the last presidential election. Those voters backed Democrats by more than 30 points.

If a pollster missed the Democratic-friendly turnout and new voters, their results could be way off. An Emerson College poll in Texas, for example, underestimated Mr. Talarico’s win by 10 percentage points, and turnout was probably a factor. The poll found that voters who had backed Mr. Trump in 2024 outnumbered backers of Kamala Harris by 11 points; Times Voter Trends and exit poll data suggest that previous Trump voters outnumbered Harris voters by a much smaller margin, probably in the mid-single digits. The Emerson poll also found new voters making up just 3 percent of the electorate, compared to 15 percent of actual voters, according to Times Voter Trends.

Maine offers another potential instance of this, with polling from Marist finding Troy Jackson, the Democrat, ahead by nine percentage points among registered voters. The same poll, when accounting for the likeliest voters, had Mr. Jackson up by only two points. He won the state by six. With a different model of the electorate, Marist might have had a more accurate result.

Another possible source of error this year is that voters shifted over time, with Democrats seeming to gain strength, sometimes after surveys were no longer in the field.

Kansas provides a good example. A Times/Siena poll taken in September found the Senate race to be even. By October, another had Adam Hamilton ahead by five percentage points. In the end, he won the race by exactly that margin. Most other polls in the state followed a similar path.

This was the case across the Times/Siena polls this year when taken as a group.

Bars show how poll results in a given period differ from the eventual results.

Source: The New York Times/Siena 2026 Senate polls. The late-June polling wave covers Iowa, Maine, North Carolina, Ohio, and Texas. The late-September wave includes Iowa, Kansas, Maine, Michigan, New Hampshire, Ohio, and Texas. The late-October wave covers Florida, Minnesota, and South Carolina. Finally, the November results encompass Iowa, Kansas, Maine, Michigan, Nebraska, Ohio, and Texas. Nebraska is the only state in the analysis where the candidate was an independent rather than a Democrat.

The New York Times

Nationally, this was clear as well. A September Times/Siena poll had Democrats with a nine-percentage-point advantage in the race for the House, with that gap growing to 11 points by October. The final Times/Siena national poll was taken in mid-October, but other national polls showed Democrats’ strength continuing to grow in surveys taken in the final week before the election.

If other pollsters had been in the field closer to the election, it’s possible they would have gotten closer to the final result.

Caroline Soler is a Times researcher focused on collecting and analyzing polling and election data.

Ruth Igielnik is a Times polling editor who conducts polls and analyzes and reports on the results.

Jillian Vordick is a graphics reporter at The Times.

Will the Supreme Court Thwart Congressional Investigations?

The New York Times November 12, 2026

Advertisement

Newsletter

Lawmakers must dodge rulings on immunity, standing and “valid legislative purpose.”

By Adam Liptak

Adam Liptak is the chief legal correspondent and host of The Docket.

Come January, a Congress newly dominated by Democrats will launch vigorous investigations of the Trump administration and its allies.

Lawmakers will face a target-rich environment, one that includes crypto deals, pardons, extrajudicial killings on the high seas, a Justice Department-led retribution campaign against the president’s political opponents, and the gift of a Qatari jet.

But they will also face hurdles and roadblocks — erected by the Supreme Court.

In the court’s 2024 decision granting President Trump substantial immunity from prosecution, Chief Justice John Roberts indicated that some subjects may be entirely off limits to congressional investigators.

“Congress cannot act on, and courts cannot examine, the president’s actions on subjects within his ‘conclusive and preclusive’ constitutional authority,” the chief justice wrote. Those subjects included issuing pardons, firing subordinates and deciding “which crimes to investigate and prosecute.”

The immunity decision “has quietly weakened Congress’s ability to conduct legislative oversight over the executive branch,” David Manners-Weber wrote on Lawfare, a nonprofit legal affairs website, just before the midterm elections.

Whatever the subjects of congressional investigations, the administration is unlikely to give Congress documents or let officials testify, a clash that could lead to lawsuits. And it is not at all clear that the Supreme Court would be willing to mediate those disputes, or if the justices would side with the Democratic Congress if it does.

Perhaps surprisingly, the court has never definitively resolved a basic question: Can Congress sue the executive branch?

In 2015, Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg noted in passing that “whether Congress has standing to bring a suit against the president” was an open question. “A suit between Congress and the president,” she observed, “would raise separation-of-powers concerns.”

Lower courts have been more receptive to suits from legislators.

In a pair of decisions in 2020, in the waning days of the first Trump administration, the D. C. Circuit ruled that lawsuits could proceed despite objections to the lawmakers’ standing.

In one decision, the court said that the House Judiciary Committee, then led by Democrats, had standing to sue Don McGahn, a former White House counsel, to compel him to testify. In the other, the court allowed the full House of Representatives to sue over Trump’s use of emergency powers to spend more public funds on a border wall than Congress had appropriated.

McGahn and the committee settled their dispute following some additional twists and turns. After the 2020 election, the Biden administration stopped building the border wall, then asked the Supreme Court to wipe out the appeals court’s decision.

The Biden administration, aware of political pendulum swings, sided with the Trump administration and argued that the House alone should not be allowed to sue the president.

Elizabeth Prelogar, the solicitor general under President Joe Biden, told the justices that letting the House sue “would inject the federal courts into fundamentally political disputes and upset the balance of power between the political branches.”

The Supreme Court granted the Biden administration’s petition and vacated the D. C. Circuit’s decision as moot. The court’s brief order said nothing about whether Congress, or parts of it, had standing to sue the executive branch.

I asked Payvand Ahdout, a law professor at the University of Virginia and an authority on inter-branch litigation, for an overview of the likely litigation.

“I largely agree that there are many roadblocks to courts rendering decisions on the merits in any of these cases,” she said in an email. “And even if Congress can overcome those roadblocks, courts frequently engage in avoidance techniques to keep from ordering a coordinate branch of government to take action.”

But she added that “the judiciary is not a monolith” and “we may see some cases where Congress finds an ally in the lower courts that moves the needle for investigations and oversight.”

So far I’ve been discussing clashes between Congress and the executive branch. Lawmakers will probably find it easier to obtain information from private parties like Elon Musk, or the law firms that settled with the administration after threats that they and their clients could lose government contracts.

But even in those kinds of cases, the court has imposed limits on the authority of lawmakers. In 2020, in Trump v. Mazars, the court considered congressional subpoenas seeking Trump’s tax and business records from accounting and financial institutions with which he had done business. Trump sued to block the release of the records.

Returning the case to a lower court for further analysis, Chief Justice Roberts stressed that lawmakers needed “a valid legislative purpose” for seeking the records.

“Congress may not issue a subpoena for the purpose of ‘law enforcement,’” he wrote, quoting an earlier decision, “because ‘those powers are assigned under our Constitution to the executive and the judiciary.’”

Got a news tip about the courts? If you have information to share about the Supreme Court or other federal courts, please contact us.

The ruling was not particularly clear about where to draw the line between the two. In general, the chief justice seemed to prefer accommodation over litigation.

“Historically, disputes over congressional demands for presidential documents have not ended up in court,” he wrote. “Instead, they have been hashed out in the ‘hurly-burly, the give-and-take of the political process between the legislative and the executive.’”

That is, he urged the parties to work out their differences and leave the courts out of it.

The quotation supporting that approach was part of 1975 testimony from a Justice Department lawyer before a Senate committee. The lawyer was Antonin Scalia, who would join the Supreme Court about a decade later.

In the Trump era, the give-and-take Scalia called for seems to have vanished.

The administration has, for instance, taken an extraordinarily broad view of executive privilege, saying it extends to the president’s discussions with people outside the government.

In August, the Office of Legal Counsel, the unit of the Justice Department that advises the executive branch on the law, issued a memorandum making the case for a vast expansion of the scope of executive privilege. It relied heavily on the Mazars decision from 2020, citing it eight times.

Photo illustration by Chantal Jahchan

Lexi Parra/The New York Times

Jimena Peck for The New York Times

Haiyun Jiang/The New York Times

Mailbag

If Congress passed a law setting term limits for justices, could the Supreme Court find it unconstitutional? — Barbara Insel

Yes, but it would be awkward. It’s not clear how a challenge to the statute would arise, or whether the justices would recuse themselves in light of the obvious conflict. That decision, in turn, could depend on how lower courts ruled.

As we saw just weeks ago, the court sometimes lets lower-court decisions stand when it cannot muster the required quorum of six justices.

These complications, to say nothing of the Constitution’s text (the justices “shall hold their offices during good behavior”), could suggest that a statute is not the right approach.

The report issued by the Biden-appointed Supreme Court commission said that some of its members had concluded that “the existence of constitutional doubt, as well as the significance and complexity of adopting a system of term limits, are themselves reasons to pursue the reform through constitutional amendment.”

“No matter which way the court came out on the question,” the report added, “these commissioners worry that the court’s legitimacy, or perceptions of its legitimacy, would be undermined.”

I would love to hear your questions on the law, the courts or whatever is on your mind. Send them my way at the-docket@nytimes. com.

Closing Argument

J. Harvie Wilkinson is a respected federal appeals court judge who was appointed by President Ronald Reagan and considered for a seat on the Supreme Court by President George W. Bush.

He is also a former journalist, having served for three years as the editorial page editor of The Norfolk Virginian-Pilot before joining the Justice Department. (That did not stop The Pilot from opposing his nomination in 1983. The paper said that he lacked courtroom experience.)

Judge Wilkinson’s background might have played a role in his opinion Tuesday limiting a court order requiring LinkedIn to turn over the records of journalists for an unidentified news organization that published an article “purporting to describe a top-secret United States military operation in a foreign country.”

The ruling did not identify the article or news organization in question. But parts of it raised the possibility that it involved a New York Times article disclosing a botched military operation in North Korea in 2019.

The government sought 18 months’ worth of information that could, Judge Wilkinson wrote, identify a vast number of confidential sources who had nothing to do with the article in question.

Judge Wilkinson, writing for a unanimous three-judge panel, made clear that he understood reporting.

“Confidentiality of sources is the lifeblood of a free press,” he wrote. “Without confidentiality, press coverage would be pushed in the direction of official handouts and outside sources. Without confidentiality, the ability of journalists to report on events of large importance and governmental behavior of dubious legality and integrity could not help but be hampered.”

He added that such reporting may be all the more urgent these days, and that a free press could not be viewed in isolation.

“Press freedom is among those things viewed by autocrats worldwide as a threat to their grip on power,” he wrote. “Criminal prosecutions freed from partisanship and retribution, a fearless and independent judicial system, and a secure and accessible electoral process all serve to supplement press freedom in distinguishing liberty from oppression.”

The decision was nothing like a complete victory for the journalists. Judge Wilkinson said a trial judge could conclude that some of their records must be disclosed. But he said the government had no “license to round up indiscriminately the identities of confidential and unrelated news gathering sources.”

Please send me your comments on congressional investigations, term limits for Supreme Court justices, confidential sources or anything else at the-docket@nytimes. com. See you next week. — Adam

Adam Liptak is the chief legal affairs correspondent of The Times and the host of The Docket, a newsletter on legal developments. A graduate of Yale Law School, he practiced law for 14 years before joining The Times in 2002.

A Warrior Secretary and a Lesson at the Tomb of the Unknowns

The New York Times November 12, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Pentagon Memo

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s highly cultivated brand took a hit during an encounter with an Army sentinel at Arlington Cemetery.

By Greg Jaffe

Reporting from Washington

Pete Hegseth is possibly the most stage-managed secretary in the history of the Defense Department.

Almost everything he does, even his wardrobe choices, seems designed to either rally his supporters or provoke his critics. There are the American-flag pocket squares, the patriotic socks, the slicked-back hair, the “This is War” T-shirts and the carefully curated videos of him doing push-ups with the troops.

So many push-ups.

So it stood out when a soldier guarding the Tomb of the Unknowns loudly scolded Mr. Hegseth and his party for laughing and talking near the solemn memorial on Veterans Day. Such interventions are a daily occurrence at Arlington Cemetery, where swarms of tourists brush up against strict military protocol.

“All visitors will maintain an atmosphere of silence and respect at all times,” the Army sentinel bellowed in the direction of Mr. Hegseth, his wife and his top advisers as they departed.

On Thursday, Mr. Hegseth awarded the soldier a Joint Service Commendation Medal. “We love soldiers. We love standards. Well done, Specialist,” Hegseth said on social media. “Carry on Patriots.”

The rare unscripted moment and its aftermath pointed to a larger truth about the military and its relationship to the country it serves.

An Iraq veteran and former Fox News host, Mr. Hegseth casts himself as the ultimate warrior and patriot, leading an elite force of like-minded souls. Today, only about one percent of Americans serve in the all-volunteer military, a fact often mentioned in Veterans Day speeches by presidents, politicians and Pentagon chiefs.

Most defense secretaries in recent decades have lamented the growing distance between soldiers and the nation they serve, citing it as a potential danger to the country’s democracy and the principle of civilian control of the military.

Mr. Hegseth, by contrast, appears to see the gap as proof of his and his troops’ moral and physical superiority.

“You are the real one percent,” he told hundreds of young officers and sergeants at his “State of the Force” speech in late September. “You feel comfortable inside the violence so that our citizens can live peacefully.”

Mr. Hegseth continued, pacing the stage in front of a giant American flag. The backdrop mirrored the portrayal of Gen. George S. Patton in the 1970 movie bearing his name.

“You don’t want to look like civilians, because you are different,” Mr. Hegseth told the troops. “You are set apart. You are warriors.”

Mr. Hegseth sounded a similar theme at a news conference on Tuesday in which he defended himself ahead of an impeachment vote in Congress. The defense secretary cast himself and the troops as targets of opportunistic politicians who would never understand their service.

He cited charges accusing him of carrying out unlawful strikes against suspected drug traffickers on boats in the Caribbean and the eastern Pacific.

“Make no mistake about what is happening. This is not about me,” Mr. Hegseth said.

The true targets, he said, were the troops who had pulled the triggers.

“If they want to come for the warriors,” Mr. Hegseth vowed, “they’re going to have to come through me.”

Some senior military officers, who were granted anonymity to speak frankly about a superior, questioned Mr. Hegseth’s motives. Instead of taking responsibility for his orders, the defense secretary seemed to be hiding behind the troops, they said.

On Tuesday, the day before Veterans Day, Congress voted 211 to 204 to shelve the impeachment effort, shielding Mr. Hegseth from a damaging rebuke and a potential ouster.

In the aftermath of the vote, Mr. Hegseth and his team declared “TOTAL VICTORY!” in a message posted to social media.

“We will always stand tall and fight to defend the Republic!” wrote Sean Parnell, the Pentagon’s chief spokesman.

The incident at Arlington Cemetery stood out as a rebuttal to this week’s unsuccessful impeachment effort and a reminder that the troops don’t belong to any single party, president or defense secretary, but rather to the nation they serve.

“Americans are lining up to serve in President Trump’s Department of War,” Mr. Hegseth declared on Tuesday at his news conference.

The statement caught the attention of Lt. Gen. Mark Hertling, a retired Army officer.

“It is not President Trump’s Department of War,” General Hertling said in a podcast episode. “It doesn’t belong to the president.”

Greg Jaffe covers the Pentagon and the U. S. military for The Times.

At least eight people were killed when a three-story building fell into a neighboring construction site Wednesday afternoon. The search for survivors continued into the next day.

By Andy NewmanAshley Southall and Chelsia Rose Marcius

The eight people killed when a building in Brooklyn collapsed into a construction site on Wednesday were like a cross-section of the bustling, fast-growing Flatbush neighborhood.

They included elementary-school-age cousins, construction workers from Ecuador and Guatemala, and a young man from Guinea in West Africa, according to an internal police report and family and friends of the victims.

Six died when the building, at 1321 Flatbush Avenue, crashed down around 4 p. m. Wednesday; workers next door had been doing excavation. Two others succumbed to their injuries after they were taken to the hospital, Mayor Zohran Mamdani said at a news conference on Thursday. Firefighters were still sifting through the rubble, searching for additional victims on Thursday afternoon as rain poured down.

“We promise,” the fire commissioner, Lillian Bonsignore, said, “with everything we have, we will not stop working until everyone is rescued or recovered.”

Mr. Mamdani said another 18 people, including some firefighters, had been injured.

Officials have not determined what caused the collapse.

Connections: Sports Edition

Connections: Soccer Edition

Connections Coach

By embracing Korean children stigmatized by the disease, she was a leader in the international adoption movement. She has died at 95.

Credit...

Supported by

By Maggie Jones

When Bernice Gottlieb arrived at a village in South Korea, Mi Yun Lee, who was 9 years old, had never seen anyone like her. Gottlieb was tall and exuded an Audrey Hepburn glamour — a scarf carefully tied around her glossy black hair, high cheekbones, large, welcoming eyes. To Mi Yun, she was an angel who had descended from the sky, holding promises of a new future.

It was March 1974, and Gottlieb had flown from the United States with her husband to visit St. Lazarus, a community for people with leprosy, as Hansen’s disease was known then. About 400 people lived in the village’s dormitories and one-room homes. There was a medical clinic (a doctor only came once a month), a church, a school.

Though it was about 15 miles from Seoul, St. Lazarus was sequestered from mainstream Korean life, its residents shunned by families and society. By the 1970s, doctors knew that the disease was not highly contagious and was treatable, especially if caught early. Still, the stigma persisted. Outside small-scale farming, jobs were limited for people in the village. Poverty was the norm. So was community, family, love.

Gottlieb learned about St. Lazarus a few years earlier at a friend’s house in Westchester County, N. Y., when the Rev. Lee Kyong-Jai, the head of the Catholic village, came to raise money and awareness for his community. He told Gottlieb he needed families in the United States to adopt children, none of whom had the disease, but who faced stigma, nonetheless. They were known in South Korea as Migam-a, children of the infected. Most were unable to attend public schools (those who did hid the fact of their parents’ disease and couldn’t invite friends to their homes).

By the time Gottlieb met Father Lee, she knew plenty about international adoption and was a leader in the burgeoning movement. She and her husband, the architect Ferdinand Gottlieb, adopted their daughter, Susannah, from South Korea in 1969. They were the first Americans that the orphanage director had allowed to adopt.

After Gottlieb brought Susannah back to the United States, where the couple already had two sons, she was inundated with questions from hopeful adoptive parents, many of whom gathered at her house in Dobbs Ferry, N. Y., on Friday nights. With few agencies working in international adoption at the time, Gottlieb became a key resource. She both helped parents navigate the adoption process and provided organizations with lists of potential parents, including those open to adopting children with disabilities.

Initially, she hesitated about St. Lazarus. The children weren’t orphans or children of single mothers, who were ostracized in South Korea. They had two known, living parents. Parts of the children’s story, though, reminded Gottlieb of her own childhood.

In 1930, just before Gottlieb was born, two of her older siblings died from polio. Her father’s business soon collapsed, and her mother sank into depression. A friend agreed to temporarily raise Gottlieb and her older brother, with the caveat that she wanted to adopt the children if Gottlieb’s mother didn’t recover. For the next three years, Gottlieb lived with the woman she called Mama Thompson, who took her for regular visits to their parents. When Gottlieb’s mother improved and brought her children home, Gottlieb cried for months, she later wrote in a memoir. Her mother never talked about Mama Thompson. And Gottlieb never saw her again.

If she was going to help the St. Lazarus children, Gottlieb insisted that they remain in contact with their Korean parents. It was a highly unusual idea in the early 1970s in both U. S. and international adoptions. Secrecy and sealed adoption records were typical. Even if they searched, biological parents and adopted children often never saw each other again.

Once Gottlieb agreed to the St. Lazarus plan, she dived in, as was her style, with optimism, determination — and a heap of naïveté. Among other things, she hoped the adoptions would be the first step toward South Korea eradicating prejudice against leprosy, which is caused by bacteria called Mycobacterium leprae that can damage skin, peripheral nerves, the upper respiratory tract and the eyes.

How The Times decides who gets an obituary. There is no formula, scoring system or checklist in determining the news value of a life. We investigate, research and ask around before settling on our subjects. If you know of someone who might be a candidate for a Times obituary, please suggest it here.

She enrolled in a leprosy medical training course at U. S. Public Health Service Hospital in Carville, La. — the sole leprosarium in the continental United States. While some doctors supported her plan, others warned that the children could still be at risk for the disease, given the long incubation period. And in a harbinger of future criticisms of international adoption, one doctor said regardless of poverty and stigma, the children should not be taken from their family, their language, their culture.

Gottlieb pressed on, creating a nonprofit for the St. Lazarus program called Operation Outreach. From 100 applicants, she chose four families — three couples in New York State and a single mother in Washington, D. C. — all of whom promised to keep ties between the children and their parents. She assigned two children — most of them siblings — to each family.

The biggest hurdle was the U. S. government. Legally, people could not adopt children from other countries with two living parents. And bringing the children in through the immigration system would take too much time: The quota for Asian immigrants had a yearslong backlog. Gottlieb lobbied, cajoled, argued, networked, begged. At one point, frustrated by the lack of progress, she planned to send the children illegally through Canada, until her husband — who was both her sounding board and the more sober and analytical one in the couple — told her it would undermine her mission. Eventually her congressman, Hamilton Fish, Jr., agreed to propose special legislation for the eight children. In 1976, Congress passed four separate bills, one for each pairing of children, creating an exemption for them to be adopted by U. S. families.

Meanwhile, in South Korea, the families had been living with their excruciating decision for more than three years. “One more kind of pain that comes with leprosy,” Cho Te Chung told a New York Times reporter just before the legislation was signed into law. “I wish they could go soon,” a mother said of her two daughters. “Every day hurts a little more.”

The parents told their children they were heading off to a beautiful future. “Everything will be happiness,” Cho said. Though Mi Yun sensed her father was hesitant about the decision, her parents promised that she’d never be hungry, have plenty of new toys, beautiful clothing, a better education. She was, they said, lucky.

Finally, in October 1976, Gottlieb flew to South Korea to get the children. By then, they ranged in age from 3 to 15. As they said goodbye to their parents, Mi Yun’s father, not normally affectionate, hugged her so hard she didn’t know how to respond. Dressed in hanboks, a traditional Korean outfit, they boarded the plane with Father Lee, Gottlieb and another escort. Gottlieb held the two youngest children, one of whom wept. Across the aisle, Mi Yun looked at a prayer book from her first communion in which she’d written her parents’ names, their birth dates, her home address. “Please, God, don’t let me forget them,” she thought as she memorized the words.

Once they landed at John F. Kennedy International Airport, it was hard for some children to say goodbye to Gottlieb. One clung to her until her new mother pulled her away. Mi Yun, now 12 and renamed Jennifer, drove with her new parents to her new home on Long Island. As she looked out the window of their Oldsmobile, she saw graffiti spilled across buildings, garbage piled high. Where is the wealth? The fancy buildings? The glamorous people wearing beautiful clothes? All the promises?

In the coming years, she and the other St. Lazarus children would make friends, learn English, bond and not bond with their new families, face prejudice in largely white schools, struggle with their identity. Jennifer loved her new parents, who wanted the best for her. But they had five adopted children in total, along with two older biological children. There was jealousy among siblings and abuse. Money was tight.

Back in South Korea, parents mourned. Whenever the mother of the two youngest girls heard a crying baby or a child say “umma,” Korean for “mom,” she turned around thinking it was one of her daughters.

True to Gottlieb’s promise, the Korean parents and children did stay connected. The children sent report cards, photos, news from their lives. In return, their parents sent letters, religious gifts, Korean trinkets.

After just two years in the United States, Jennifer’s adoptive parents brought her to St. Lazarus to visit. She struggled to find the Korean words to speak to her mother and was angry about the promises her parents made about the United States. But, like many of the adoptees, she kept returning (one adoptee moved to South Korea permanently) and softened as she understood her parents’ difficult lives and painful choices. (Her parents did eventually climb out of poverty.) She was in South Korea for her father’s burial and to nurse her mother as she died.

For another adoptee, her trips to South Korea convinced her of two things: Her biological parents loved her, and adoption had been the best choice. But to Jessica (she asked that only her first name be used to protect her privacy), the youngest of the group, it is more complicated. She wonders what life would have been like if she hadn’t been adopted. How does losing a lifetime with her mother, her first language and her culture compare with living in the United States without the poverty and the stigma that would have marked her Korean life? “We were at the bottom of society,” she said. “But we would have that parent-child bond. I wonder if I would have felt more loved.”

Gottlieb was, for many years, on the periphery of Jessica and the adoptees’ lives. By the 1980s, after working on anti-leprosy campaigns, including for the United Nations, she left the adoption world. Later, she was horrified by reports of adoption corruption, her daughter said. South Korea, as it became clear, has used adoption to lower the country’s social welfare costs. Some adoption agencies, eager to meet American and European parents’ demand for adoptable children, trafficked in stolen babies, taking them from hospitals and off the streets. At times, they coerced mothers and made false promises. They lied to adoptees about their origins. In total, South Korea sent about 200,000 children abroad, more than any other country. The government is now phasing out international adoption.

Gottlieb, who died on Aug. 25 in Santa Monica, Calif., at 95, never believed adoption should be a moneymaking business or that it was the only way to help children in need. After two organizations invited her to India in the late 1970s to consider starting a program there, she decided against it. Gottlieb saw that the stigma against leprosy was less pronounced than in Korea. Children were welcome at schools, but many families couldn’t afford the supplies they needed to attend. So, rather than an adoption program, Gottlieb established a fund to support children’s education, providing school uniforms and books.

By the 1990s she had moved in a very different direction, becoming a Realtor in Westchester County and writing two novels about a crime-busting real-estate agent. In addition to her daughter, Susannah, her two sons, Peter and Richard, survive her.

She is survived, too, by a group of adoptees, now in their 50s and 60s, who thought of Gottlieb as a surrogate mother, a godmother, a fairy godmother. She was a magnet that held them together. As they got older and reconnected with her, she organized reunions, invited them to her home, told stories of their childhood. She attended the wedding of and hosted a baby shower for the youngest of the group. She reminded them that their parents didn’t send them away for lack of devotion, but out of desperation. Perhaps most important, she was the person who created a pathway — one that few international adoptees would ever receive — to keep the children of St. Lazarus connected to their past, to the Korean parents who had always loved them.

Lee Jiyoun contributed reporting from Seoul.

What Does Memory Sound Like?

The New York Times November 12, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Op-Docs

Video by Taliesin Black-Brown

Text by Hank Lentfer

Mr. Black-Brown is a filmmaker and photographer. Mr. Lentfer is an Alaskan author and sound recordist.

If our eyes are the front door of perception. Our ears are the back door.

We open our eyes to a familiar world of shape and color, streets and homes, faces and bodies. Sounds can slip in unannounced, rearrange our emotional furniture and let themselves out before we’ve even realized they were there.

There are voices far older than any human tongue.

Demoiselle cranes, for instance, called from African skies for millions of years before our ancestors descended from the trees and eventually set forth on two legs. Sandhill cranes greeted the first humans to find their way to North America. Along with robins and chickadees, rain and surf, elk and wolves, whales and gulls, they form a gorgeous, unending chorus. These ancient voices can, for a keen listener, help unlock memories we didn’t know we had. They remind us we are part of a lineage of sound that will continue long after we are gone.

We titled our short documentary “Listen” for a reason. We’re inviting you to slow down and really listen to what’s there. Use headphones if you have them. Better yet, grab a friend, hook up the best speakers you can find and let these wild voices rearrange your furniture.

Taliesin Black-Brown is an Emmy Award-winning filmmaker. Hank Lentfer is an author and sound recordist based in Alaska.
