The Face of the A. I. Boom Powering the U. S. Economy Is Gone

The New York Times November 12, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s ousted leader, was a unique rhetorical and financial booster for investments that are driving economic growth.

By Ben Casselman

As investors have pumped trillions of dollars into artificial intelligence companies, chipmakers and data center developers, the economy has come to rely on the industry as its primary — some would argue only — reliable driver of growth.

No company has been more central to that growth than Nvidia, whose chips fill the data centers that power A. I. and whose money helps to finance them. And, at least until this week, it was impossible to imagine Nvidia without Jensen Huang, its high-flying, leather-clad co-founder and chief executive.

All of which means that Mr. Huang’s resignation on Thursday, following a made-for-Hollywood series of scandals, matters not just for the company and its investors, but for virtually every American.

Or, as Aaron Klein, an expert in financial regulation at the Brookings Institution, put it: “Can one C. E. O.’s sex life take down the economy?”

The answer, in a literal sense, is almost certainly no. No one believes that Mr. Huang’s resignation will, by itself, bring the A. I. boom to an end, let alone plunge the economy into a recession. Nvidia’s stock price tumbled on Thursday, but the broader market barely budged.

But Mr. Klein’s quip spoke to the unique role that Mr. Huang played at Nvidia, and that his company has played in the A. I. build out.

Nvidia controls about 90 percent of the market for the most advanced chips used to train and run A. I. models. The turmoil at the company could create an opening for competitors such as AMD and Intel to encroach on that market share. But there is little reason to think that Mr. Huang’s resignation will threaten Nvidia’s ability to develop and produce the chips it has promised its customers.

But Nvidia isn’t just the dominant chipmaker. It is also the “central bank of A. I.,” helping to finance the industry’s growth through a series of complex deals with its customers and suppliers.

When OpenAI signed a lease for a 10-gigawatt data center in Ohio in August, it was Nvidia that provided $105 billion in loan guarantees. Days later, the company teamed up with several Wall Street firms to create a $500 billion fund to help finance A. I.-related infrastructure. Nvidia owns a more than 10 percent stake in CoreWeave, a big data center operator, and has guaranteed billions of dollars in its loans.

Its loan commitments and financing arrangements would make Nvidia the 10th largest bank in the country, according to an estimate from Ryan Cummings, the chief of staff for the Stanford Institute for Economic Policy Research.

“Nvidia is at the center of this circular financing, and obviously at the center of Nvidia is Jensen Huang,” Mr. Cummings said. “He has been the driving force, pretty inarguably, behind a lot of the A. I. build-out.”

Without Mr. Huang in charge, Nvidia’s role could change, Mr. Cummings said. And while it is possible that other companies will step in to fill the gap, that isn’t guaranteed.

Mr. Huang’s departure comes at a delicate time for the A. I. industry. There have been signs in recent months that investors are growing more skeptical that companies will deliver returns that justify the huge investments they are making in A. I., or at least that those returns could take longer than expected to materialize.

And Democrats’ sweeping victories in last week’s midterm elections could lead to new restrictions on data center construction, which could jeopardize the industry’s boom.

“At a point when people are already on edge about this trade, it’s another piece of uncertainty,” Mr. Cummings said.

In the past, when confidence in the A. I. story has wavered, Mr. Huang and Nvidia have been the ones to calm doubts, reporting huge sales figures or stepping in to provide financing to data center projects whose future seemed in jeopardy. This time, it isn’t clear who will fill the void.

“Could the single largest A. I. company C. E. O.’s impropriety be the start of the pop of the bubble?” Mr. Klein asked. “Yes, as crazy as that sounds. Particularly when one company is so central.”

Bubbles are inherently unpredictable: It isn’t clear, ahead of time, what will flip the psychological switch that causes them to burst. The muted market reaction of financial markets to the news on Thursday suggests that investors aren’t losing faith in the A. I. trade.

But Mr. Klein said the Nvidia mess should be a warning that the complex web of A. I. financing arrangements is threatening financial stability.

“It looks like the financial regulators are sleeping through the alarm clock,” he said.

If Nvidia’s new leadership takes a more cautious approach to financing, that could have implications for the broader economy. The data center boom has helped to prop up the construction and manufacturing industries, at a time when tariffs, high interest rates and uncertainty have limited demand from other sectors.

Still, the breakneck pace of the A. I. build-out has also pushed up inflation and raised borrowing costs. Many economists argue that a modest slowdown would be healthy.

The more immediate risk, economists say, is that a loss of confidence in the A. I. story leads to a steep drop in the stock market. The strength of the market has helped prop up consumer spending even as wage growth has cooled.

If the A. I. trade unravels because of an abrupt curtailment in investment, “that is more recessionary,” said Pooja Sriram, an economist at Barclays. “That’s when there is a more material shakeout in the stock market that transcends to how consumers feel. Balance sheets are hit and that could escalate very quickly into a downturn.”

Colby Smith contributed reporting.

Ben Casselman is the chief economics correspondent for The Times. He has reported on the economy for nearly 20 years.

SpaceX Plans $74 Billion Investment to Build Data Centers in Texas and Arizona

The New York Times November 12, 2026

Artificial Intelligence

Advertisement

Supported by

Elon Musk’s rocket and artificial intelligence company has spent billions to develop the giant warehouses full of computer servers that power the technology.

By Grace Kay

SpaceX said on Thursday that it planned to invest $74 billion to build new data center campuses in Arizona and Texas as the company continued to pour money into the global artificial intelligence race.

The projects, proposed by Elon Musk’s rocket and A. I. company, would be among some of the largest data center projects in the United States.

In Texas, SpaceX plans to invest $24 billion in a data center campus on 444 acres of company-owned land near the Starbase rocket site in the Rio Grande Valley. The data center in Texas will generate its own power rather than rely on the public grid, the company said in its announcement. It is not immediately clear whether the project needs any further regulatory approvals.

In Arizona, SpaceX plans to build a $50 billion campus in Cochise County, which will create 5,500 construction jobs and 1,000 permanent jobs, the company said. The Arizona project still requires approval from the county.

SpaceX, which went public this year in the biggest initial public offering in history, has quickly grown its business leasing out computing power to other A. I. companies like Anthropic and Google. In October, SpaceX reported that its A. I. business accounted for more than half its revenue.

Anthropic has committed to paying up to $120.5 billion through 2029. Google is also paying SpaceX $920 million per month for computing power.

SpaceX did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

SpaceX’s A. I. unit — xAI — has been at the forefront of the data center build out and operates four data centers near Memphis, Tenn., and Southhaven, Miss. Amazon, Meta, Microsoft and other tech giants have spent tens of billions of dollars on their own data center campuses.

The build outs have proved costly. SpaceX said in October that capital expenditures had risen to $19.6 billion during the third quarter, nearly three times its spending from the previous year. Mr. Musk said in October that the company had also closed $40 billion in debt financing to help fund the chips needed for its data centers.

SpaceX’s chief financial officer, Bret Johnsen, has said the company will continue to spend heavily on its data center build out. In October, he said the company was likely to spend $35 billion to $40 billion in the three months ending in December.

I'm a New York Times reporter, covering Elon Musk's companies with a focus on AI and emerging technology from New York.

A Frantic Search in Brooklyn

The New York Times November 12, 2026

For hours, hundreds of firefighters and rescue workers tore through steel and concrete searching for survivors.

A wall of an apartment building had been sheared off, exposing clothes hanging inside a closet.

In a pit below, a refrigerator laid on its side, nestled between broken furniture and other remnants of the apartments that were destroyed.

Portions of a construction site, including a portable toilet and office, remained intact, even as its workers went missing.

On city streets outside, medical workers waited to take away the people who were injured or killed.

Supported by

At one moment, an apartment building was standing. At another, it had tumbled into a hole. Ruin, and death, followed.

By Ana Ley and Dave Sanders

Devastation arrived Wednesday afternoon on a Brooklyn street. A construction crew had dug a deep hole, and, suddenly, an apartment building next to it tumbled in.

The body of one person was found soon after, and as the hours passed, the death toll rose. On Thursday, Mayor Zohran Mamdani said that eight people had been killed, including two children, and 18 had been injured.

Hundreds of firefighters and emergency workers scoured a large pile of rubble overnight and into the morning as they sought to rescue victims at the site, in the Flatbush neighborhood. Relatives and friends of the missing stood nearby, bleary-eyed and awaiting news. One woman sobbed as strangers tried to console her. She was later told her husband, a construction worker, was among the dead.

Dozens of police vehicles, ambulances and fire trucks bathed the area in red and blue light late into the night. Canine units, drones and helicopters swarmed the site with teams of firefighters wielding axes and pickaxes. Specialized vehicles and bulldozers combed through the wreckage as the frantic rescue operation continued.

Ana Ley is a Times reporter covering immigration in New York City.

What to Know About the Deadly Building Collapse in Brooklyn

The New York Times November 12, 2026

Building Collapse in Brooklyn

Advertisement

Supported by

At least eight people were killed and more than a dozen others injured when a three-story building in Flatbush collapsed, officials said.

By Maia ColemanCaitlyn Freeman and Max Bearak

A three-story apartment building collapsed and largely fell into an adjacent construction site in the Flatbush neighborhood of Brooklyn on Wednesday, killing at least eight people and injuring 18 others, Mayor Zohran Mamdani said.

Emergency workers were still sifting through the rubble on Thursday morning as they searched for the remaining victims. Officials said they did not immediately know how many people had been in the building, at 1321 Flatbush Avenue.

Mr. Mamdani said that the Department of Buildings and law enforcement officials would investigate the cause of the collapse.

“There are no words for a loss of this magnitude,” Mr. Mamdani said on social media on Thursday morning. “My heart is with the families and loved ones of those we have lost, those who are injured and everyone grieving today.”

The collapse occurred while an excavation was taking place at the adjacent construction site on Bedford Avenue, where the city had approved plans for a three-story building.

At 4:01 p. m. on Wednesday, the Fire Department received a 911 call about a building collapse at 1321 Flatbush Avenue, Mr. Mamdani said at a news conference later that day.

Canine units, drones, helicopters and fire trucks were used in the search, alongside excavation machinery, in a search and rescue operation that continued into Thursday. The adjoining wall of an adjacent building was sheared off by the collapse, leaving a staircase, a bedroom and closets exposed to the open air.

It’s not clear yet. The Department of Buildings said that its engineers were conducting structural stability inspections of nearby buildings, but city records suggested that there had been at least some concern about the condition of the collapsed building.

The building that collapsed was built in 1930 and had four apartments, according to city records. It is in the Little Haiti section of Flatbush, on an avenue lined with shops.

The Department of Buildings said the developers of the adjacent construction site had an active permit for excavation and foundation work. The agency’s commissioner, Ahmed Tigani, told reporters that workers were excavating that site at the time of the collapse.

Marco Hernandez and Jillian Vordick / The New York Times

An inspection related to the construction site and filed with the Buildings Department in March noted that the north facade of the collapsed building was in “poor condition with noticeable cracks.”

A full stop-work order has been issued for the construction site, the department said.

The authorities have not released the names of the people who were killed or injured, but at a news conference on Thursday, Mr. Mamdani confirmed that six adults and two children had died in the collapse. Two of the dead were construction workers, he said.

Six of the victims were found dead at the site while two others died later at local hospitals, the mayor said. Eighteen people were also injured in the collapse, including four firefighters, and at least one of the injured was in critical condition on Thursday.

The city has lost “our friends and our neighbors,” Mr. Mamdani said, noting that several victims appeared to be immigrants from Central or South America.

Flatbush is home to a large number of immigrants, according to Rodneyse Bichotte Hermelyn, a local assembly member. After the collapse, Ms. Bichotte Hermelyn said she saw emergency responders pull a toddler from the rubble and a pregnant woman whose husband was searching for her.

Lillian Bonsignore, the city’s fire commissioner, said on Thursday afternoon that emergency responders were still conducting search and rescue operations and had not yet transitioned to recovery efforts. But a rainstorm on Thursday afternoon was likely to complicate and slow that process.

On Thursday afternoon, many residents near the site of the collapse remained indefinitely displaced, though some further down Flatbush Avenue had returned to their homes. The city’s emergency management agency and the American Red Cross have opened a reception center for affected and displaced residents at the Flatbush Y. M. C. A., at 1401 Flatbush Avenue.

The authorities are encouraging people who are unable to reach someone they believe to be affected by the collapse to call 311. People outside the city can call 212-639-9675.

Mr. Mamdani said the city had begun to investigate the disaster, with an additional focus on the construction site. The Buildings Department has identified “five entities” associated with the project, and city officials plan to conduct sweeps of 100 other sites the groups are involved with to ensure they are safe.

“If there is anyone or any entity operating in this city that bears responsibility for what happened, we will hold them fully accountable,” Mr. Mamdani said.

Sharon Otterman, Ishani Desai, Sarah Chatta, Mihir Zaveri, Troy Closson, Emma G. Fitzsimmons and Ana Ley contributed reporting.

Maia Coleman is a reporter for The Times covering the New York Police Department and criminal justice in the New York area.

Caitlyn Freeman is a Metro reporter for The New York Times and part of the 2026-27 Times Fellowship, a program for journalists early in their careers.

Max Bearak is a correspondent for The Times focusing on breaking and international news.

Trump Says He’s Pulling Vance Off Iran Talks to Focus on Fraud Campaign

The New York Times November 12, 2026

War in the Middle East

Advertisement

Supported by

The announcement on social media deepened questions about what the president’s plan is to end the war. “We don’t need a deal with Iran,” he wrote.

By Luke Broadwater

Reporting from Washington

President Trump said on Thursday that he had pulled Vice President JD Vance back from engaging in potential peace talks with Iran, saying that his time would be better spent investigating fraud in Democratic-run jurisdictions.

“We don’t need a deal with Iran,” Mr. Trump wrote on social media. “Those days have long since passed.”

The post deepens questions about what Mr. Trump’s plan is to end the war. The president has been weighing a number of options, including ramping up military strikes, withdrawing and leaving the matter to Arab allies or simply maintaining the status quo.

It also signals a pivot on his instructions to Mr. Vance, after the vice president publicly blamed the war for the Republican Party’s devastating midterm election losses in a striking critique of the administration’s agenda and messaging.

Mr. Trump had assigned Mr. Vance, who privately expressed opposition to going to war with Iran, to lead negotiations earlier this year. The vice president traveled to Pakistan in April and met with Iranian leaders in a marathon session that ended without any resolution.

Mr. Vance recently contacted a top Iranian political and military official to propose a renewal of comprehensive peace negotiations. In a letter sent from Mr. Vance via Qatari meditators to Gen. Mohsen Rezaei, the secretary of the Supreme National Security Council, the vice president suggested that American and Iranian officials meet soon, adding that he would lead the talks for the United States.

But Mr. Trump said on Thursday that he was ending that effort.

“I have asked Vice President Vance to focus his complete and total attention on the Massive Corruption and Crime taking place in Democrat run Cities and States throughout the U. S.,” he wrote on social media.

While there is a high-profile fraud investigation in Minnesota that has resulted in scores of arrests, federal data does not support the president’s suggestion that fraud is more prevalent under Democrats than Republicans. Mr. Trump also has granted clemency to more than 70 allies, donors and others convicted in fraud cases, often involving high-dollar totals.

The president’s instruction to back off negotiations with Iran came as other travel plans by Mr. Vance had been scuttled.

Mr. Vance had explored traveling to several countries in the Caribbean and South America during Thanksgiving week, officials said. Those plans are now off, the officials said.

The trip had been in the planning stages since October. Last week, officials were told to cancel a stop in the Dominican Republic. Then on Monday, officials canceled the rest of the stops, in Colombia, Argentina and Chile. All those nations are run by right-wing governments considered partners of the Trump administration.

“The vice president’s team regularly explores potential travel opportunities in support of the administration’s domestic and foreign policy agendas,” Mr. Vance’s office said in a statement. “While potential trips may be in various stages of consideration, no trip is considered final until announced by the vice president’s office.”

Shortly after Republicans suffered heavy losses in the midterm elections, Mr. Vance placed the blame for Republicans’ wipeout in the midterm elections squarely on the war with Iran.

“The reason we lost is the war,” he wrote in a social media post, adding, “If you’d like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next six years was worth it, then do so.”

Mr. Trump told reporters that he was not upset by the post. “A lot of people didn’t like his comments,” he said. “But not me.”

Mr. Trump’s announcement on Thursday added further uncertainty to an already muddled situation. The United States and Iran have recently avoided large-scale fighting, but skirmishes, a naval blockade and a struggle for control of the Strait of Hormuz have continued.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Gen. Dan Caine, the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, have presented the president with a menu of military options that Adm. Brad Cooper, the commander of U. S. Central Command, developed in recent months, if Mr. Trump wants to ramp up the war again.

But in a recent “60 Minutes” interview, Mr. Trump suggested he was no longer worried about the country’s nuclear capabilities, his stated reason for starting the war.

Still, the Strait of Hormuz, the key oil shipping waterway that Iran closed after the United States and Israel began the war, remains contested.

In response, the United States has set up a naval blockade that prevents Iran from exporting oil, while American escorts and patrols try to ensure that a healthy amount of non-Iranian oil gets through.

About two weeks ago, Iran said it was prepared to fully reopen the strait in two days if the United States agreed to a set of demands.

After the midterm elections, Iran’s foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, wrote on social media: “American voters have made their choice. Time for the White House to make its own.”

“Our 2-day proposal stands: meet the requirements, including end to war on all fronts, and you will see results,” he wrote. “Or choose war, and see our alert and battle-hardened Warriors rain down hell.”

Edward Wong contributed reporting from Washington, and Maria Abi-Habib from Mexico City.

Luke Broadwater covers the White House for The Times.

Takeaways From the Times’s Report on Aviation Safety

The New York Times November 12, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

How alarmed should we be about the state of air travel?

By James Fallows

When an Army helicopter and a commuter jet collided over the Potomac last year, killing all 67 people aboard both aircraft, a historic era of airline safety came to an end. American commercial airlines had gone without a fatal crash for 16 years, the longest disaster-free period ever for U. S. air travel.

In the nearly two years since, the strains on the system, which have been mounting for decades, have become acute. One of the best measures of aviation safety is the rate of “runway incursions,” close calls on the ground where planes come dangerously near each other. After a spike in 2023, those incidents fell sharply in 2024 as the F. A. A. and airlines tightened procedures. Since 2025 they have climbed again, and the most serious kind of incursion, where a collision is only narrowly avoided, is running even higher this year than last.

Air travel has been so safe in large part because of a profound commitment from the people in charge to learn from tragedies — what aviation experts call “lessons written in blood.” But the Trump administration has been slow to learn new lessons, and in some cases it seems to be unlearning the old ones.

“We are seeing the vulnerabilities in real time,” Jennifer Homendy, the chair of the N. T. S. B., told me. “We have a duty to act before another tragedy occurs.”

How alarmed should we be? Over 30 years I’ve logged more than 2,000 hours as pilot-in-command of single-engine aircraft, and written three books on aviation. What I have seen since the Potomac crash is something new and worrying.

In a story for the magazine, I take readers through some of the system’s vulnerabilities:

The morning after the Potomac crash, President Trump blamed the disaster on D. E. I. hiring practices during the Obama and Biden administrations. The National Transportation Safety Board found that the real culprit was overcrowding.

Aircraft at the most in-demand hubs were taking off and landing back to back, often using authorized shortcuts to speed up traffic flow. This was especially risky in the narrow air corridor between National Airport and restricted airspace over the White House and the Capitol, and the N. T. S. B. recommended 33 separate equipment and procedure changes that the F. A. A. should undertake to make future such accidents far less likely.

But the F. A. A. has not implemented one-third of these recommendations, a response the N. T. S. B. categorizes as “unacceptable.” (The F. A. A. told me that it is still evaluating how to address the remaining recommendations.)

On Trump’s first day in office, his acting Homeland Security secretary fired all of the members of a key airline security advisory committee, as part of the department’s “commitment to eliminating the misuse of resources.”

A month later, the F. A. A. fired some 400 probationary employees who had not yet won civil-service protection, including 132 members of the Professional Aviation Safety Specialists union.

“We’ll look back on choices like these as the first step in some future accident chain,” Bruce J. Holmes, a lifelong aviator and 30-year NASA veteran says of such changes.

Elon Musk, when he was leading the so-called Department of Government Efficiency, promised to “make rapid safety upgrades to the air traffic control system.”

He repeatedly derided Verizon, which had won a contract on that very project, and installed several SpaceX engineers at the F. A. A. as “special government employees” with ethical waivers to work on projects that might financially benefit Musk’s businesses.

In the end, SpaceX did not get a contract, but the F. A. A. did change a regulation that affected the company: Now more commercial flights are allowed to pass through areas where they face an accident caused by debris from a failed space launch.

In April, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy announced a new effort to address a longstanding shortage of air traffic controllers: he would recruit video game enthusiasts. Gamers, he said, are used to looking at screens and talking when there’s a lot going on around them — “and that’s actually what you’re doing in a tower.”

A veteran controller was less sure. “This is real life and death,” he told me. “It actually is different from getting shot on a screen.”

In August, Duffy said the F. A. A. had “supercharged” the hiring process and reached its staffing target in record time. He didn’t mention that the F. A. A. had cut that target by more than 2,000, betting that new technology, including A. I., would make up the difference.

The Pentagon has in repeated instances surprised commercial aviation authorities with unannounced maneuvers over the Caribbean, in one case forcing a JetBlue plane to take evasive action to avoid a collision.

Without notifying anyone in the F. A. A., officials from Customs and Border Protection fired a laser-powered anti-drone weapon system, on loan from the Pentagon, in the area around El Paso, forcing the local airport to shut down completely. It ultimately emerged that the system had been deployed to shoot down a party balloon that C. B. P. had mistaken for a cartel drone.

The Trump administration has also deployed aircraft in displays that experts described as reckless, bending rules to allow administration officials to fly their own jets in restricted air space or, most recently, allowing the Qatari-donated 747 that has been serving as Air Force One to fly directly over the White House in airspace where no commercial airliner would ever be allowed, for what it called an “epic” photo op.

In a statement, Singapore said it held Alice Huang’s passport months after President Trump was briefed that she was a spy.

By Paul Mozur

Singapore’s government said on Thursday the United States had provided little help in its investigation into Alice Huang, the woman at the center of a spy plot that has led to the investigation of Nvidia’s chief executive, Jensen Huang.

Singaporean authorities held Ms. Huang’s passport to prevent her from leaving the country from June 2025 until February over “potential false declarations” in relation to her company, Megaspeed, which is based in the country, the government said in a statement. She was ultimately released with a “stern warning” and barred from re-entering Singapore.

The statement raises new questions about the response of the Trump administration to the case and why the U. S. government did not more forcefully intervene. According to the timeline in the statement, Singaporean authorities had been holding Ms. Huang’s passport well after President Trump was briefed last fall about her relationship with Nvidia’s chief executive and the belief that she was a Chinese intelligence asset.

The New York Times has reported that Taiwan began monitoring Ms. Huang in 2024 at the guidance of the U. S. government.

In its statement, Singapore said that it had sought information from an American server maker and close Nvidia business partner, Supermicro, but that the company had provided “limited cooperation.” Supermicro, a firm that packages Nvidia’s A. I. chips onto servers that can be used in data centers, has been at the center of a number of chip smuggling investigations across the globe.

Supermicro was a supplier to Megaspeed, a company incorporated in Singapore and run by Ms. Huang, according to two people with knowledge of the matter.

Singapore said in the statement its authorities raised Supermicro’s “limited cooperation” with the U. S. Department of Justice and Federal Bureau of Investigation in July 2025 and “requested their assistance in securing the company’s cooperation.”

“Despite these repeated requests, Singapore has to date received limited information or assistance in respect of the company,” the statement said.

Supermicro denied that Megaspeed had ever been a customer. “Supermicro did not sell any products to Megaspeed and has operated in compliance with all applicable U. S. export and re-export control laws,” the company said in a statement.

During questioning, Ms. Huang sought to downplay her role in Megaspeed, according to Singapore’s statement. She was ultimately released because of “insufficient evidence relating to the possible inaccurate declarations for which Megaspeed was being investigated.”

She was issued a “stern warning” and barred from re-entering Singapore. The country’s police are continuing to investigate Megaspeed.

Paul Mozur is the global technology correspondent for The Times, based in Taipei. Previously he wrote about technology and politics in Asia from Hong Kong, Shanghai and Seoul.

Connections: Soccer Edition

Connections Coach

Most Democrats abhor the health secretary’s stance on vaccines, but some see an opportunity to win voters from his MAHA movement by joining with him on food and environmental issues.

Credit... Haiyun Jiang/The New York Times

Supported by

By Sheryl Gay Stolberg

Sheryl Gay Stolberg covers Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and his MAHA movement.

Three days after last week’s “blue wave” election, Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. posted a warning on X to anyone suspecting his Make America Healthy Again movement had been weakened. “It’s time to unleash the Kraken,” he wrote.

The phrase, a reference to the 1981 move “Clash of the Titans” that gained currency in 2020 among far-right internet personalities who claimed Democrats stole the election, suggests Mr. Kennedy will fight for his agenda and has no intention of leaving his job despite the defeat of several MAHA-backed candidates.

The question now is whether Democrats will use their new majorities in Congress to try to push him out.

Many want to investigate him, saying his vaccine agenda and handling of measles outbreaks have put American lives at risk. Some, including Senator-elect Annie Andrews of South Carolina, want to impeach him. Senator Angela Alsobrooks, Democrat of Maryland, wants Mr. Kennedy removed, but has not said how.

“The time is now,” Ms. Alsobrooks wrote on X the day after the election. “RFK Jr. must resign or be fired. End of discussion.”

But others want to work with Mr. Kennedy in areas where they can agree. They believe his food and environmental policies, which have run into roadblocks with the Trump White House, have a natural home with Democrats, and they see a chance to win over some of the health-focused coalition that helped propel President Trump to a second term.

Democrats like Representative Chellie Pingree of Maine, a regenerative farmer, and Tim Ryan, a former congressman from Ohio, believe the party should not squander an opportunity to woo MAHA voters on those issues. Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan, a doctor and former state public health official, has proposed his own MAHA agenda under a different name: Build a Healthier America.

“This makes no sense,” Mr. Ryan wrote in response to Ms. Alsobrooks, adding, “Why wouldn’t we work together to see what wins we can get?”

Emily Hilliard, a spokeswoman for Mr. Kennedy, said the secretary would “continue to serve the American people and welcomes working with all members of Congress to turn shared priorities into lasting MAHA reforms.”

MAHA activists across the political spectrum have soured on the Trump White House for stalling Mr. Kennedy’s effort to regulate ultraprocessed foods. Many so-called MAHA Moms, who believed Mr. Trump when he said he would let Mr. Kennedy “go wild on health,” felt betrayed by the president when he issued an executive order ramping up production of glyphosate, a weedkiller that some scientists link to cancer.

“Women feel like they were lied to,” Alex Clark, a conservative podcaster and MAHA influencer, said in February, after the glyphosate order.

Two prominent MAHA leaders, Vani Hari, a cookbook author and healthy eating activist who calls herself “the Food Babe,” and Zen Honeycutt, an environmental activist who founded the group Moms Across America, are former Democrats who followed Mr. Kennedy into Mr. Trump’s camp. Both say they vote the person, not the party.

“I’m frankly tired of reporters asking me, you know, whether I’m loyal to the Republicans, whether I’m loyal to the Democrats,” said Ms. Hari, who was a delegate for Barack Obama at the 2012 Democratic National Convention. “I’m loyal to my children.”

On the day after the election, Ms. Honeycutt joined a webinar for leaders of MAHA Action, a nonprofit advocacy group that supports Mr. Kennedy. She implored Democrats to join forces with the secretary.

“I just urge every Democrat that is considering working against him to sit down and talk with him,” she said. “I think you’re going to love him. I think you’re going to enjoy working with him.”

The blue wave sent a string of Democratic doctors, scientists and health professionals to Congress, who arrived in Washington for freshman orientation this week. But working with Mr. Kennedy may be a hard sell to many of them.

In the past, most of the doctors in Congress have been Republicans, often self-employed and driven to run by business concerns. The new crop of Democrats with professional health backgrounds are animated by the cost of care, access to treatments and in some cases antipathy toward Mr. Kennedy. Ms. Andrews, the senator-elect from South Carolina, a state hit hard by the measles epidemic, ran on a platform of impeaching Mr. Kennedy.

“He’s a clear and present danger to public health,” Ms. Andrews, a pediatrician, said during the campaign.

After the election, Erik Polyak, the executive director of 314 Action, a political action committee that backs scientists and health professionals who run for public office, predicted a rough road ahead for Mr. Kennedy. “We’re going to see R. F. K. Jr.’s head on a platter,” Mr. Polyak told Politico.

The comment ricocheted across the internet, as news organizations declared that “Dems smell blood” and were “coming for” the health secretary. But in an interview, the founder and president of 314 Action, Shaughnessy Naughton, dismissed Mr. Polyak’s statement. “That is not rhetoric that belongs in this conversation,” she said.

Still, Ms. Naughton, who is a chemist and former congressional candidate from Pennsylvania, saw the election results as a repudiation of Mr. Kennedy’s policies, including his attacks on the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and the National Institutes of Health.

“We have been warning Republicans for months that voters were going to hold Republicans responsible for the recklessness of R. F. K. Jr.,” she said.

For the moment, Democrats are more focused on impeaching Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth than Mr. Kennedy. “I don’t think Democrats can spend their time trying to impeach the entire cabinet, and if there are any impeachments, it should start with Secretary Hegseth,” Ms. Pingree said.

But Mr. Kennedy’s detractors may soon get some ammunition. Early next week, an arm of the World Health Organization is expected to strip the United States of its designation as a nation that has eliminated measles. The disease has killed 11 people in the country since Mr. Kennedy took office.

Senator Bernie Sanders, the Vermont independent who caucuses with Democrats and is likely to become the next chairman of the Senate health committee, told CNN on Sunday that he is “absolutely open” to impeachment. In a statement to The New York Times on Saturday, Mr. Sanders sidestepped questions about whether he would rather impeach or work with Mr. Kennedy.

“R. F. K. Jr. is, by far, the most dangerous health and human services secretary in our nation’s history,” Mr. Sanders said in the statement, adding that his committee “will hold Secretary Kennedy accountable.”

While the election confirmed the rupture between the MAHA movement and Republicans, paradoxically, Mr. Kennedy’s hand inside the White House may now be strengthened. Last week, Mr. Trump announced that he was replacing his chief of staff, Susie Wiles, who has been accused of blocking some MAHA policies, with Stephen Miller, the architect of the administration’s hard-line immigration policies. Mr. Miller’s wife, Katie Miller, was Mr. Kennedy’s spokeswoman during the transition.

“Next to me, Stephen Miller is the strongest MAHA supporter in the administration,” Mr. Kennedy wrote on X, in his “unleash the Kraken” post.

Some Kennedy allies are urging the secretary to take advantage of MAHA’s fractured relationship with Republicans, and the switch in the White House leadership, to advance his agenda. Ms. Clark sees two options for Mr. Kennedy. One is to quit, and plan a run for president in 2028. “The other option,” she said, “is to go in, guns a-blazing, I don’t care, I’m going to treat every day like the president is going to fire me.”

Even Tony Lyons, the conservative publisher and close Kennedy ally who runs MAHA Action and its sister political action committee, is noticeably shifting his rhetoric.

Early in the election cycle, Mr. Lyons vowed to raise $100 million to elect “MAHA-aligned, Trump-endorsed” Republicans. The MAHA PAC did help elect one Republican, Julia Letlow, the senator-elect from Louisiana, though she did not flip a seat. She will replace Senator Bill Cassidy, who lost to her in a primary.

But some of the MAHA PAC’s marquee Republican candidates lost last week. They include Senator Roger Marshall of Kansas; Ken Paxton, the Texas attorney general who was running for Senate; and Zach Lahn, who hoped to become Iowa’s governor. At the MAHA Action post-election event, Mr. Lyons blamed corporate influence and “Big Food, Big Ag, Big Pharma” for the outcomes.

He did not talk about Trump-endorsed Republicans. “We have the building blocks of an incredibly powerful, independent movement that is beholden to no one,” he said.

Mr. Kennedy seems unbowed. At a MAHA Action party in Washington on Monday night, he was surrounded by fans, jockeying to take selfies; one young woman posed holding a small rabbit. He spoke for about 10 minutes, praising Mr. Miller and Ms. Wiles.

But in addition to criticizing Democrats, Mr. Kennedy also took aim at Republicans, who refused to confirm several Trump health appointees, and suggested he may have a freer hand now that the president’s party is no longer in power.

“Every time I tried to do something robust, I would get calls saying, ‘If you do that, we’re not going to confirm your appointees,’” he said. He added: “The Senate no longer has any leverage over me. And you know, that’s a big deal.”

Dani Blum contributed reporting from Washington.

Sheryl Gay Stolberg is a correspondent based in Washington for The Times, covering Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and President Trump’s health agenda.

Nvidia Shares Plunge, Shaking Up Tech Stocks

The New York Times November 12, 2026

Nvidia C. E. O. Resigns

Advertisement

Supported by

News that the chipmaker’s chief executive, Jensen Huang, resigned drove Nvidia’s stock down, though the broader market rose slightly.

Notes: Data is delayed at least 15 minutes.

Source: FactSet.

The New York Times

By Aruni SoniEshe Nelson and Jason Karaian

Nvidia’s shares plummeted Thursday, sending tremors through global markets, as the company’s chief executive, Jensen Huang, stepped down from his role.

Shares in Nvidia dropped as much as 14 percent when markets opened for trading on Thursday, extending a decline that has wiped out more than $1 trillion from the company’s market value this month alone. The stock began to reverse most of its losses by late morning.

The broader market rose slightly, too, as investors began to conclude that the fallout of Mr. Jensen’s departure would not fundamentally undermine the artificial intelligence trade. Yields on the 10-year U. S. Treasury rose above 5 percent on Thursday for the first time in weeks. Yields go up when Treasury prices go down.

Nvidia has emerged as central to the A. I. economy because its chips — or graphic processing units — help train and power models across the industry. It has also become a central bank of sorts for several A. I. companies, because its finances are deeply intertwined with those of everyone from frontier A. I. labs to neoclouds, which rent out computing power.

“This is an Nvidia problem before it is an A. I. problem,” said Mark Malek, chief investment officer at Siebert Financial. But he added that Nvidia’s woes could trickle through to other companies.

“Where I would be careful is with the smaller A. I. cloud companies that leaned on Nvidia’s checkbook,” he said. “If the new regime gets more conservative about financing its own customers, that is where it shows up first.”

The company’s board named Colette Kress, Nvidia’s chief financial officer, as its interim chief executive.

With the change in Nvidia’s leadership, investors face uncertainty about one of the poster children of the A. I. trade and how its problems could affect the broader economy.

Among the hardest hit stocks on Thursday were cloud computing providers that have strategic partnerships with Nvidia. Coreweave sank nearly 8 percent, and Nebius plunged nearly 17 percent. Nvidia’s rivals, on the other hand, ticked higher. AMD rose nearly 3 percent and Broadcom gained more than 4 percent on Thursday.

The broader U. S. market, initially weighed down by Nvidia’s troubles, inched higher on Thursday afternoon. The S&P 500 was up 0.2 percent and tech-heavy Nasdaq up 0.1 percent.

Nvidia’s woes reverberated through global markets as well. Taiwan’s TSMC, which produces chips designed by Nvidia, fell nearly 2 percent. But South Korea’s Samsung, which competes with Nvidia on some business lines, gained 1 percent. Shares in Europe’s largest tech company, ASML of the Netherlands, fell less than 1 percent.

Mr. Huang, who co-founded Nvidia in 1993, has become one of the most influential forces in the A. I. boom, which has helped to drive U. S. stock markets to new highs in recent years.

Nvidia’s board deliberations came after revelations that Mr. Huang had an affair with an executive who reports to him as well as with a woman whom U. S. intelligence has identified as a Chinese spy.

Some market analysts covering Nvidia have begun to downgrade their forecasts for its stock. Though the chipmaker is expected to remain a critical part of the A. I. build-out, some noted rising concerns about its governance and lack of a clear succession plan. They argued that these revelations have fundamentally changed Mr. Huang’s position in the tech world, and it was unclear what the implications of his departure from Nvidia could be.

Analysts at Bernstein downgraded Nvidia and sharply lowered their target for its share price. “Our gut tells us that we probably haven’t yet fully probed the depths of what might be found here,” they wrote. “We’ve had enough, and prefer to watch from the sidelines.”

Analysts at RBC Capital Markets also slashed their forecast for the stock, citing the lack of a formal succession plan for chief executive. “Whether any individual can replicate Huang’s singular combination of technical vision, ecosystem-building acumen and ability to serve as the global face of the A. I. revolution remains an open question,” they noted.

Nvidia’s stock is down about a third from its peak at the start of October, putting the company deep in a bear market, defined as a drop of 20 percent or more from a recent high.

The chipmaker retains a central role in the A. I. revolution, said Ken Mahoney, chief executive of Mahoney Asset Management, but he added that there could be more “rumblings” under the surface for investors looking to buy the dip.

“Ultimately, a lot depends on your investment time horizon,” he said. “Short-term traders face tremendous uncertainty, while longer-term investors may find opportunity if the company’s underlying fundamentals remain intact.”

Nvidia became the world’s largest public company by market value for the first time in 2024, exerting an outsize influence over major indexes like the Nasdaq Composite and the S&P 500. Analysts still expect Nvidia to make a profit of well over $200 billion this year, with its chips in high demand as tech companies rush to build giant A. I. data centers. It reports its quarterly earnings next week.

During last week’s market turmoil, Nvidia fell below Apple as the world’s biggest public company.

Aruni Soni is a business reporter and a member of the 2026-27 Times Fellowship, a program for journalists early in their careers.

Eshe Nelson is a Times reporter based in London, covering economics and business news.

Jason Karaian is a deputy business editor at The Times, based in London.

Democrats Plan Investigation Into Climate and Science Cuts Under Trump

The New York Times November 12, 2026

Trump Administration

Advertisement

Supported by

Letters sent by two key House committees tell companies and officials not to destroy documents.

By Evan Halper

Reporting from Washington

Congressional Democrats have alerted more than 60 companies, individuals and agencies that they are potential targets of investigations into the Trump administration’s cuts to scientific research, rollback of environmental protections and pursuit of unorthodox business deals.

The letters reveal where Democrats, soon to be empowered with subpoena authority after their sweeping wins in last week’s elections, intend to focus as they examine some of the administration’s most unabashed deals and policy changes. The notices sent from top Democrats on two key House committees demand preservation of any documents that could be relevant to congressional oversight next year.

The attempt to dismantle one of the world’s leading climate and weather research institutions, a lucrative White House deal with a rare earths company and an organized campaign to delegitimize climate science ahead of a sweeping regulatory rollback are among the concerns related to letters sent by the House Science Committee Thursday morning and reviewed by The New York Times.

“This administration has engaged in an assault on the science enterprise in this country,” said Representative Zoe Lofgren, Democrat of California, who is expected to chair the House Science Committee next year. “There have been firings, coercing people to resign, impounding money and possible corruption.”

Democrats have been in the minority in both chambers of Congress for almost four years. Lawmakers said potential targets ignored previous requests for information related to the Trump administration because they lacked legal authority to compel a response. That changed with last week’s election.

“If Democrats choose to pursue sham investigations and radical left policies, they are choosing to work against the American people,” Lauren Bis, a White House spokeswoman, said in a statement.

The Science Committee asked about the rare earths deal after several Democratic lawmakers warned that the arrangement the White House struck has the appearance of corruption. The deal calls for the government to invest as much as $1.6 billion in USA Rare Earth, a mineral company based in Oklahoma, in exchange for a 10 percent stake in the firm. Democrats say the company leveraged the government investment to raise $1.5 billion in private funds, using Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick’s former firm, Cantor Fitzgerald, as a placement agent. Cantor Fitzgerald is now run by Mr. Lutnick’s sons, and Democrats have accused Mr. Lutnick of using public funds to bolster his former firm.

The Commerce Department has denied wrongdoing, saying Mr. Lutnick complied with ethics requirements and that Cantor Fitzgerald played no role in the government’s investment decision.

The committee is also pursuing an investigation into a report published by the Energy Department that appeared designed to undermine the credibility of climate science while the administration prepared to roll back landmark rules limiting carbon emissions.

Energy Secretary Chris Wright handpicked five researchers to work on the report in secret. The Environmental Protection Agency then cited the report to justify a plan to repeal what’s known as the endangerment finding, a scientific determination that serves as the legal foundation for the E. P. A.’s power to regulate climate pollution.

A federal judge ultimately ruled the report was illegal, citing a 1972 law that prohibits agencies from relying on secret groups for policymaking. In response, the E. P. A. dropped the report from its justification for scrapping the climate rules. But environmental groups have sued to try to reinstate the rules, and they could make use of any information that comes out of the oversight hearings.

One of the scientists who helped draft the report, Judith Curry, said in an email that she will comply with the committee’s request. But she dismissed its investigation as “a massive waste of everyone’s time,” noting the scientists have already publicly disclosed their emails and other documents as part of the litigation, and that the lawsuit has “thwarted” them from drafting a report that answers concerns critics have raised about their work.

Travis Fisher, an energy economist who helped organize the report, noted one of the scientists who worked on it was a senior energy official in the Obama administration. “Scientific debate deserves a hearing at the highest levels, and I look forward to working with the committee,” Mr. Fisher wrote in an email.

An emailed statement from the E. P. A. said the agency is reviewing the committee’s letter “and will respond through appropriate channels.”

The committee also expressed interest in the administration’s efforts to dismantle the National Center for Atmospheric Research in Colorado, which Russell Vought, the director of the White House Office of Management and Budget, called “one of the largest sources of climate alarmism in the country.”

A federal judge has issued a preliminary injunction blocking the administration’s plan. Democrats have also expressed alarm over what they say is evidence provided by a whistle blower that the administration is trying to improperly transfer the agency’s space weather program to a private company.

The targets of Ms. Lofgren’s letters did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

On Monday, the top Democrat on the House Committee on Natural Resources put his own likely targets on notice to preserve documents, including some agencies also contacted by the Science Committee. Among the recipients of letters from Representative Jared Huffman of California are companies including Lithium Americas, a mining operation in which the Trump administration has claimed a 5 percent equity stake, and SoftBank, a $50 million donor to Trump’s presidential library that is receiving help from the administration in fast-tracking the world’s largest data center development.

Large oil companies that have been among the biggest beneficiaries of the administration’s regulatory rollbacks were also sent directives to preserve documents, as was the Trust for the National Mall, a nonprofit that Democrats claim the administration sought to use unlawfully to conceal the identity of corporate donors to its ballroom project.

Lithium Americas and SoftBank declined to comment. The Trust did not respond to a request for comment.

“For the past two years, the Trump administration has repeatedly failed to provide Congress with information necessary to conduct its oversight responsibilities and obstructed numerous congressional investigations,” Mr. Huffman wrote in the letters.

Evan Halper reports on the policies and politics shaping our response to climate change for The New York Times.

For Democrats, Economic Populism Is Cutting Through Party Divides

The New York Times November 12, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

News Analysis

Moderate Democrats and progressives have long feuded over who should drive their party’s economic agenda. But many newly elected members say they share the same big goals.

By Catie Edmondson

Reporting from the Capitol

Claire Valdez, a democratic socialist assemblywoman from Queens, was listening to a campaign speech by Cait Conley, a centrist Army veteran from the Hudson Valley, when she felt a pang of recognition.

“She was talking about billionaires,” Ms. Valdez, who was elected last week in her solidly Democratic district, recalled of Ms. Conley, who flipped a Republican seat in a conservative-leaning area. “It’s like, this sounds like Bernie 2016.”

Now both women are headed to Congress after a Democratic sweep that handed their party firm control of the House and Senate but quickly gave rise to a debate in their ranks about whether progressives or moderates will have the upper hand in driving the agenda come January.

Unlike in the past, however, members of both factions — centrist Democrats who captured competitive districts and the most liberal members in safe seats — appear to have coalesced around a common theme many of them agree won their party the midterms and should be their focus: economic populism.

The last time Democrats controlled both chambers of Congress, under President Joseph R. Biden Jr., bitter policy disagreements between moderates and progressives over how expansive their legislative plan should be prompted intraparty feuds that threatened to derail their economic agenda.

Democratic leaders in both the House and Senate are already navigating some of those same rifts. Representative Hakeem Jeffries and Senator Chuck Schumer, the centrist New York Democrats who are now their party’s leaders in the minority, are facing resistance from the left to their bids to keep the top posts in the majority. Some progressives have demanded that they commit to embracing specific far-reaching policy changes on the heels of overwhelming electoral victories.

But for all of the policy disputes that Democrats will still be forced to confront when they take power in January, there is broad agreement among many of the newly elected members on an agenda focused on cutting costs and combating corruption.

Senators-elect Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan and Troy Jackson of Maine — both left-leaning leaders who won in more competitive states — ran on Medicare for all. Senator-elect James Talarico of Texas, a moderate who prevailed in his Republican-dominated state, campaigned on allowing every American, regardless of age, to join Medicare. In heavily Republican Kansas, Senator-elect Adam Hamilton called for expanding Medicare to cover vision and dental care. Nearly all of them railed against billionaires and corporate greed.

“They say it differently, but they are all on the same theme,” Mr. Schumer said in an interview. “It echoed from one end of the country to the other. It set an echo chamber.”

Voters almost uniformly reported that tackling government corruption was one of their top issues in the midterms. A memo issued by House Democrats’ super PAC after the elections said that in focus groups and interviews, “voters cast blame far and wide” for rising household costs, “from greedy corporations and their wealthy C. E. O. s, to corrupt and conflicted politicians.”

That dynamic has already created some unusual ideological crosscurrents in the party. Representative-elect Sam Forstag of Montana, who flipped a conservative seat, told his constituents in a video recorded during new member orientation in Washington this week that he planned to join both the Blue Dog Coalition — a centrist group traditionally made up of southern Democrats — and the liberal Progressive Caucus, two factions that are often at odds with each other.

“The overlap is, well, giving us the chance to fight for populist economic policies that are actually going to help working people, and finally put us back at the front of the line in terms of who Congress should be working for,” Mr. Forstag said.

The approach is also shaping how newly elected Democrats are thinking about using their oversight power in the new Congress. In the past, the most liberal Democrats have clamored for impeachments to punish misconduct.

Now, even progressives are arguing that their party should train their focus on government and corporate wrongdoing that has driven up costs for Americans.

“We really need to look at any specific instance of corruption that can be tied directly to the material circumstances of working families today,” said Representative-elect Melat Kiros of Colorado, a liberal who won a primary race against a veteran Democratic congresswoman.

“I don’t know necessarily that investigating the Qatari jet has a direct impact to the material circumstances of a working person right now in the country,” Ms. Kiros said, referring to the luxury jet given to President Trump by the Qatari royal family. “But I do think if we talk about the role that some of these health insurance companies have been having in the dramatic continuing rise in health care costs today, the collusion that takes place between the big four meatpacking companies and the rise in groceries and meat specifically, right? These are very specific harms that the American people and the American consumer is facing.”

Those issues may also orient Democrats should they choose to try to dare Mr. Trump to veto affordability legislation — around health care or otherwise — through the budget reconciliation process, which allows a party to circumvent the Senate filibuster when passing bills.

The last time Democrats attempted to pass filibuster-proof domestic policy legislation, when the party had a governing trifecta in 2021 under Mr. Biden, progressives and centrists clashed. Liberals refused to support a bipartisan infrastructure measure prioritized by the moderates until the Senate passed their top priority: a behemoth package to fund climate programs, health care, education and child care.

But with Mr. Trump in the White House, Democrats sound more willing to put aside such disagreements and find measures they can coalesce around and pressure the president to accept.

“People just feel like we’re being scammed all the time, and the quality of the things that we enjoyed is getting worse, and people are getting incredibly rich off of it,” Ms. Valdez said. “Even if we won’t agree 100 percent on the specifics with everyone in our caucus, I think we’ll have a lot of places of agreement in tackling this corporate greed.”

Michael Gold and Carl Hulse contributed reporting.

Catie Edmondson covers Congress for The Times.

One Shot Dead and Four Wounded Around Washington, D. C., Condo Building

The New York Times November 12, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

The shooting in a busy neighborhood took place at a gym and two nearby locations. A suspect was found with a fatal gunshot wound after barricading in a building, the police said.

By Billy WitzAishvarya KaviMadison Malone Kircher and Christine Hauser

Aishvarya Kavi reported from Washington, D. C.

One person was killed and four wounded in a shooting on Thursday in a busy neighborhood of Washington, D. C., the police said.

The violence, which began before 8 a. m., took place at a gym in the Logan Circle section, but also at a construction site across the street and in the lobby of a nearby building, officials said, and it prompted a widespread response by law enforcement officers.

The police officers who first answered the call found a man dead inside the VIDA gym, said Jeff Carroll, the city’s acting police chief.

One of the wounded victims was in critical condition; the others suffered non-life-threatening injuries, the police said. The suspect, who barricaded himself in the building, was found with a fatal self-inflicted gunshot wound, the police said. They did not give his identity.

Authorities said that the shooting appeared to have stemmed from a conflict between the gunman and the homeowners association of the apartment building in which he lived and where he was found barricaded on the seventh floor. Officials did not provide more details.

The Logan Circle area where the shooting occurred is a primarily residential neighborhood less than a mile from the White House and home to coffee shops and other businesses.

The New York Times

During the manhunt, dozens of law enforcement vehicles, some from federal agencies, blocked the streets, including several SWAT units. An emergency alert to cellphones in the area instructed people to shelter in place.

Helicopters circled overhead as ambulances arrived, and snipers were spotted atop the roof of a nearby condo building.

Phil Morton, 37, said he had just arrived at work when he heard a “parade of police cars” and screeching tires outside his office. Mr. Morton, a vehicle safety engineer, said he initially thought the activity might be a presidential motorcade.

The gym, housed within the Metropole building, is typically moderately busy on a Thursday morning. Usually, several dozen occupants are spread out across three floors.

Suzanne Garwood, 55, said that she had been in a locker room when she heard “an enormous bang.” Outside the room, she smelled gun smoke. Another patron told her there had been a shooting.

Gym staff members ushered Ms. Garwood, an attorney who lives in Arlington, Va., out a side door and into an alleyway. She walked back toward the gym to grab her bike and heard what she believed to be more gunshots, Ms. Garwood said.

She then took shelter in an apartment building with about a dozen other gym goers.

Elisabeth Pinsker, a resident of the condo building above VIDA, said that fire alarms sounded before 8 a. m., and a short time later, officials were evacuating the residents.

“Pound, pound, pound,” she said, describing the sound at her door. “’Get out of the building,” said the officer. As she left the building, she saw police coming in, with “with big guns, not just handguns,” she said.

Michael Gold, Erik Wemple and Clarence Williams contributed reporting. Kirsten Noyes contributed research.

Aishvarya Kavi works in the Washington bureau of The Times, helping to cover a variety of political and national news.

We Were Warned of Deceptive A. I. Fakes. We Got Memes.

The New York Times November 12, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

The surge of A. I. fakes that emerged this election season was different than what researchers had feared. The results are also a reckoning.

Source: TBC_on_X

By Stuart A. Thompson

First came the election results, then came the meme party.

In the wake of the Democratic wave of support on Election Day, content creators used artificial intelligence to flood the internet with fake videos, depicting candidates and celebrities in various states of celebration.

One A. I.-made skit, featuring replicas of the cast from the hit TV show “The Office” showed the boss adjusting to a progressive society, wearing a Pride flag sweater and calling for an emergency Diversity Day. It received more than 16 million views in one post on X.

After Democrats swept the midterm elections, meme-makers flooded the internet with A. I.-generated fakes. It was emblematic of the kinds of fakery produced this year.

An A. I. version of Senator-elect James Talarico pushes aside Ken Paxton, his Republican opponent.

An A. I. version of Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed, of Michigan, dances with Zohran Mamdani, New York City’s mayor.

Source: TBC_on_X

The video was emblematic of the kinds of A. I. fakes that have coursed through social media during the midterm season. Many of the most popular videos spreading online vied for laughs and sometimes jeers — an absurd mix of outlandish events that obviously never happened.

The results are a minor relief for researchers who monitor the spread of A. I. fakery, and also a reckoning.

Experts have warned ahead of every U. S. election since at least 2020 that A. I. replicas of real people — “deepfakes” — and other deceptive content generated by the technology could upend democracy, misleading voters about scandals that never happened or salacious fake comments.

Some ads published this year depicted realistic A. I. versions of candidates. But far more of the videos circulating online were parodies, jokes and memes that were too absurd to be believed.

“The case that everyone’s worried about is a highly inflammatory or incriminating deepfake going viral on the eve of an election and truly moving the needle on how people have voted,” said Henry Ajder, an expert on A. I. and the founder of Latent Space Advisory, an A. I.-consulting firm. “That has not yet come to bear.”

Memes have spread widely online showing real candidates in bizarre situations, like one series mocking President Trump as a small business owner with Vice President JD Vance as his son and employee. Creators who opposed Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed’s bid released a flurry of videos disparaging the candidate, often deploying racist stereotypes.

A. I.-generated depictions of President Trump mocked issues important to voters this year, like affordability and the war in Iran.

Source: Ari Kuschnir

Hundreds of A. I.-generated campaign ads also flooded the internet and airwaves, including some that were deceptive and not disclosed as A. I.-made, according to a report by the Wesleyan Media Project, a research group at Wesleyan University. A vast majority of the ads were obviously fake, depicting impossible scenes.

Some were more grounded in reality, including an ad showing an A. I. version of Vikki Goodwin, then a Democratic candidate for lieutenant governor in Texas, purportedly supporting a “death tax.”

“There are a lot of people who don’t know me yet, who might think this is me,” she told The New York Times in September. The campaign behind the ad said at the time that it was “an obvious parody produced to entertain.”

Ms. Goodwin ultimately won her race by more than six percentage points.

One frequent target of attack ads, Senator-elect James Talarico, a Texas Democrat, won his election handily. Though there is plenty of material available of Mr. Talarico with which to generate A. I. fakes or audio clones, experts could not find evidence of a deceptive deepfake of him that posed as genuine footage. Instead, the candidate was featured in dozens of A. I.-generated videos dancing and singing, which were viewed millions of times online.

A television ad paid for by Ken Paxton’s campaign depicted an A. I.-generated version of James Talarico repeated comments he made in the past.

Source: Paxton for TX Senate

Those A. I. fakes can still have political power, rallying supporters and bringing to life criticisms made against candidates, which can stick in voters’ minds.

“That’s something that political campaigns have done forever — that’s nothing new,” Mr. Ajder said. “The means of production are new, the ability to scale, the access — the viscerality is different.”

The memes match content published during primary elections in the United States and in recent general elections in other countries. A report from Canadian researchers at McGill University and the University of Montreal found that A. I.-generated content made up about 6 percent of election-related images on X during the country’s federal election last year. But more than 90 percent of the views went to more innocuous content, like memes, jokes and fake depictions of candidates as superheros or supervillains.

Experts have pointed to a handful of past cases where A. I.-generated fakes seemed to mislead voters. In 2023, an A. I.-generated audio clip was credited with potentially turning the course of an election in Slovakia. In 2024, an A. I. replica of President Joseph R. Biden’s voice was used to call voters in New Hampshire, advising them to skip the primary election.

This year, a political group created a phone line for an A. I.-powered version of Nithya Raman, the Los Angeles mayoral candidate who ultimately won her race. On the phone line, she had appeared to endorse tent encampments.

Such fakes tend to target partisans who are more likely to believe them, rather than reaching swing voters who tend to show more skepticism. They may be spread more easily in group chats or private groups, researchers said.

And online videos with a more comedic edge have collected millions of views.

“The threat of deepfakes has not disappeared,” said Shaina Raza, a research scientist at the Vector Institute of Artificial Intelligence, who has studied A. I. risks. “It is taking different forms than what we expected.”

Stuart A. Thompson writes for The Times about online influence, including the people, places and institutions that shape the information we all consume.

Democrats, Take the Deal

The New York Times November 12, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

The Editorial Board

By The Editorial Board

The editorial board is a group of opinion journalists whose views are informed by expertise, research, debate and certain longstanding values. It is separate from the newsroom.

In his election night victory speech, Representative Hakeem Jeffries of New York said he and his fellow Democrats would fight to “make this country affordable for every single American.” They have an opportunity to start now, before they take control of Congress in January. They should seize it.

The Senate this week is debating a bill on a subject that is more important than it sounds: permitting reform. The bill would make it easier to build solar energy farms, battery storage, power lines and more. As a result, it would reduce energy prices. The status quo is expensive, dirty and unstable. The country needs to build a lot of big, new things to make its future cheaper and cleaner.

The bill has the support of some of the Senate’s most environmentally minded members — and of the White House. This political miracle reflects years of bipartisan negotiations, false starts and near misses. But following their party’s whopping midterm victory, some Democrats are tempted to scrap this legislation and wait to act until they take control of Congress next year. Democrats would then draft a new bill more to the liking of some environmental groups.

The current bill has a good chance to pass the Senate. By a margin of 73 to 25, senators approved a procedural measure on Monday, with a final vote expected in the coming weeks. The situation in the House is murkier. Among the potential no votes on the bill is Mr. Jeffries, the Democratic leader, who has raised concerns about it.

The bill’s Democratic skeptics are making a mistake. President Trump would almost certainly veto a follow-up bill next year. And time matters, especially for the climate. Congress should pass this bill now. It can then return next year and pass other bills that would do even more good.

The country’s current permitting regime is the result of many good intentions. Legislators wrote laws intended to protect water, air, endangered species and precious land. Over the years, though, the rules have become so complex and restrictive that the country cannot build the future it needs. This complexity feeds cynicism about whether government can get anything done.

Today, for instance, it typically takes between five and 13 years to build a long-distance power line, like the one that transports clean hydropower from Quebec to New England. That line took about a decade to finish, and opened in January. It has enough capacity to meet about one-fifth of Massachusetts’s electricity demand, and it’s projected to save consumers $50 million a year.

Many other valuable projects, unfortunately, remain incomplete or were never begun because of permitting bureaucracy. The slowness weakens the fight against climate change. Without lines to transport clean power from sunny and windy regions to other parts of the country, the country ends up using dirty energy in its place. Democrats who call climate change an emergency should not defend a permitting system too slow to build the clean energy that would address it.

Many of the country’s permitting rules were written at a time when industrial development usually caused environmental harm. In response, the environmental movement developed a habit of opposing new projects. Today, though, inertia often benefits fossil fuel companies. They, too, can use the regulatory state to tie up clean energy projects in permitting purgatory.

The costs of today’s bureaucracy are broader than its effect on the climate. A more robust, cleaner grid would make American energy more reliable and less dependent on hostile foreign nations. No country can embargo the wind. Better permitting rules would improve traffic and road safety: A road signal project in Connecticut that would fix a dangerous highway intersection — but would also affect nearby wetlands — was proposed in 2024 but may not be finished until 2032. And public health can suffer too. In January, a Washington sewage line burst after a repair was delayed for eight years, sending hundreds of millions of gallons of waste into the Potomac River.

Finally, the current permitting system raises costs for Americans — the issue that dominates politics today. The status quo increases their energy costs by making it harder for new projects to come online, including inexpensive renewables such as wind and solar. The bill in Congress would make progress against these problems and begin to deliver on Democrats’ promise to address affordability.

The bill also has a provision addressing data centers, another subject on which Democrats made many promises during this year’s campaign. It would force data center operators to pay the full costs of the electricity they use, protecting the average electricity consumer.

Opponents of the bill, such as the Sierra Club, complain that it might harm the environment. That concern is misplaced.

Yes, the bill would ease the construction of a range of projects, including fossil fuel infrastructure. But the United States will not stop using oil or natural gas anytime soon, and adding unnecessary costs to those projects serves little purpose. On net, the bill would cut greenhouse gas emissions from power plants by as much as 18 percent by 2040, according to the Rhodium Group, a research firm. It would do so in part by nearly tripling the construction of high-voltage transmission lines, which whiz electricity from often remote wind farms and solar plants to cities that need power.

Common sense supports that finding. Oil and gas companies have built their infrastructure over decades; renewables need to catch up quickly. The country currently gets less than a fifth of its energy from zero-carbon sources. Rapidly increasing that share will be impossible if it takes a decade to build a transmission line.

This is why the bill draws support from passionate climate crusaders such as Senator Martin Heinrich of New Mexico, Senator Brian Schatz of Hawaii and Senator Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island. Both of Georgia’s senators, Jon Ossoff and Raphael Warnock, voted to advance it this week. Practical-minded environmental groups such as the Citizens’ Climate Lobby and the Center for Climate and Energy Solutions have endorsed it, as has Consumer Reports.

The bill’s supporters recognize that it is merely a first step toward a much broader agenda to reduce carbon emissions and lower energy costs. But anyone who cares about climate change should cheer this bill. And a party that just won an election on affordability should not pass up a chance to start delivering immediately.
